column121: While descending into LGA we had a very close RA. we were level at 10;000 feet at roughly 290 knots when ATC gave us a traffic advisory as well as a descent to 8;000 feet. Captain was PF and immediately began slowing to 250knots in order to go below 10;000. Maybe two seconds after the ATC communication we were notified of traffic on the PFD (Primary Flight Display) immediately followed by the RA. I quickly notified ATC that we were responding while I was looking for traffic. Captain did a great job following the RA and making prompt control inputs. If I remember correctly that aircraft was within 300 feet of us and I was never able to make visual contract. We also accelerated over 260 knots while executing the descent RA. After completion; I notified ATC and asked if they still wanted the descent to 8;000 which they did and the flight continued normally.

column121: I was flying Aircraft X on a practice approach into CHS (VOR 21) and had been cleared for the option for runway 21. I had a view limiting device on until approach minimums (440 ft) but was flying with an instructor acting as a safety pilot. Upon reaching minimums I removed the View Limiting Device and executed a touch a go landing. Shortly after rotation at roughly 100-200 ft AGL; I spotted Aircraft Y on the southeast side of runway 21 at approximately 400-500AGL. When I initially made visual contact with Aircraft Y it was on a course to cross the runway directly in front of our path of flight. I immediately leveled off to avoid further loss of separation and at about this time contacted tower to advise them that Aircraft Y was overflying the runway. I received no response to this radio call and continued to visually avoid Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y passed across the centerline of runway 21 and I subsequently began to reestablish a climb and once again contacted tower to advise of the near miss. The tower controller then told Aircraft Y that they 'were supposed to remain south of 21'. Upon hearing this; Aircraft Y began to turn back towards runway 21 (and our flight path) to cross back over to the south side. We once again had minimal separation as Aircraft Y flew directly in front of us a second time to return to the south side of the runway. After Aircraft Y transitioned to the south side of the runway no further loss of separation occurred and we returned to our original point of departure uneventfully.At no point before; during; or after the incident were we advised of any helicopter traffic to be aware of nor did the controller seem to realize Aircraft Y's error until well after our first report of the loss of separation.

column121: Got to the airplane about an hour before a scheduled departure and Maintenance was on board fixing a problem with our Elevator Aileron Computer (ELAC) system. This caused a delay of about an hour. Flight was not very full but we were boarded up and had to stay at the gate until Maintenance finished their job and paperwork was signed. We eventually pushed back and everything was normal. 2 engine taxi out to runway XXR for departure. There were 2 other planes waiting at the end to takeoff but we were given a takeoff clearance by tower since they were waiting for en-trail spacing. I remember thinking that our takeoff clearance was given a little early; as we were still probably 500'-800' or so from the end of the runway. CA was PF and I was PM on this leg; our first flight together. CA pushed the throttles up and we began the takeoff roll. Everything was normal up until about the 50-65kt range when the Takeoff Hold Lights suddenly changed from green to red. At this point I was looking at the engine pages but I remember seeing the change from green to red happen out of my peripheral vision. I also remember looking down the runway and even though it was dark; I saw an airplane crossing downfield. The captain immediately used MAX braking to slowed the plane to a stop. We skidded a little bit due to the wet runway. He set the parking brake and made a PA in the back. At the same time; I advised ZZZ Tower that we were aborting the takeoff on the runway. They seemed a little confused but one thing that stuck with me is that they NEVER asked us why we discontinued the takeoff. I asked Tower to roll the fire trucks in case our brakes were hot or locked up or there was any other outside damage they were able to see. We were able to taxi so we decided to turn off the runway on an upcoming taxiway and that's where Airport Rescue and Firefighting met us. They could see no such damage and our brakes were not on fire or anything like that. We sat on the taxiway for a while to gather ourselves and to run appropriate checklists. We decided that it was best to go back to the gate because we were getting close to our min fuel for takeoff and we also wanted Maintenance to do a quick inspection of the plane in case one of the wheels locked up since we skidded during the abort. We taxied back to the gate without issue and myself and the captain walked up to the terminal to debrief what had happened.In my opinion; there needs to be better communication between controllers and pilots. I'm still not sure if this was a case where ZZZ ground cleared a plane to cross XXR while ZZZ Tower cleared us for takeoff; or if the crossing plane did so without a clearance; or what exactly happened. It was very strange (in my opinion) for tower not to ask us a reason for the abort. They NEVER recognized the reason why we had to abort the takeoff or maybe they did and said nothing about it. Either way; there was a massive communication breakdown between ground; tower; us; and another aircraft.

column121: I was working Sector 79 to provide relief to Sector 94's higher volume.  During this session; Aircraft X reported seeing what they believed to be a balloon at 'eye level' with their aircraft; estimated 100-200 ft off their left wing (est at OTO165018). I immediately notified the supervisor; who then went to a few of the different balloon tracking websites available.  The Supervisor did have paperwork on a balloon; but it was never made clear whether the balloon launched or not. The balloon did not have a transponder on it.  At the time of the incident; the Supervisor found on the tracker website that the balloon was estimated well above FL410 (estimated around FL700); and a bit further North than where the report was made.  Aircraft X also made it seem like the balloon was unusually small for being at that altitude; so it may not have been the same balloon/object that was known and being tracked. I made the announcement over frequency regarding the unmanned derelict balloon; and made it known more specifically to some aircraft nearby at varying altitudes (FL380; FL400; and another one further north at FL410) and no other aircraft was able to identify/spot the balloon.  Aircraft X wasn't able to tell if the object/balloon was in a climb or a descent as they just caught it out of their peripheral. The aircraft and pilots were unharmed; and they requested an estimated location of the event for their reporting as well.I have heard it suggested several times; and agree; that any balloon that is being knowingly launched into Class A airspace needs to have a transponder attached so that we can more accurately know its location and altitude. It's incredibly unsafe to have something climbing uncontrolled/untracked through controlled airspace that could cause an accident should it get draped over a windshield/engine/control surface etc. I don't think balloons should be allowed to be launched without a transponder; period.

column121: I was the pilot flying on flight to LBB.The flight and approach to landing on runway 26 in LBB were all standard and normal. ATIS was reporting gusty winds about 25-35 kts. right down the runway and low level wind shear advisories.We briefed the go-around procedure in case we did get a wind shear advisory.The weather for LBB was reporting VFR.I turned the autopilot off around 200 ft above the minimums. At approximately 200-300 AGL we received a wind shear warning. I called for a go around and pushed the thrust levers forward and pitched up for the recovery.I initially pushed the auto throttle button when I pushed the thrust levers forward on the go around. While the plane was climbing I realized I hadn't pushed the TOGA button so I did; and at the same time while I was doing that my FO said push the TOGA button.Tower instructed us to climb runway heading to 5000 ft.During the climb out around 1200 ft the airspeed got slow and the shaker went off. I lowered the nose and my FO assisted in pushing the thrust levers forward.After we recovered; the FO re-engaged the auto throttle and engaged the autopilot. We climbed to 5000ft and cleaned up the aircraft. We got vectored back around for runway 26.We landed uneventfully with no further encounters of wind shear.Suggestions: I should of had my finger on the TOGA button.

column121: I was the pilot monitoring for this flight. Toward the end of the climbout of ZZZ; somewhere above 2000 feet; flaps had been retracted on schedule and we were climbing at 240 KIAS. Weather was IMC. I was prompted to switch to departure; then we were given direct to ZZZ [VOR]. I was about to call '3000 feet' and prompt for the after takeoff when this occurred. After I had got confirmation and executed the direct; my FO said something about the autopilot being degraded. I then looked at the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) and saw 'ALT HOLD' with an amber line through it indicating a degraded vertical mode; then noticed our airspeed was quickly rolling below 200 kts and nearing 180 kts. We were in the amber airspeed band with the Performance Limiting Indicator (PLI) visible. There was a startle effect and a moment of disbelief or confusion in what I was seeing; but I called out the speed; and prompted the FO to accelerate as the PLI was floating near the limit. I remember saying something like 'lower the nose'. When the PLI contacted; I called 'STALL' took control; and rolled wings level to initiate the recovery. It took a few seconds for me to realize we were not accelerating at which point I realized I was unconsciously working against the auto throttle at which point I pushed the throttles all the way forward and clicked the autothrottles off. The aircraft began accelerating; the descent arrested and began climbing. During this I also had to tell ATC we were responding to a situation and we'd get back to them. They gave us a vector to 270 and to advise them when everything was okay. Airspeed reached approximately 270 kts as we were climbing again where I started to easy the climb and the airspeed to re-automate. I called for Autopilot Center Command; and once it engaged it resumed the turn to the heading we had been assigned (270). However we immediately got a 'bank angle' aural alert; which confused us because although the Autopilot was banking slightly beyond the Flight Director; the angle was not any higher than 25 degrees while at about 240 knots. Nevertheless; I disconnected the automation again; eased the bank and hand flew with the Autothrottles engaged at 240 kts. Once rolled onto our heading of 270 and steadily climbing to our altitude (we had gotten 7000 and then 11000 assigned during this); I called for the Autopilot again; and then never had another issue. I asked the FO if they were ready to retake the controls; and they took over just before 10;000. We then accomplished the after takeoff checklist. I did not notice at what point we went into altitude capture; when the vertical mode degraded; or when airspeed began rolling back as I was in the middle of ATC responses etc as is typical for this phase of flight. The events all happened very quickly. I only remember seeing the degraded mode; and then the pitch and airspeed which I was immediately fixated on along with the VSI and the altitude; the usual instrument scan. Automation modes were secondary to me at the time as they were being disconnected. I did not think to reset flight directors or try other autopilots since I was focused on the recovery and keeping the plane flying. We descended about 700' during recovery starting from about 3700' regaining altitude at about 3000' and climbing. We talk about; and practice upset recovery in every sim session. We talk about startle effect in CRM every year and in sims. We are trained to expect the unexpected; but it's not until it happens to you in the real environment where you fully realize the effect it has on you.

column121: I was flying my personal airplane to ZZZ1 for repair of intermittent right engine not starting issue and occasional auto pilot disconnects. During the flight at flight level 390 while in Cruise with a 75 KT tail wind; the auto pilot suddenly disconnected. The airplane immediately started to drift and climb. The FMS also disconnected and I lost the flight command level bars; I manually took control of the side stick and tried to reengage the autopilot with no success; I was successful in engaging the FMS system; and the flight bars returned; I immediately leveled the wings and stabilized the attitude; during this 30 second or so the airplane climbed approximately 500 to 700 feet. I stopped the climb and arrested the sudden climb and immediately started to descend at the same time that ATC called and asked me what the problem was and I told them I had an auto pilot failure and they said to immediately turn 40° to the left and descend to 390 which I immediately complied. My copilot pulled the QRH manual and looked up the procedure for auto pilot failure and I flew the airplane manually while he troubleshot the issue. He continually tried to turn the autopilot on and within a few minutes it reengaged. Along the route we had 3 other similar disengagements but did not have a severe up draft and altitude issue. I was able to immediately engage the FMS and fly the command bars and keep the altitude and track constant; especially after the first unexpected incident; I was prepared for this potential issue. The auto pilot disconnected one more of the times while in RVSM airspace but it reconnected fairly quickly so I continued the flight in RVSM. It disconnected several more times below RVSM on the way to ZZZ1. The airplane is at the service center currently; I spent time with maintenance going over the issues. I also downloaded the computer Data Storage Unit (DSU) of the flight and gave it to maintenance DSU so they could trace the cause of the autopilot failures.

column121: After landing at ZZZ on Aircraft X; we received taxi instructions to proceed via Taxiway 1; 2; 3; and 4 to gate XX. We turned off engine No. 1 after 2 minutes and continued taxi on a single engine.As we approached the turn from Taxiway 1 onto Taxiway 2; the EICAS displayed a HYD 1 FAIL message. This was followed by RUDDER SYS 1-2 INOP; AIL SYS 1-2 INOP; and STEER INOP indications. Upon recognizing the messages; we stopped the aircraft and advised Ground that we needed time to accomplish the checklist due to a maintenance issue.The Captain and I reviewed the QRH and confirmed that the procedure called for directional control using differential braking. After evaluating the situation; we determined that towing the aircraft to the gate would be the safest course of action.While I handled radio communications and coordination with ATC and airport personnel; the Captain kept the flight attendants and passengers informed of the situation and provided updates as needed. Airport operations coordinated for a tug to respond; and once it arrived; we accomplished the tow in accordance with the AOM Gate Tow-In Procedure. The aircraft was then safely towed to the gate without further incident.Suggestions: Crew coordination and communication were effective throughout the event. Given the loss of hydraulic system 1; the decision to discontinue taxi and request a tow helped reduce operational risk and ensured a safe arrival at the gate. Continued emphasis on prompt checklist use; clear CRM; and conservative decision-making during abnormal ground operations would be beneficial.
column123: After landing at ZZZ on Aircraft X; we received taxi instructions to proceed via Taxiways 1; 2; 3; and 4 to Gate XX. Approximately two minutes after clearing the runway; Engine No. 1 was shut down and we continued taxi on a single engine.As we approached the turn from Taxiway 1 onto Taxiway 2; an EICAS message for HYD 1 FAIL was displayed. This was followed by RUDDER SYS 1-2 INOP; AIL SYS 1-2 INOP; and STEER INOP indications. Upon recognizing these messages; we stopped the aircraft; set the parking brake; and advised Ground that we required time to accomplish the appropriate checklist due to a maintenance issue.The HYD 1 FAIL message subsequently cleared from the EICAS; however; upon reviewing the hydraulic page on the MFD (Multi-Function Flight Display); we observed no pressure in System 1.The Flight Attendant was informed of the situation; the plan; and the expected delay to the gate.We coordinated with Ground and airport operations to arrange a tug for the short tow to the gate and requested a GPU due to the APU being inoperative. After completing the QRH procedures and coordinating with operations; I made a PA informing the passengers that we had arrived early into ZZZ; but would need to stop to address a steering issue and would be towed the remainder of the way to the gate. I also thanked them for their patience.Once preparations were complete; we accomplished the tow in accordance with the AOM Gate Tow-In Procedure. Due to the APU being inoperative; both engines were shut down prior to the tow; which resulted in the aircraft being on battery power for approximately eight minutes. Electrical load was minimized as much as possible to preserve battery life during this time.The aircraft was safely towed to the gate without further incident.Suggestions: Crew coordination and communication were effective throughout the event. Given the loss of Hydraulic System 1; the decision to discontinue taxi and request a tow reduced operational risk and supported a safe arrival at the gate. Continued emphasis on prompt checklist execution; clear CRM; and conservative decision-making during abnormal ground operations is essential.

column121: As we were rolling out on the final landing of the day and exiting the runway; the first officer and I were alerted by the low oil pressure" annunciation on the upper engine panel with all three yellow annunciators blinking. After looking down at the lower engine panel; we both noticed the oil quantity very low and the oil pressure very low. The oil quantity was eventually replaced with a "lo" annunciation; and the oil pressure was outlined with a red box and read 7 psi. At that moment; we had already started the APU and decided to immediately shut down the engine. The relief pilot referenced the low oil pressure QRH; but there was no further guidance in that checklist other than to reference the "engine failure or shut down" checklist. All steps were already accomplished in the "engine fire  or failure shut down" checklist for the conditions of the flight. As we taxied into parking spot; I noticed a large amount of smoke coming from behind our plane. I directed the first officer to call operations to see if we could have anyone do a visual inspection of our aircraft. The ground crew was already in place; and they marshaled us into parking where we set the brakes and shut down the remaining motor uneventfully. The maintenance representative came on board and told us that he saw a tailpipe fire as we were taxiing with a lot of oil underneath the number two engine on the ramp. We both concluded it was the oil that was dripping on the hot engine and exhaust area that caused the smoke and tail pipe fire. We had no indications of any type of fire or high EGT inside of the aircraft since the tailpipe fire was outside of the internal core of the engine. The maintenance representative left and returned telling us that the fire had reignited and he wanted to get everyone off of the aircraft quickly. We were already in the process of deplaning the aircraft; but I made an announcement over the PA that we had smoked coming from the right side of the aircraft and we needed to expedite the disembarking of the aircraft. All passengers exited through the primary door attached to the jet bridge without incident. After all of the passengers had deplaned; I; along with the Purser; exited the aircraft. I was unable to enter a logbook entry through my iPad because more than 10 minutes had elapsed since the flight closed out; so I contacted Maintenance Control and explained the situation and he said that he would enter the write up into the logbook."

column121: After pushing back from gate X; we were getting ready to taxi out towards the north line at the gates. The pushback crew put us at a standard 45 degree angle. We started engine #2 and configured for a standard single engine taxi. After completing the after start checklist; scanning for traffic; and turning on our taxi lights; we commenced our taxi with a right hand turn (towards the operating engine) towards the north line. Due to the adverse yaw; forward momentum was required to make the right turn. As the airplane moved forward and I began my right turn; a baggage truck with two individuals came from my left side and failed to stop. I abruptly brought the plane to a stop to avoid contact with the ground personnel. The cart identifier was noticed and this happened at around XA:15 local time. After watching the baggage cart drive away; I cleared for traffic and commenced (again) the process of inching forward to gain momentum to make my right turn. Since I had already moved forward a few feet; my left wing encroached the service road as I made the right turn. As I completed the right turn; I observed a catering truck driving on the service road towards my wingtip; again; without stopping. I began to bring the airplane to a stop and observed the truck completely go off the service road to avoid my wingtip. Even with all my lights on; not a single car / truck stopped to give way. As we taxied north; I observed another aircraft that had just pushed back from gate Y make the right turn towards the north line. Even without inching forward much; their left wing tip encroached; although slightly; the service road. I observed multiple catering trucks drive around the service road instead of stopping and waiting for the aircraft to exit. This is an incredibly unsafe situation that apparently has become normal practice for the ground handlers to drive in such a careless way in one of the most congested ramp areas in the world.

column121: Departing Runway 15 at Martin State Airport. Given takeoff clearance after holding short of runway for several minutes. After lining up and confirming runway; controls were handed to SIC and I was pilot monitoring. Upon SIC applying power we received aural taxiway" notification while accelerating. Power was instantly pulled back instinctually but we thought the warning was in error because we thought the runway was simply displaced for landing operations. We did not see any sort of large yellow chevron markings indicating that we were on a taxi only portion of the runway surface before reaching the runway threshold. ATC had not given us any sort of instruction to taxi forward and then depart either. We did not want to remain on an active runway longer than was necessary or cause a timing or separation problem for the tower controller so elected to continue takeoff. As we later approached what we thought was the displaced threshold for landing only; not takeoff; we did see small yellow chevrons which were impossible to see from where we were previously holding short of the runway. Remainder of the takeoff; departure and flight was normal after that.I would suggest better markings or signage at Martin State Airport. Have large yellow chevrons painted on the taxiway portion leading to the threshold or a sign indicating the nonstandard displaced threshold that can give pilots a heads-up while they hold short of the runway. I also don't recall seeing any sort of hotspot circle in that area on the Jeppesen airport diagram. A notation on the company flight planning brief or notation in the flight release package from dispatch would also be helpful. I would think this is a relatively common mistake made at this airport and that it could be better addressed and mitigated."
column123: Cleared for takeoff on Runway 15. column121: Our flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ was uneventful until we started our approach.  The First Officer and I planned and briefed our approach to Runway XXR.  When we got handed over to ZZZ Approach; we were advised to expect Runway XYR.  After a runway change and new briefing; we completed the Before Landing Checklist to the line.  Shortly after we were instructed to descend to 4000 feet and fly direct to ZZZZZ to intercept the XYR localizer.  We were instructed to cross ZZZZZ at 4;000 feet and cleared for the ILS.  At 4;000 feet; I selected LNAV/VNAV and closed the speed window to engage VNAV PTH but remained in VNAV SPD.  Approach instructed us to reduce speed to 170 knots. I opened the speed window to reduce speed.  While slowing down; I requested Flaps 1; VNAV PTH engaged and I selected 2;300 feet for the FAF altitude.  At this point; the Master Caution light illuminated; extinguished and then illuminated again; we saw the HYD light illuminate of the Right Annunciator panel.  The aircraft had already started a descent on the approach path but no more that 100 to 200 feet; we requested to abandon the approach and maintain 4;000 feet as well as a vector to the right.  Autopilot was disengaged momentarily and then re-engaged when established on an altitude and heading.  We selected the systems page on the Lower DU (Display Unit); at this time we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was zero and we had lost pressure in Hydraulic System B.  At this time the LOW-PRESSURE lights on the overhead panel also illuminated.  I declared my aircraft and communications and requested the LOSS OF SYSTEM B QRH procedure.  While completing the QRH procedure; we noticed the Flap Indicator needle was between the Flaps Up and Flaps 1 position.  We requested priority handling with ATC and advised them of the aircraft status and intentions; we requested ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) shortly after.We completed the QRH procedure; I then transferred control and communications to the First Officer; I proceeded to complete the NON-NORMAL LANDING CONSIDERATIONS procedure contacting Dispatch and Maintenance Control and informing our cabin crew and our passengers of the current situation.  ATC advised us to expect the ILS to Runway XXL; we selected and briefed the new approach.  ATC vectored us for the approach; we lowered the gear and landing flaps while on base leg and completed the Before Landing Checklist.Our landing on Runway XXL was normal; we vacated the runway and were able to vacate to the left and stopped on Taxiway 1.  We asked Fire Command to inspect the aircraft exterior and were informed of smoke coming from the right landing gear but did not detect excessive temperatures with their thermal imaging.  ARFF requested we shut down the right engine which we did after the 3-minute cool down period; at which time they advised smoke was no longer detected. We decided to continue our taxi to our assigned gate as we were confident in our ability to stop the aircraft normally.  Even though we had no issues stopping the aircraft; we requested to stop on the ramp short of the gate area and have the aircraft towed to our parking position.  After parking; we completed the shutdown checklist; completed the logbook and our maintenance team took over the aircraft.Cause: Mechanical failure of the onboard hydraulic system.  I believe the airlines training for non-normal procedures was evident in this situation.  A recommendation for myself as a new captain was to have let the First Officer fly the aircraft and communicate and I complete the QRH procedures.

column121: Normal takeoff; cruise and approach.  No anomalies and completely routine.  RNAV XX.  Normal touchdown and roll out.  Taxi off runway on Taxiway 1; joined Taxiway 2 east bound.  Ground advised Taxiway 2 to right on Taxiway 3 to taxi to gate XX.  Upon turning onto Taxiway 3 we heard a faint thud.  I suspected a *single* tire failure.  The gate was approximately 200 yards away.  As we approached the gate we noticed the airplane seemed a little tilted to the left.  Following the marshallers commands; I got the takeoff config warning inadvertently.  I immediately pulled the engines back to 40% N1. At 40% N1 the aircraft came to a stop on its own without brakes.  Completed the shutdown checklist.  The jet bridge could not reach the airplane.  Once stairs were placed; I went outside to find the number 2 main was shredded and the number 1 tire was off the rim bead.  Once passengers deplaned a visual inspection found multiple tire marks on the top of the engine cowl; under wing; flaps; fuselage; gear arm and elevator.  Pieces of rubber were found inside the fuselage wheel well area.  A hole around 5 inches was found in the rear wing fairing.  Closer inspection found the trailing edge of the flap to be cracked at a stringer.  During a conversation with company officials; I recommended a runway inspection of XXL in ZZZ.  Remains of a tire were found mid field on RWY XXL in ZZZ at the approximate rotation point.  I suspect this tire failed at rotation although there were no indications to the flight attendants or flight crew.  The fact that a large tire mark was found on the top of the left engine cowl near the inlet this event could have played out very differently.  I suspect the number 1 tire was the only wheel doing the braking on the left side during landing and the blow out plugs popped due to overheating on the taxi in on the remaining tire.  Cause: Better tires.

column121: We had a normal departure from the gate and a normal taxi out to runway XXL. When it came time to do the before takeoff final items checklist I tested the takeoff warning horn by advancing both throttles individually. Our aircraft did not have a takeoff warning horn button to test it. When I advanced both throttles individually the takeoff warning horn did not sound. My first officer tested the master caution system during his flow and we did not have any caution lights stay illuminated.We were cleared for takeoff off runway XXL. I advanced the throttles to approximately 40 % and let the engines stabilize. As soon as I started advancing the throttles again toward the takeoff setting the takeoff waning horn sounded. I immediately said reject and reduced the throttles to idle. We did not get above 30 knots. I estimated it was about 20 knots. My first officer informed the tower and we exited the runway at Taxiway 1. This was more of a discontinued takeoff at a normal taxi speed.We had a master caution light and two door lights on the overhead were illuminated. The Left FWD Overwing and Left AFT Overwing both were illuminated.We exited the runway and came to a stop on taxiway 1. My first officer informed tower that we were addressing a maintenance issue. I made an announcement to the passengers that we had to exit the runway to address a maintenance issue and that I would give them more information when I could.My first officer ran the rejected takeoff checklist as I followed along. We then ran the abnormal checklist for the Overwing exit lights illuminated. Then with the parking brake set I called dispatch on my phone and explained to him what happened and asked for a conference call with Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control came on the line and I explained to him what happened and what we had. He informed me we would have to return to a gate and he would advised station maintenance. I asked the dispatcher to inform the station that we would be a gate return and he said he would. I informed my first officer and then I called my purser and informed them. I then made a PA to the passengers and told them I had some unfortunate news and that we needed to return to the gate and have maintenance address the issue and that I would have more information for them when we got back to a gate. We coordinated with station ops and we returned to gate XX. Station maintenance came on board and we briefed them on what happened. I entered two separate ELB (Electronic Log Book) entries; one for each Overwing door light; and informed station maintenance over the radio. I then made a PA and informed the passengers and gave them an explanation of what happened.Maintenance informed us that they found a servo that was malfunctioning that would need to be replaced and gave us a time estimate of over an hour and once they replaced the servo they would need to pressurize the aircraft. I informed the gate agent of this information and we both agreed to deplaned the passengers. After the passengers deplaned I called the Chief Pilot on the phone and briefed them of what happened. I then debriefed my entire crew in first class before we left the aircraft. They found us a new aircraft to take to ZZZ1. The aircraft this event happened in was a B737 Max 9.
column123: This event occurred in a 737 max 9. Aircraft was swapped due to maintenance after event.Preflight duties went routinely from aircraft setup to taxi out. Captain called for the before takeoff checklist where he completed the takeoff configuration warning test the horn did not sound and no indication of doors were open. We were cleared to line up and wait and shortly after given clearance to takeoff on XXR. The captain advanced the thrust levers to about 40% and then advanced them further; we immediately got to takeoff configuration warning on and master caution; door annunciation. Captain immediately brought the thrust back to idle and called reject. We had at most been doing 40 knots. I notified atc of the reject and we taxied to exit the runway at Taxiway 1. Once parking brake was set Captain and I discussed what the issue was and determined that the flight attendant go check the left over wing exits to make sure they weren't actually open once we had confirmation on that. We ran the rejected takeoff; checklist and verified did not need to take any further action from that checklist as the rejected takeoff was less than 80 knots. Captain then got in touch with maintenance. Let them know what the issue was and they let us know that we need to be returning to the gate and most likely there is a sensor that went out on the over wing exits. We also checked the non-normal checklist for over wing amber light; which did not give us any further guidance while on the ground. After running checklist we discussed if there's any further action we need to take before starting a taxi back to the gate; we came to the conclusion that we had done all the appropriate actions for the situation.  Taxi back to the gate and parking  was normal.

column121: ZZZ1-ZZZ flight; I was flying as PF. While cruising at FL350; after returning from a bathroom break; the captain briefed me on any changes. He was currently on heading mode deviating to the left from a vertical developed cloud after requesting and receiving authorization from ATC to do so. We accomplished positive exchange of controls. The captain made a PA telling the flight attendants to take their seats. A few moments later; we started hitting turbulence while flying to the left of the cloud. I had my hands on the thrust levers and yoke ready to take over. As the turbulence became severe; the CA told me to hand fly; because AP would most likely disengage. At this point; the turbulence was severe. My focus; as discussed with the CA; was to try my best to maintain wings level and control over aircraft. We caught a strong updraft and hit FL356. Once the turbulence became less; as I was recovering to initial heading and altitude; ATC called us that he saw us 600ft above our altitude. Captain answered; explained we hit severe turbulence and were unable to maintain heading or altitude; but were already out of that area and correcting. ATC didn't say anything else about it. We reengaged the AP once conditions no longer showed any turbulence. CA called the flights attendants; who notified us that everyone in the back was ok with no injuries. Cause: Squall line passing by ZZZ. Our route took us south; then west before heading back toward ZZZ. We were monitoring radar; but had a lot of distance from any thunderstorm cells. Cause of severe turbulence was the vertical build up that we were deviating from.
column123: Cruising at FL350 and having been cleared direct the ZZZ vortac a request was made and granted by ARTCC to deviate left of course for a thunderstorm building up. Position was 30 nm west of ZZZ2 and 20 nm south of ZZZ [VOR]. The turn took the aircraft near the edge of the thunderstorm at which time the aircraft encountered an updraft which caused a 700 foot uncommanded climb to 35700. The pilot flying disconnected the autopilot to initiate a descent to 35000. ARTCC called on the radio to inquire about the altitude deviation. The updraft was reported along with a response about descending back to 35000. There was light turbulence. Flight attendants had been advised to be in their seats. No flight attendant or passenger injuries were reported. The seatbelt sign was on and an announcement was made about the upcoming turbulence. ARTCC did not comment further and there was no notice about a pilot deviation.Cause: Misjudged the amount of distance from the edge of the thunderstorm. Suggestions: Make a more pronounced turn away from the thunderstorm so as to achieve a wider gap (20 nm minimum) and increase the margin of safety.

column121: During installation of the RH engine upper outboard start fuel nozzle; the new nozzle assembly was damaged.  During installation of the new nozzle the mounting ears of the nozzle got bent due to an unseen misalignment of the nozzle.  It was found that either during removal of the old nozzle or during insertion of the new one that there is a tapered boss on the burner can internal to the engine that floats in a flange; this boss was shifted and causing the new nozzle to not correctly engage into the engine.  From the aft edge that is visible the nozzle was sitting flush with the engine case but it was lifted on the backside (fwd) edge where you couldn't see without a mirror.  The mounting nuts were run down and damaged the mount ears of the new nozzle during this process.  No damage occurred to the engine mounting boss. The nozzle was removed and after researching found that the floating tapered boss can be moved back into position and another replacement fuel nozzle was inserted without issue.Suggestions:  Add a warning note in the MX (Maintenance) manual to notate that the internal alignment of the floating tapered burner can boss can be moved if pushed on during removal/install causing the reinstallation of the nozzle to not align in its bore correctly.  Suggest a process to realign the tapered boss if it inadvertently gets shifted.

column121: On Day 0; at approximately XA:20; I was pilot in command of Aircraft X; a Cessna 172S NAV III; departing Runway XXR at ZZZ on a personal flight with one passenger. I hold a Private Pilot certificate; ASEL; with approximately 163.5 total flight hours; all in Cessna 172 aircraft; and 16.6 hours in the preceding 90 days. I was well-rested; of sound mind; and had completed the IMSAFE checklist prior to flight with no concerns. No hazardous attitudes were recognized.The aircraft was rented from the FBO at ZZZ. Prior to flight; I taxied to the fuel tank where the FBO personnel topped off the fuel. A preflight inspection and walkaround were completed with no abnormalities. Fuel was sumped with normal results. Engine oil was observed at approximately 6.5 quarts; one quart was requested and added. A weight and balance computation was completed and confirmed the aircraft was within limits. The fuel selector was verified on BOTH. Aircraft loading was as follows: PIC at 180 lbs; one passenger at 255 lbs; and approximately 20 lbs of baggage in the rear seat area; with full fuel.ATIS Information 1 was current at XD:53; reporting winds 120 at 10 gusting 18; variable between 070 and 140; visibility 10 statute miles; ceiling broken at 4;000 ft; broken at 7;500 ft; temperature 27°C; dew point 17°C; altimeter 30.18. Increased bird activity was noted in the vicinity of the airport. The wind presented a right crosswind component on Runway XXR. Density altitude was elevated due to the 27°C temperature; however; the conditions were within the normal operating envelope for the aircraft type and loading.During the engine run-up at 2;000 RPM; a magneto check was performed. The left magneto dropped to 1;930 RPM and ran smoothly. The right magneto dropped to 1;910 RPM and ran rough. The idle check was satisfactory at 840 RPM. A second magneto check was performed; during which the right magneto ran smoothly. Both drops and the differential were within limits.I contacted ZZZ Tower and reported holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1; ready for departure. Tower instructed line up and wait due to traffic on the downwind. Subsequently; Tower cleared me for takeoff on Runway XXR with an assigned heading of 080.I began the takeoff roll from the full length of Runway XXR. Full throttle was applied with mixture full rich; flaps up; and trim set for takeoff. Engine instruments were checked and indicated in the green. Airspeed was confirmed alive. The takeoff roll felt normal in terms of acceleration. I noticed the crosswind component during the roll consistent with the reported winds.Rotation was initiated at 55 KIAS with approximately 10 degrees of pitch. Immediately after liftoff; climb performance was sub-optimal and the aircraft was barely gaining altitude. At a few feet AGL; the stall warning horn activated. I reduced the angle of attack; but airspeed was not increasing. I observed the engine RPM between 2;400 and 2;500. The engine sounded smooth and was not surging or running rough. The aircraft drifted left of the runway centerline.Within a few seconds; recognizing the aircraft was not climbing and was drifting off centerline; I made the decision to abort the takeoff rather than risk running out of usable runway or being forced to land off-surface. I pulled the throttle and mixture fully out; shutting down the engine. The aircraft touched down on the remaining runway approximately abeam Taxiway 2; roughly 1;600 feet from the Runway XXR threshold. I continued on Runway XXR; slowing down and turning right onto Runway XY; where I came to a full stop.I transmitted to Tower that I was aborting the takeoff. Tower initially instructed a right turn at Taxiway 3 to contact ground; then corrected to exit on Runway XY and contact ground. I acknowledged and advised that the engine was off. I contacted ZZZ Ground and reported engine-off on Runway XY after the aborted takeoff. Ground asked if I needed assistance; I requested a moment to assess. After confirmingeverything was in order; I successfully restarted the engine and requested taxi back to the Southeast ramp. Ground cleared me to taxi via Runway XY and Taxiway 3.Upon return to the ramp; I completed a squawk write-up documenting the event. Maintenance was contacted. The aircraft is pending inspection and the cause of the degraded takeoff performance has not yet been determined. No injuries were sustained by either occupant. No aircraft damage was observed.Chain of Events and Contributing Factors:The problem first arose during the run-up when the right magneto ran rough on the initial check. Although the second check was smooth and within limits; this may have been an early indication of a fouled spark plug or developing magneto issue. The problem became apparent immediately after rotation when the aircraft failed to achieve a normal climb rate despite full throttle application; and the stall warning activated at a few feet AGL. Engine RPM was observed at 2;400-2;500; which; combined with the initial rough magneto; suggests a possible partial power issue such as a fouled spark plug or intermittent magneto malfunction.Human Performance Considerations:I was well-rested and had passed the IMSAFE checklist with no concerns. My perception of the initial rough right magneto was that it had cleared on the second check; and I judged the engine fit for flight based on the smooth recheck and all indications being within limits. In hindsight; the initial rough magneto warranted additional scrutiny. My decision to abort was made quickly once I recognized the convergence of poor climb performance; stall warning activation; and lateral drift from centerline. I prioritized remaining on the runway surface and bringing the aircraft to a safe stop over attempting to continue a climb that the aircraft was not performing.Corrective Actions and Prevention:The aircraft has been squawked and is pending maintenance inspection; which should identify the mechanical cause. In future operations; if a magneto runs rough during the initial check -- even if a recheck is smooth -- I will perform an additional magneto verification while holding short prior to takeoff to confirm the issue has truly resolved rather than accepting a single smooth recheck. This additional step adds minimal time and could catch an intermittent ignition issue before committing to a takeoff. I will also establish a more deliberate go/no-go gate at the hold-short line for any anomaly observed during run-up; treating an initial rough magneto with greater caution.

column121: While conducting Flight Instruction in a helicopter (CFI positioned left seat; Pilot-Student Right Seat) at the local high traffic-use un-towered airport; we had conducted our approach to the predominant wind use runway XX; making the CTAF radio report of the approach; and runway XX mid-field intersection termination point.    The mid-point area of the runways intersect; with Runways XX and XY crossing; with the winds indicated by windsock on the airfield of 350-010°; 10 knots with occasional gusts during our traffic pattern training.  The runway alignment angle of Runways XX and XY does not allow a direct view on final for Runway XY if positioned near the intersection or north on Runway XX for reference.  This positioning makes it necessary to verify conflicting approach path is clear of course; if directly holding short (responsibly announced) or prior to an initial departure intention from runway XX; neither of which was the case in this situation.  Upon completing our approach to the mid-field intersection on Runway XX; I was allowing the student pilot to stabilize their hover in the wind prior to our take-off checks and prepare for next departure / right traffic pattern.  I heard an aircraft in-bound over the CTAF; making a call with the intent to use Runway XY; despite the winds and traffic pattern in use already; so as to avoid back-taxing to parking; as only Runway XY has a parallel taxiway directly accessible easily to & from the apron / ramp area.  I made another CTAF call stating we were a momentary delay; midfield intersection RWY XX.   I did not hear another CTAF call; however just a few moments later the American A-5 Tiger landed in front on us on Runway XY; (from my right; angled and blocked by the Pilot-Student / Door) rolling directly by within 50' or less from our hovering position on Runway XX; just south of the intersection.   The pilot while; rolling out after landing; proceeded to chastise us over CTAF; stating we 'were too close to the runway and shouldn't be there'.  I restated we literally had called our position on our approach and again just prior to his approach; stating we were still occupying the predominant wind runway at the intersection; using the crossing runway XX as established by us and other aircraft in the recent traffic pattern operations.    The other pilot continued to berate us over the radio; saying we should have moved 'off to the side' since he 'was landing'; insisting that despite the crossing runway in use; the runway stated as occupied and he saw us in position on runway (XX); implied it was his right of way to continue his approach regardless  apparently in lieu of considering a CTAF call about our holding position or the option to go-around since the runway area was already occupied.  There was no inquiry about if we were holding short on Runway XY; or if we could reposition away from the crossing runway (which we can & will do routinely); nor any attempt to abort his landing approach; despite knowing we were still there.   This continues to pose an hazard to flight operations at the airport; where airplane traffic will force repeated runway changes during established traffic pattern operations; in order to simplify their ground taxi to parking.  The airplane traffic continues to demonstrate no intention of clearing final approach or the runway environment on multiple occasions; insisting their landing gives them the right of way to an occupied runway; regardless of any aircraft already present. This has developed into a stigma; instead of addressing the core safety issues of communication; runway / pattern operations in use; traffic flow courtesy and clarifying intentions or going around versus forcing a situation into a Near Mid-Air Collision or Runway Incursion to a known occupied runway.

column121: Arrived at ZZZ for preflight. Preflight was normal with no abnormalities. Oil level was at 4 quarts; which led me to add 2 more quarts to bring it above the normal 6 quart range. No contaminants found in fuel during sump. No oil leaks in or around the engine. Aircraft had full fuel tanks and I was the only occupant in the aircraft for this flight.Started the engine; contacted clearance and ground frequencies for taxi to run-up area. The taxi was normal with no abnormalities.The run-up went smoothly with no abnormalities. Magneto checks were very smooth and well within range. The engine sounded normal and I continued my taxi to the runway.Departed ZZZ with no abnormalities. The engine sounded completely normal during climb out. I exited the airspace and started to head North-West towards ZZZ1; which was my destination for this flight. 4 minutes after my departure; I reached my cruising altitude of 2;000 feet due to a cloud layer above me and my relatively short flight plan to ZZZ1. My RPM setting for the flight was 2300 rpm's; and the mixture was leaned slightly due to the high density altitude for the day. 12 minutes after my departure; I noticed a steady decrease in rpm's. The drop started at 2300 rpm's and decreased on its own to about 1500 rpm's. I checked to make sure that the throttle did not back itself out. Everything looked normal. The engine started to shake violently. I immediately added full mixture and pulled the carburetor heat. Neither of those inputs made the problem any better. I backed off the throttle enough that the shaking wasn't as violent; but kept it high enough that I could mostly maintain altitude. I first thought that the propeller could have been knocked out of balance; however I decided that that was more than likely not the issue. There was too much shaking for it to be a normal bad magneto; so I also ruled that out. However; in case there was a bad magneto; I did not attempt a magneto check. I checked my engine gauges and the fuel pressure was green; the oil pressure was green; but the oil temperature was gradually decreasing. I monitored the gauges throughout the remainder of the flight. I was monitoring guard on 121.5 as soon as I had gotten the frequency change call from ZZZ tower. ZZZ approach responded to me on 121.5 and asked what kind of aircraft; how many souls were on board; and how much fuel I had. I responded that I was a Cessna 172; 1 soul on board; and full fuel as I had just departed ZZZ. I did my best to report my location before I was contacted by approach; however they made radar contact with me fairly quickly. They eventually asked me to switch to their frequency.I started to look for somewhere to land near me in case my engine decided to quit. I eventually made my way to the Highway that leads into the Bay and the city. I observed traffic patterns of the vehicles on the highway to see if it would be a safe option to land on. Traffic was relatively light; so I stayed over top of the highway until I could find a possible landing location at an airport. Approach gave me a few options to the North. Those airports were private strips. After hearing my options; I decided that ZZZ2 was the best option. Approach informed me of runway length; width; and winds available to the best of their knowledge. About 6 miles away from ZZZ2; I started to turn towards the airfield. I utilized the 3D imaging on ForeFlight to see what the strip would look like since it was private. I made visual contact with the field and continued my flight towards it. Approach informed me that an aircraft was above me and following me in case I had to ditch elsewhere.I had enough power to maintain my altitude for a normal left downwind entry for the field. I added 10 degrees of flaps to help me maintain my altitude while the aircraft slowed down. Once I was confident that I could make the short runway; I added full flaps. There was nearly a 90 degree crosswind for the runway (runway XX). The landing was smooth and did not require any substantial abnormal procedures. I taxied the aircraft off of the runway and shut down immediately. Postflight inspection resulted in seeing that there was a substantial amount of oil pooling on the ground on the right side of the nose wheel coming from the cowling and around the exhaust. I was not able to take the cowling off of the aircraft due to the amount of screws and lack of tools. Nothing looked abnormal in the engine other than the obvious oil leak. I believe that most of the oil leak came after the engine stopped; or at least when I was on the ground. The oil pressure never fell out of the green range and the engine stayed on throughout the flight until I was on the ground and shut it down myself. To my knowledge; I do not believe that any FAR's were broken or deviated from.

column121: Aircraft X cleared for the RNAV-Visual runway 12C into IWA. Aircraft Y squawking 1200 not in communication with ATC maneuvering outside the Class B. In my opinion. Aircraft X came into an unsafe proximity to Aircraft Y. Traffic was issued; and the pilot had Aircraft Y in sight and maintaining visual separation. No TCAS-RA was announced. The RNAV-Visual approach into IWA barely touches the PHX Class B airspace. It provides minimal protection from VFR aircraft not in communication with ATC. The majority of this procedure is in Class E airspace. There is high intensity training activity in the area of the approach. This area is a known 'hot-spot' to controllers due to the frequency of TCAS-RA's and traffic alerts. Maneuvering aircraft routinely change trajectory and/or altitude placing them into unsafe proximity into airliners descending or departing from IWA airport. There is a huge risk currently of unpredictable; non-participating aircraft intersecting with high-speed traffic flows. I propose 3 solutions to help mitigate this safety issue. Listed from most effective to least effective:1) Implement Class C airspace at IWA. A standard Class C airspace design would fully contain the approach procedure. IWA meets the FAA requirements to become Class C. In 2025; IWA recorded 15;309 air carrier operations; presumably all of which were IFR; and 95;618 air taxi operations; unknown with publicly available information how many were IFR. The threshold is 75;000 IFR operations. Additionally; IWA had 2;036;218 passengers in 2025; dramatically above the threshold of 250;000 enplaned passengers. 2) Expand the Class B airspace to more fully encompass the approaches at IWA. This may be difficult because IWA is not the primary airport; but the airspace should be studied to more fully accommodate jet traffic in the Phoenix area. 3) Implement a Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) or Special Air Traffic Rule (SATR). Mandate that pilots communicate with ATC near the IWA airport. 4). Charted Hot Spot on the sectional/TAC chart. The current traffic mix near Gateway airport presents a systemic and increasing safety risk. Proactive mitigation now reduces the likelihood of a future serious incident or accident.

column121: An Aircraft X departed SDL requesting VFR flight following. Aircraft X established communications with me approximately 10 miles northwest of SDL in a slow climb and moving quickly. I radar identified Aircraft X and issued traffic. Relevant traffic was Aircraft Y; who just terminated flight following a couple minutes earlier and was off my frequency. The pilot of Aircraft X said 'radar contact'. I subsequently issued a traffic alert and the pilot indicated he had the other aircraft in sight. In my recollection; the aircraft at the closest proximity were target merge and 200 feet. In my opinion; this is a 'near mid-air'.   Recommendation: There are several things at play here. Firstly; Aircraft X called me in the blind for flight following. UHF radio stepping on the VHF frequency. It took several transmissions for me to determine his callsign and type aircraft. Contributing to this difficulty was poor radio and reception quality making it difficult on first listen to determine the callsign if you aren't expecting it. Secondly; Aircraft X was not transmitting an ADS-B callsign. If the aircraft was transmitting the ADS-B callsign; I would have determined his callsign much quicker. ADS-B is required to operate in the airspace Aircraft X was flying in. Because of the delay in inputting the necessary information into STARS; I was unable to issue the aircraft control instructions to more effectively avoid traffic. Recommendation: SDL Tower should solicit high performing aircraft for flight following and input; or have Biltmore input flight plan information into STARS/NAS. This would eliminate the back and forth the radar controller has to do to determine the pilots callsign and intentions. In turn; we could provide a much better service. IWA tower does this already and it is very helpful. SDL tower should too. Alternatively; SDL tower can give the Biltmore controller a heads up of what's about to happen.

column121: This report is to point out a safety concern we as a crew of this flight experienced and would like to bring to attention.Distributing factors: IAH-ZZZZ flight close to maximum takeoff weight.During our departure from IAH on RWY 33R; we experienced a situation that presented a significant safety risk; which we believe warrants attention.After being cleared to line up and wait; and subsequently cleared for takeoff; we observed two aircraft stopped at the far end of RWY 33R; appearing to be positioned on Taxiway NB in direct alignment with the takeoff runway. A subsequent query with ATC confirmed these aircraft were indeed on TWY NB.Both aircraft remained in that position during the takeoff roll of the preceding aircraft. Given our aircraft was near maximum takeoff weight; these stationary aircraft were directly in line with the runway overrun area in the event of a rejected takeoff. This created a completely avoidable additional risk factor that could have resulted in a serious incident.As a precaution; we elected to not accept our takeoff clearance(prior to initiating the takeoff roll); until the aircraft could be moved. ATC instructed us to taxi off RWY 33R via WL and proceed back down WA for resequencing. Ground control successfully contacted the stationary aircraft; which were moved clear of the potential overrun area before any further departures. We were resequenced and departed RWY 33R a few minutes later without incident.

column121: During the initial climb-out from Runway XX at ZZZ; ZZZ Tower attempted to contact Aircraft Y (a helicopter) to establish visual contact with our aircraft. Aircraft Y did not initially respond to Tower.Upon hearing the call; I initiated an immediate visual scan. I located the target on the TCAS display off the right side and subsequently acquired visual contact with Aircraft Y. At that time; the helicopter appeared to be in a stationary hover. We continued our climb via the SID.Shortly thereafter; the helicopter began a turn toward our flight path before abruptly maneuvering to pass behind us. This maneuver triggered a TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) to 'Descend'We received a 'Clear of Conflict' shortly after the descent was initiated. After clear of conflict; we resumed our climb on the ZZZZZ X departure.The Captain; the Pilot Monitoring; notified ZZZ Tower that we were responding to a TCAS RA. At this point; Aircraft Y responded on the frequency; however; the audio quality and timing suggested the helicopter may have been on a different frequency or experiencing a communication lag with ZZZ Tower during the initial conflict.
column123: Climbing out on ZZZZZ X departure we heard ATC communicating with a Aircraft Y helicopter. It seemed that ATC had lost communication with the helicopter. ATC made several calls to Aircraft Y with no response. At approximately 2600 ft we got a traffic; traffic on TCAS. We visually acquired the helicopter at our approximate 3 o'clock position. He was approaching our departure path. Almost immediately we got a 'descend; descend' command from TCAS. We executed the maneuver and informed ATC of TCAS RA twice. We then saw the helicopter make a sharp left hand turn behind us. ATC then established contact with Aircraft Y and I believe Aircraft Y said he was on a different frequency. After our TCAS event we climbed and continued the departure. I have been flying for over 40 years and this was the closest I've come to another aircraft while airborne.

column121: I was completing a round trip flight from LGB in Aircraft X. My right-seat passenger was an instrument-rated private pilot. We were descending to land at Long Beach 26L with VFR flight following; on SoCal Approach. Route of flight was direct from the southeast; descending through 3000 on a 303 degree heading; descent to 2500 authorized. ATC issued a traffic alert for a converging aircraft at 2500 feet indicated. I added power and held 3000 feet until further advised. I never saw the other traffic; so turning away was not an option. As the other aircraft (Aircraft Y) passed directly beneath us; my copilot snapped a ForeFlight screenshot showing the tracks crossing; the other aircraft was shown at 2600' on ADSB-in.The other aircraft was not in communication with SoCal so far as I could tell. It is possible the other pilot was on the practice area CTAF; though I was not. The near-miss happened very fast. Collision was avoided due to my evasive action of aborting descent in response to the ATC alert. My analysis is that my choice to use ATC flight following; and a quick response to the ATC traffic alert; likely saved our lives. My attention was divided between managing the descent; visually scanning outside; descent checklist; navigation; and communications. My iPad was not showing traffic consistently; as it would not maintain a steady WiFi connection to my Sentry Plus. Yet I should have been able to note the conflicting traffic on my own ADSB-in on the G1000 Multi-function Flight Display (MFD). Had the other aircraft been on frequency; likely there would have been ATC intervention to deconflict. Had I been monitoring the CTAF; I might have heard the other aircraft make a position announcement; but the extra radio work would have increased my workload and delayed my imminent handover to LGB Tower.See-and-avoid is a fantasy in situations like this one. Again; though I was actively looking; I never saw the other traffic. I will redouble my own efforts to maintain situational awareness of traffic using all resources available. I would support a requirement for all aircraft to transmit ADSB-out in all US airspace. I would also support a change in the FARs to allow general aviation copilots to log Second in Command (SIC) time; in order to encourage pilot-passengers to serve as Pilot Monitoring. Thank you.

column121: I took off IFR from HEF; the departure procedure was to climb to 800 ft and continue a climbing right turn toward CSN.  The tight turn was required because of R-6608A.  When I reached 800 ft I began my left turn by turning the heading bug.  The heading bug did not respond. At the same time I was a full power and clean for the climb.  I got disoriented briefly because the heading plane wasn't responding and failed to increase the altitude to the next altitude of 2000.  So I was 800 ft off the ground and gaining speed. I focused ouside for obstacle clearance I called ATC; let them know I was having trouble. The gave me vectors and prompted a climb.  Those controller are so great!Anyway. I was very well prepared for the departure procedure. I don't do them very often so I studied it hard and set up the nav properly.  The first mistake was setting the altitude to 800 ft; the first point the climb was supposed to stop was 2000 ft.  The second mistake was turning the wrong knob for heading change (two identical knobs - one does altimeter the other heading).  The third mistake was trouble shooting the autopilot.  I should have disconnected it and hand flown.  If I had done that I would not have veered far off course. What I did well was call ATC quickly and they helped me get my head back on straight.I discussed with two respected ATP/CFI's and gained additional insight.  I've shared my story with other pilots.

column121: We were being vectored to the final approach course for ILS 32 at TBR; and I cancelled IFR when the field was in sight as there was no other traffic in sight or indicated on my traffic display (ADS-B and Garmin 800). I switched to VFR on the transponder and switched to the CTAF to report my position and intention to land on Runway 32. A few seconds after I reported my position and intentions on CTAF the runway lights came on bright. I had not activated that so I concluded that someone at the non-towered airport had heard me and out of courtesy turned the lights up bright.As I turned onto the final approach course at the final approach fix I noticed a single white strobe light at the departure end of the runway. I wondered if it was an aircraft on the runway or a single Runway End Identifier Light. Since I had not heard any other transmissions or position reports on the CTAF and observed no traffic on my traffic display I concluded it must be a single REIL; even though I had never seen such a thing.I made a short-final position report but still was unsure what the strobe like was. Just before crossing the runway threshold I looked down and saw what I thought was an aircraft at the end of the runway--the source of the single strobe light.I immediately added power and initiated a go-around. I climbed out and turned to a left downwind. At that point I questioned if I had tuned the correct CTAF; so I checked Airport Info on Foreflight and discovered I had tuned 122.75 instead of the correct frequency; 122.72. I reported my position and intention to land on 32. A helicopter pilot responded and said they had been on the runway. I explained my frequency mistake and apologized. The pilot said something to the effect of 'No problem.' I saw the strobe light move off the runway onto a closed diagonal runway so I continued my downwind.Just before touching down another voice transmitted; saying he was the instructor in the helicopter and claimed we were just 10 feet above them when I initiated the go-around. Given that I was busy with the landing I did not respond. And that was it. No other transmissions from the helicopter.The next day I attempted to find out who was flying the helicopter so I could discuss the situation with the instructor; but the airport said they do not know of anyone who is training there in a helicopter.My mistake in tuning the incorrect CTAF frequency was obvious. But the sudden change in runway lighting made me think someone heard me and turned up the lights; so I had no reason to think I had the incorrect CTAF. Plus; I wasn't surprised that no other aircraft responded to my initial calls because it was nighttime and there was no traffic shown on my traffic display. I've learned from that to double check every frequency input. But I wonder why the helicopter would remain at the very end of the departure runway for several minutes without any movement; and why they did not appear on my traffic display. That's what I wanted to talk to the helicopter instructor about.That experience was a dramatic and sobering example of how an unrelated series of events and circumstances can lead to a disaster. Pay attention to details!

column121: ZZZ. Runway in use XX SID ZZZ Day 0 XA:47. We have on board 4 Display Units (DUs) (screens) but as soon as we took off we lost without any warning 3 out 4 DUs; with only the right front DU working but the information that we were getting was limited and NOT ACCURATE in terms of speed; altitude and heading... the altitude indication showed 5;000 ft. but we were absolutely positive that was a wrong indication so we were not able to comply with the SID right away; we managed to turn right using the magnetic compass; but altitude indications continued not being reliable at all; our main concern at that time was to promptly to recover our failed DUs in order to have accurate navigation info. So we executed the proper check list for EACH DU and we were able to recover all of them ONE AT THE TIME; when we reached about 7 or 8;000 ft. everything was working in perfect order again; and we were able to continue our 2:30 hour flight to ZZZ1 without any further malfunction at all.Up to now we still don't know what was the cause of the problem; the Embraer Legacy 500 is very computer and technologically fly by wire aircraft; I have talked to a couple of mechanics and their best guess is that after being parked for 9 days in the cold humid and rainy weather there was some kind of glitch in any of the computers that cause the problem when the aircraft was airborne. I must mention that the departure ZZZ controller did in fact a great job that day he was completely BUSY at that time; we didn't have any TCAS advisory or resolution at all mainly thanks to him. I have been flying for over several decades and my co-captain for over more than several decades and this was for me the most stressful situation I have ever encountered in the cockpit as a PIC; we even thought for a brief moment to declaring an emergency but the frequency was so busy and crowded; so meanwhile we focused on recover our DUs and being as safe as possible!!

column121: On Day 0 at XA:55 (calm winds and clear) while departing the ZZZ Airport in my Bonanza; I had a very close encounter with a business jet departing in the opposite direction on the same runway. To back up a little; I started the engine in front of the hangar and set up the NAV along with some of the other preflight items while the engine was warming up. On taxi out; I made a radio call announcing that I was on the south ramp taxiing to Runway XX for departure via Taxiway 1. A  Mooney immediately came back saying he was doing the same thing. I saw him taxi out from between a row of T-hangars and followed him to the run-up area. While taxiing; a cub announced that he was departing (opposite direction) on Runway XY. It is worth noting that a Zenith experimental aircraft had previously departed Runway XX and was on a downwind departure. After completing my run-up checks; I continued taxiing to the runway checking for traffic in the pattern and announced that I was departing Runway XX with a left crosswind departure. On the takeoff roll at about 40 to 50 mph a business jet came flashing overhead; opposite direction; about 200 or 300 feet above me. Way too close! The TRAFFIC TRAFFIC alert went off after the jet had passed overhead. I continued the takeoff and as I was turning crosswind; the Mooney announced his takeoff. I called him and asked if he heard the jet make a takeoff call. He said no. I never heard any communication from the jet before; during; or after the encounter. Did he not make a call or was he on a different frequency? At the ZZZ Airport most of the aircraft are parked or hangared at the opposite end. Runway XY is the most convenient runway for departure. The remarks section of the airport information states that Runway XX is the preferred calm wind runway. Almost nobody pays any attention to this. Aircraft in the Runway XY run-up area are difficult to see from Runway XX. Turbine aircraft on the ramp departing Runway XY typically taxi from the ramp right onto the runway and depart without stopping; traffic permitting. What could I have done better? Look harder at the opposite end for traffic? If the jet had been on CTAF; perhaps a second call that I was rolling on Runway XX for takeoff would have helped.

column121: During departure from ZZZ; the aircraft was operating with a deferred item: ENG 2 FIRE LOOP (no indication as to which loop) along with other unrelated deferrals.Shortly after departure; we received multiple intermittent ECAM alerts for ENG 2 FIRE LOOP B. The alert appeared and cleared several times; prompting further review of the aircrafts maintenance history and current status.Upon re-examining the aircraft logbook; I noted that a similar discrepancy involving ENG 2 fire loop B had been recorded two pages prior out of ZZZ1. The associated maintenance comment indicated the issue had been entered into the maintenance software; however; there was no clear documentation specifying the corrective action taken and if that was the current deferral we had. This lack of clarity made it difficult to determine whether the previously recorded issue corresponded to the currently deferred LOOP A; or if there had been an error in deferral.I cross-checked the Deferred Item (DI) list and logbook entries and discussed the situation with my First Officer. To clarify information; I contacted Dispatch; who confirmed that LOOP A was the deferred system. However; due to the ambiguity in the maintenance records and absence of a clear timeline or action history; uncertainty remained as to whether the correct loop had been deferred or if both loops were potentially inoperative.Given the possibility that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 could be non-functional; effectively leaving the engine without fire detection capability; we assessed this as a potential safety-of-flight concern. We communicated our concerns to Dispatch; including the possibility of an incorrect deferral and the operational implication of having no fire detection on ENG 2.Dispatch concurred with our assessment and requested a return to ZZZ; with an amended release issued. The return was conducted uneventfully.Upon arrival; we coordinated with Maintenance to clarify the discrepancy. After additional review; Maintenance confirmed that the deferral was correct and that both fire detection loops on ENG 2 were inoperative; LOOP A having been placed on deferral a while ago; and LOOP B being inoperative now without deferral. To me this event highlighted a significant gap in flight crew access to detailed and time-stamped maintenance actions and deferral history. The absence of clear documentation regarding when a system was deferred; what exact corrective actions were taken; or whether previous discrepancies were related to current deferrals. It created uncertainty during an in-flight abnormal situation.In my opinion this lack of transparency led to an unnecessary increased cockpit workload during a critical phase of flight by the difficulty of verifying a system status and MEL applicability.I would like to see an improvement of flight crew access to detailed maintenance records; to enhance our situational awareness and support more informed and timely decision-making.

column121: Leg was briefed and flown as first flight of the day.  Flight was uneventful until parked at gate. Upon stopping; I neglected to set the parking brake (although I thought I had); gave the marshaller the parking brake set sign; and proceeded with the shutdown flow. Upon calling for the Shutdown checklist; I noticed unusual movement peripherally at the same time the marshaller also noticed the aircraft rolling backward. I immediately applied the toe brakes and brought the aircraft to a stop. I made a PA to request the passengers return to their seats. The aircraft had rolled approximately 10 feet backward and needed to be repositioned. In coordination with the ground crew; we attempted a start of the #1engine. When it failed to start; we started the #2 engine; turned on the #1 hydraulic pump and repositioned the aircraft. I set the parking brake; shut down the engine; and accomplished the Shutdown checklist without further incident.  Cause: This event was caused by my inattention; distraction; and lack of attention to detail. Inwardly; I was focused on other shutdown tasks and confirming my next assignment (deadhead to ZZZ1).Suggestions: Continue to maintain situational awareness until all shutdown tasks are complete. No matter how many times a task in a shutdown sequence has been repeated; confirm switch position and indication after accomplishing a task. Always be cognizant of parking brake position and indication. DO NOT PAY LIP SERVICE TO CHECKLISTS!

Since we were actively navigating to a VOR; we placed the frequency in and monitored it as a back up in case we lost all GPS sensing. Approximately 100mi from the coast; all messages cleared and GPS 2 began getting information again. We continued with no further issues or erroneous information. Upon checking the GPS jamming/spoofing website; we found that we had crossed along the edge of an active area.

I immediately did a go around and went missed. After getting myself sorted; I called up the center and explained that I was on the published missed approach. They asked why I went missed; and I said there was a grader on the runway; and asked if I would like to shoot the approach again. The grader then came on the radio and let me know that he was now clear of the runway; and that he had his radio volume turned down; so he didn't hear our calls. On my second approach; I landed without issue and took off without incident.Cause: The cause of this incident was the grader's radios being turned down to where he did not hear my inbound radio calls. This; paired with low visibility and ceilings; left me in the dark about whether he was in the runway environment.Suggestions: Suggestions that could prevent this event from occurring again would be to make sure that the grader's are required to have their radios on and turned up when on the runway; or moving in the runway environment.
