column121: I was holding short of rwy XX at ZZZ getting my ifr clearance/release for a flight. The field was 1000 overcast.  I was on the phone (through my headset) with ZZZ clearance delivery and radio background noise and poor telephone connection were very distracting and makde for difficult communication. I turned the volume on comm 1 way down to hear ZZZ. Once I got my release; I heard no traffic on ctaf (I didn't realize that comm 1 volume was at zero); and I announced my taxi onto the runway for departure. With a quick glance; I saw no traffic on final and taxied onto the runway. Sight of the traffic on final was blocked by the airframe and I gave a cursory; at best; visual check of final. I didn't expect to see any traffic and therefore I didn't.  As I turned on the runway; I saw a flash of an airplane overhead and stopped immediately. After a few seconds to analyze what I'd done; I realized that comm 1's volume was at zero. Therefore; I hadn't heard the traffice making their calls. Unbelievably; I had taxied onto the runway with an aircraft on short final. I realized my mistake; corrected my comm 1 volume; and taked with the aricraft that was on the go and going back into the pattern. I told them of my error and thanked them for being aware and taking corrective action for my mistake. They were quite gracious. I then took  quick second to analyze things and decided to proceed with my departure. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Background distractions with comm 1 and the telephone both in my headset caused communication difficulties and I turned comm 1 volume to zero. There was a failure to check comm 1 volume before taxiing onto the runway. I felt rushed (self imposed) because of a 5 minute void time; and my connecting flight pilot (leg 3) was up against a tfr at the final destination. I was trying to gain as much time for him as possible. I allowed myself to feel rushed in the moment and made a critical error that could have had terrible consequences. Only a cursory glance of final was a factor since i didn't expect to see any traffic because I hadn't heard any radio calls in several minutes. I will not turn the volume on comm 1 or 2 to zero ever again. Turn it down a bit perhaps; but never to zero. I have an acute awareness now of the issues with being rushed in the cockpit. I will be very careful to not allow myself to rush. I am incorporating a slow and methodical final cockpit check before taking the runway.A slower and more intentional check of final before proceeding onto the runway will also be a corrective action. I never imagined (wiht my varied experience) that I'd make such stupid and compounding mistakes leading to such an incident. I believe that I am a more diligent; aware and intentional pilot moving forward.

column121: When departing ZZZ Airport in Cherokee; an engine incident occurred during the initial climb out. During taxi from the ramp to the runup area just off of runway XXR at Taxiway 1; there were no bad engine indications on either the standard engine gauges or the installed engine monitor. The engine runup was conducted; and all indications were normal and in the green; including Fuel Pressure; Oil Pressure; Oil Temperature; and Cylinder Head Temperature. Magnetos were also checked and were within specifications. After the runup; we were told to cross XXR at Taxiway 1 and hold short of XXL at Taxiway 1. Before we entered XXL for departure; I verified that the aircraft was properly set up; including the electric fuel pump on; the fuel selector on the fullest tank; and the mixture full rich. We were then cleared for takeoff on XXL at Taxiway 1. We rolled onto the runway centerline and smoothly increased power to take off. My student is fairly new; so I pointed to each engine indication and called out each of the following for him. Fuel pressure in the green; Oil temperature in the green; Oil pressure in the green. I then verified with the digital engine monitor. We climbed on the departure leg to 1;100 feet indicated; then started our left climbing turn out to the southeast. Up to this point; there were no indications on the engine gauges other than positive indications. While in the left-hand turn; there was a loud bang and a thump that I felt through my seat. This was followed by shaking throughout the aircraft and the flight controls. Oil began spraying onto the windshield. This was followed by smoke filling the cockpit. My first action was to turn downwind and reduce power. I contacted ZZZ Tower and requested a short approach to land on Runway XXL. The tower responded; saying they were unable due to landing traffic. I then responded to the tower; informing them that I would need a short approach to Runway XXL. The tower then told the landing traffic to go around. I made a left turn toward the runway and landed safely. At the time of the landing; I did not know if there was a fire due to the smoke in the cockpit; so I used full braking power using the parking brake handle and exited Runway XXL at Taxiway 2. As I was rolling off the runway; I brought the mixture lever back to idle cut; turned the magnetos off; and removed the key. At this point; I saw that there was no fire; and smoke was coming from the hot oil and exhaust gas. I notified Tower that we would not be needing emergency services. I then turned off the master switch; opened the door; and my student and I exited the airplane. I; as Pilot in Command; did everything in my power to properly pre-flight the aircraft; including verifying that the required inspections were complete; required documents were in the aircraft; and the aircraft was airworthy; verifying the engine was running properly before takeoff; and swiftly and safely returning to the airport when the incident occurred. After landing; I inspected the engine and found that the #1 cylinder had cracked and the pushrods had been forced from their seat. There was nothing further I could have done to prevent this issue from occurring.

After finishing ECAM actions I had the FO go to the follow up items as I continued to fly and communicate to ATC. After a brief discussion with the FO I favored the notifying ATC option and communicated that with ATC followed with Souls on Board and 1.5 hours of fuel. We did three turns in holding which allowed for us to finish everything we needed to do inside and outside the aircraft to include the comms to dispatch; FAs; the passengers and ZZZ ops to make sure they were ready for us. We setup the arrival and approach and slowly worked towards ZZZ. We completed all checklists and landed without incident. Tower wasn't sure as to our plan for leaving the runway after landing so we told them we would clear immediately after landing. Fire trucks still responded even though they weren't requested; followed us to the gate and we shutdown the engines.The FO and I did a post flight inspection walk around of the aircraft specifically the right engine and saw no anomalies. I communicated with chief pilot who passed on the info to the IOC Duty pilot; dispatch informing them the plane was grounded awaiting contract maintenance; and Maintenance Control due to the out of base write up.The FO did a great job of remaining calm and helping me work the issue. His input and dedication to the task at hand was perfect and the interaction between us was seamless. SIDE NOTE: Major issue with the wording on the ECAM vs what's on the switch- wording is mismatched which caused an unnecessary distraction and wasted time in proceeding to the 2nd ECAM which was turning off AUTOTHRUST; which almost led to an MMO overspeed. The ECAM says: ENG 2 N1 MODE ONENG 1 N1 MODE ONWhile we presumed this was actually the Full Authority Digital Engine Control (FADEC)s it doesn't say that and I was concerned about the result of turning them on during flight (it's labeled GROUND POWER and a guarded switch for a reason?!) and possibly exacerbating this issue or creating another issue. So I had the FO scrub the manual to confirm that N1 MODE= FADEC during holding in an attempt to complete the first ECAM action. Meanwhile the airspeed was slowly creeping up as we delayed doing the third item of the 1st ECAM - move the thrust levers; since we hadn't resolved the 1st two items of the first ECAM . This distraction brought us real close to an MMO overspeed but I caught it prior to it occurring. I retarded the thrust levers appropriate to the speed needed. We then circled back to the 1st two items of the first ECAM and the search for N1 MODE.Cause: there seems to be a mismatch of ECAM procedures and the name of the switch which should be looked into further.

column121: I was the instructor on a VFR instrument training flight flying the RNAV runway XX approach to LPV minimums into ZZZ my student was flying the aircraft under the hood as I operated as safety pilot and instructor in the right seat. Before hitting minimums about 2 miles from the airport we were cleared the option runway XX and after the option we were told to fly runway heading. It was very busy at the airport; from the ATIS I knew they were landing and departing runways XY and XX which intersect. As we continued passed minimums I told my student that he had the airport in sight simulating breaking through the clouds. Since we were cleared the option I decided to have my student continue the approach to landing where we would touch and go then continue as cleared on runway heading. As we descended to the runway I noticed a Cessna on the ground to our aircraft right rolling down runway XY. I had not been told about any traffic though I had been listening to the tower frequency and had known that the primary runway in use was runway XY. I made the snap judgment that the aircraft had possibly just landed and was about to taxi off the runway which seemed odd since we were so low on the approach. As I continued to watch the Cessna on runway XY I noticed it was accelerating and clearly about to take off which would have been right throughout our landing path. I glanced at my IPad which has ADS-B traffic information and saw that the plane was company traffic. I told my student the go missed and climb immediately. I then told my student to turn right to avoid the Cessna; my student had not seen the Cessna as from his prospective the aircraft was to his right and under the nose. My student responded to my command to side step to the right telling me we had been instructed to fly runway heading. I grabbed the stick bumping it right while telling my student there is aircraft below us we need to side step. I keyed the mic announcing we had gone missed. The tower frequency was extremely busy and it was clear the controller was having a difficult time. I chose not to ask what had gone wrong in that moment as I knew it would do no one any good. My student finally saw the Cessna as it climbed to our altitude as it passed behind us and to the left. It was clear from the angle that we had been right over each other at some point over the runways and could not have had a separation more than 200 feet. While side stepping to the right I lost visual with the Cessna due to the low wing of our DA40. After talking to the instructor of the Cessna and his student I came to find he was unaware of my presence landing runway XX and did not see us at any point. The classic high wing; low wing conundrum played a roll in this event as I could not adequately maintain visual separation and take evasive action at the same time.If I had not seen the Cessna or taken corrective action the separation between our aircraft and the Cessna would have been extremely close.I have a few takeaways first for myself; I should have been listening more intently on the radio of what other traffic was cleared to do. I did not know what the Cessna was doing until I saw it on the ground accelerating I should have had a better mental picture of the traffic around me.We should not have been cleared the option for runway XX; in my opinion we should have been told to break off and been given a heading prior to the threshold that would have avoided overflying runway XY. I have received this kind of clearance at ZZZ before and would have accepted it. If we could not fit into the traffic flow we should not have been cleared the approach or not have been told to continue when checking in with tower. It would be frustrating but I would rather be told that we need to break off early than be put into a situation such as this. There is no substitute for looking outside. I have heard this countless times as a pilot and I now fully appreciate why.

column121: Yet again I have to write a report because the safety culture of management; Traffic Management Unit (TMU); and the command center is severely lacking. The FAA does not have safety as its number one priority. They care more about efficiency and running plans to keep stakeholders happy than controller workload and safe sector flow.On Day 0 multiple areas in ZTL worked extremely high volume traffic that was not predicted or well managed due to the special event. I had already been working steady traffic flow at Spartanburg with CLT departures and arrivals; and ATL departures as well as numerous point outs on AGS/AIK/DNL/HQU arrivals going into East Departure. I was called by the Macon sector to say that East 16 had told them to hold AGS and I would need to hold one in my airspace; once I got them in the hold I called East to let them know ATL departures would be delayed climbing due to the holding pattern; East said we're not holding AGS put them on a 180" which I did. Not two minutes later Macon called again to say we are holding AIK; put another in the hold and then the supervisor said were running AIK but 25 Miles in Trail (MIT). I called East and they said that they had never been holding AIK. This was just the start of an extremely chaotic and unsafe 45 minutes where it became clear that TMU and OMs were not aware of the traffic volume and did not have a plan to appropriately mitigate it. The sector Spartanburg has a Monitor Alert Parameter (MAP) value of 14; we started at a 20 and briefly went up to a 24 which is absolutely not safe; an unacceptable risk for no reason.When I finished up with the holding mess I looked back to the east side to see about 8 AGS area departures flashing at me all looking for higher and with a mess over overtakes and bad speeds. All of these departures would cross the standard ATL departures with everyone wanting higher. I had to vector a few to maintain separation but this was an absolute disaster where my D-side and me were barely holding on to the sector. I left that session feeling extremely stressed and frustrated that we did not get support from TMU and ZTL management to stop sectors from being overloaded.This happened because the command center; facility management; and TMU do not care about safety and do not care about sector overload. Their number one priority seems to be keeping as many aircraft moving as possible; especially when it involves special events. TMU is forcing normal ATL and CLT traffic flows which already put our sectors near capacity and then adding significant event volume on top of that; is not a safe combination.Additionally we do not have the staffing to support overloaded sectors with D-sides and trackers. We had XX people on this shift and needed two more than that positions open but we couldn't do it.Recommendation: When there are special events regular traffic flow must be reduced to not overload sectors; even something like 30 MIT off ATL and CLT would have helped in this case. It is unsafe for a controller to work normal traffic flow plus 100s of additional flights for the special events.From what I can discern TMU has no tools to plan for departures pushes off of smaller airports; especially with a special event they need to be able to see these departures and meter them to manage sector overload. When a sector starts getting overloaded the first move should be shut off departures; re-evaluate the situation and then resume with needed restrictions in place; this did not happen in this event.Local facilities need more say on what restrictions to implement from the command center; especially when it involves safety. I can't count how many times I have told an Operations Supervisor (OS) or OM that some situation is unsafe but the answer is that's what the command center wants so we have to do it.Traffic volume needs to match controller staffing; we need to reduce traffic on low staffed days and this needs to be variable depending on numbers. If we have 9/12 then we should have 75% of traffic volume; this way demand can better meet capacity as opposed to the current method of we will put in a staffing trigger if you are at 50%."No notice holding" needs to be an absolute last resort; we should have the tools to see when too many aircraft will get to an airport at the same time and manage that well in advance to reduce last minute holding and vectors which increase risk.The MAP is a useful tool but it is too slow to update and does not properly capture departures from small airports. Today 32 Spartanburg was showing green for most of the day with the exception of the current block that was a red +5 - 10 above MAP. How can we use this tool to manage sectors if it can't accurately look at departures?Overall I cannot wrap my head around the fact that on a normal day if we are 1 over the MAP number on a combined sector they will split it; if a sector appears red on the board they will add a D-side but on a day like today where we exceeded the MAP values on multiple sectors we are just a "little busy" and managers say "well we made it through; thanks for the hard work" this is UNACCEPTABLE we cannot have it both ways. If exceeding MAP values is a big deal on a normal day than it also needs to be a big deal on special events and weather days. We cannot keep working sectors that are too overloaded to safely separate traffic; someday there will be an error that is unrecoverable."

column121: I was training on sector 40/41. During the session; Aircraft X was handed off to us from NCT with destination to APC. The pilot stated he had the ATIS for APC. I cleared the pilot direct RRIBT; a transition fix on the RNAV 19R.The pilot said he could not find RRIBT on the approach plate; I spelled it for him and he was able to find it and go direct. I then cleared him to cross RRIBT AOA 060 and cleared him for the approach. During this time we were sequencing for STS and went into holding for SFO. We were also discussing sector operations and procedures given that SFO/Norcal was in an unusual/uncommon configuration (landing SE). At some point my trainer observed Aircraft X descending below 059; which was low for the segment of the approach he was on; but still above the MVA. My trainer brought it to my attention; at which point the pilot descends below the MVA; and we issued a safety alert. The pilot climbs to 045 as instructed; but does not follow the lateral guidance of the approach; at which point I canceled the approach clearance. I vectored him back around for the approach; he flew it with no problems this time and landed at APC.Recommendation: Confirm pilot is familiar with approach being given. Notify pilot of deviation from approach segment altitude prior to it requiring a safety alert.Better low altitude alert phraseology. Wouldn't have prevented it; but could've been better regardless.
column123: We were flying inbound on the REBAS1 arrival and were told to join the approach after REBAS. We had briefed and loaded the approach loaded via vectors; so we didn't have anything loaded in the FMS prior to OIINK we asked the controller how he wanted us to join the approach and he told us to go direct RRIBT. Due to how we had the approach loaded we didn't have RRIBT. At this point we were behind the airplane and ended up loading RRIBT manually to get headed in the right direction. We looked in the FMS to try and load it via RRIBT but we were not able to since it wasn't a IAF. We ended up manually putting in BARKZ and POPES. Because we had manually put in the points they had no altitude protection. We were VNAVing down to 1900 at NAAYY. Because we had fell behind we didn't catch the altitudes at BARKZ and POPES. We got as low as 3700 feet before OIINK and had the TAWS page pulled up and got no terrain warnings so we didn't think anything of it until we received a low altitude alert from ATC and were told to climb and maintain 4500 feet. We ended up being told to climb to 6000 and got vectored back to POPES to do the RNAV 19R again. The second time we understood where we went wrong and complied with the remaining altitude restrictions and eventually landed with no issue. After landing we were then told to copy down a phone number. This could've been prevented had we loaded the approach Via the IAF Rebas. We also could have asked for delay vectors and taken the time to figure out how to set up the approach correctly.

column121: On visual approach to approach to Runway XX at ZZZ; I was PM(Pilot Monitoring)  and Line Check Pilot (LCP) conducting Operating Evaluation (OE) training for my FO(First Officer) who was PF.(Pilot Flying).  During the approach we were slowing and configuring to land.  Upon calling for Flaps 30; we encountered a wind gust that increased our airspeed and caused a 'FLAP RELIEF'  EICAS CAUTION message.  I return returned the Flap handle to Flaps 25 until we got out of the gust and slowed back to return the Flaps to 30.  At this time we received a 'LE SLAT DISAGREE' and 'TE FLAP ASYM'  EICAS  Caution Messages.   We executed a Go Around and per SOP retracted the Flap handle to Flaps 20.  The Flaps retracted to about 21 degrees and stayed stuck there as we tried to retract them on the Go-around.  I returned the Flap Handle to correspond with the Flaps at the '20' detent.   We retracted the gear and flew the missed approach per ATC instructions and remained at 180 KIAS.  We advised ATC of our condition and requested priority handling.  After completing After Takeoff Checks we ran the QRH procedures for the above listed malfunctions.  They directed us to accomplish an approach and landing using FLAPS 20 Ref + Target speeds.   We completed all checklists.  I spoke to the Flight Attendants and advised them of our situation and used our brief model.   I then spoke to the passengers and advised them of the situation.  I sent an ACARS message to dispatch to advise them of the situation and we were in the pattern for landing and would speak on ground if needed.   We finished our briefs and checklists and I took over the aircraft as PF due to my FO being a student on OE .  We then advised ATC we were ready to return for landing.  They vectored us to a visual approach to Runway XYC as we had requested that as a longer runway per our configuration.  We landed uneventfully and cleared the runway where we spoke to and were followed to the gate by the airport responding vehicles.  We taxied safely to the gate without further incident.
column123: On a visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ Airport; I was the First Officer acting as PF while undergoing Operational Evaluation (OE); with the Captain serving as PM and Line Check Pilot (LCP).During descent and landing configuration; I called for Flaps 30. column121: While completing cruise duties at initial level-off and preparing for ETOPS entry; the PM checked the status page on the lower EICAS as part of normal system checks. It was then that both pilots noticed the status message 'AIR/GND DISAGREE'. After checking circuit breakers; we discussed the meaning of the message and the fact that status messages are not controlling in-flight and do not require crew action. However; we discussed the possibility of the issue developing into an 'AIR/GND SYS' EICAS Advisory which drives a non-normal checklist. We considered about 10 minutes into discovering the discrepancy that we may need to air return. We considered the weather forecast at ZZZ1; ZZZ2; and ZZZ. ZZZ1 and ZZZ2 were forecasting rainy and gusty conditions with thunderstorms in the vicinity; ZZZ was dry with light winds. We also considered that if we received the EICAS Advisory that our auto brakes; auto speed brakes; and thrust reversers would be inop all while navigating near thunderstorms approaching ZZZ1. We completed an HF phone patch to Maintenance Control to discuss the issue; attempt to gain more awareness about this message; and rope in dispatch to get their latest information about local weather. We researched more and discussed the risks which worked in our favor to burn more fuel to get our gross weight below max landing weight. At about 1+30 into the flight; we decided that the workload to take this potential issue into the islands with unfavorable weather would not be the safest course of action. Additionally; the MEL mentioned that the issue does not have MEL solutions once on the ground. We coordinated with dispatch; ATC; and flight attendants to start heading back to ZZZ. On the approach; we configured early including gear to see if the ground/flight mode anomaly would appear and force the AIR/GND SYS advisory. It was a normal approach; however; I noticed that the aircraft sank faster than usual while pulling power during the flare. This may have been because the jet allowed the engines to go to ground idle before touchdown; but I added power to re-establish a normal flare and descent rate then gradually reduced power to idle as the jet touched down. While deploying thrust reversers; the EICAS Advisory 'AIR/GND SYS' appeared and remained on until we cleared the runway. We passed all this info to maintenance who was able to capture it in the write up.
column123: Leveled off at FL330 waiting to accomplish a cruise check and begin departure using the ZZZZZ guide.  I noticed  a status message alerting us AIR/GND SYS.  FO continued flying while I looked up the status message approaching ZZZZZ1.  We had been radar service terminated from ZZZ CTR.  FM was not much guidance so we decided to contact ZZZ radio for a SELCAL check and position report as we elected to continue on the track.  After establishing contact with ZZZ radio; I requested an HF Phone Patch and was given a separate HF frequency at which time a phone patch to Dispatch and Maintenance Control was established.  The phone patch was limited and we could barely hear Dispatch and Maintenance Control.  Maintenance Control was not sure nor could verify if the aircraft was in air mode or ground mode.  We tried several times to check circuit breakers and EICAS to see if we could determine which mode the aircraft was in and what to expect when we put the gear down.  We were not sure if we would get Air/Gnd System which would affect braking and thrust reversers.  The Wx in ZZZ1 was gusty winds with rainy showers and wet runway.  The Wx in ZZZ2 (Mx base) was worse and forecasted to get worst.  We continued flying given we were tankering fuel with 14;000lbs extra which put us landing over weight with an air return and also landing heavier than normal with rainy weather and gusty winds with terrain.  Given these threats; we elected to continue towards the fix to burn fuel down.  The extra flying time would allow us to brief an air return; close out the HF phone patch by also notifying the company and dispatch; speak with FAs; and develop a plan.  We accomplished all; referenced the diversion guide in the FOM; and communicated our plan with ZZZ radio.  We executed a diversion from our track turning right flying directly North and returning back to ZZZ.  We requested an early descent while also encountering holding for traffic delays in ZZZ which was to our advantage to burn fuel down to help with our overweight landing.  We held for ten minutes at 10;000 ft and took delayed vectors landing runway XXR about 300 lbs overweight.  We put the gear down early to make sure no further issues or status/EICAS messages were present.  We received AIR/GND SYS on the EICAS upon putting the landing gear down.  In anticipation; we previously referenced the AIR/GND SYS checklist and had already prepared for non-normal landing distance and any configuration differences.  We accomplished the landing checklist while configuring early and landed with no issues.Of note; approximately 50-40ft above touchdown; we did notice the aircraft loose airspeed and drop unexpectedly to which the FO added slight power to arrest the descent due overweight landing considerations.  I briefed a shallow touchdown due to overweight landing as a threat and to use the entire runway for braking.  We landed and stopped turning off at taxiway 1 with no issues using minimal braking.  No emergency was declared.My decision to air return was based on several considerations; mostly unknown conditions from the air/gnd computer with bad weather in the islands.  The FO was excellent in executing the air return as the PF allowing me to coordinate the divert with no issues.

column121: The SFO VOR has been NOTAMed out of service for a while and will continue to be due to construction. Because of this; there are also NOTAMs for alternate missed approach instructions for ILS 28L and ILS 28R.In my experience; very few pilots are briefing these or even know they exist - because thoroughly reviewing NOTAMs is not one of our strong suits. This is partially the fault of the pilots; but primarily the fault of the system. There are way too many NOTAMs; many of which are irrelevant to pilots; and they aren't sorted at all. Today there are 66 active NOTAMs (5 pages) for SFO; and the majority of them are about construction cranes. It's no wonder people miss the important ones.So how can we make this easier; specifically in SFO?I suggest modifying these two NOTAMs so they say right at the top applies only to non-RNAV aircraft" or equivalent. Every jet landing at SFO is capable of using RNAV as a primary means of navigation in the terminal area. Why are we briefing (or not briefing; as is usually the case) some alternate procedure when we are fully capable of flying the published procedure even with the VOR out of service? Furthermore; I bet if a jet actually flew the alternate procedure in accordance with the NOTAM; ATC might be surprised because they're not expecting that.Please forward this to the responsible people in ATC. Let's work together to simplify things where possible. Make these two NOTAMs apply only to non-RNAV aircraft."

column121: We were about 30 miles from destination ZZZ we were descending through 6000ft spoilers were fully deployed and engines were at idle speed was around 230kts. When I looked at the speed I wanted 250 until 10nm from destination so I slowly brought in power. This was first sign of a problem. We got a weird fluttering noise. Brought power back.. I looked at the other pilot said that's not right. I proceeded to stow the spoilers to see if they had anything to do with the noise but they did not. The I slowly added engine power same noise. Back to idle. Then I added power on the number 2 engine no noise power smooth. Next I added power to number 1 engine and it made a lot of noise like a helicopter. At that moment I smelled oil in the cabin. I looked all the engine parameters and both engines in the green and matched up. I then made a decision having the runway in sight and a good number 2 engine to shut number 1 down as to avoid fire or damage . I told Person A to use the fuel cut off. column121: This was the last leg of a 4-day trip. Boarding was normal. We were completely full plus a Company X Pilot in the cockpit jumpseat. We were cleared for takeoff full length on runway XXL at approximately XA:06 UTC. We were cleared on the ZZZZZX RNAV departure out of ZZZ. Takeoff was normal. We were instructed to contact ZZZ departure at approximately 1000 ft AGL. I checked in with ZZZ departure; the controller instructed us to climb to 5;000 ft. As I was replying to that instruction I received a call from the cabin. I answered the call and the purser alerted me that they may have a fire in the cabin. The forward galley was filing with smoke and it appeared that it was coming out of one of the ovens in the forward galley. I told the captain what was going on in the cabin. At that time we began smelling a strong acrid odor as well as seeing a haze of smoke in the cockpit. The captain; myself and the jumpseater all donned our oxygen masks and established crew communications. The captain told me that they wanted to return to ZZZ immediately. I alerted ATC that we would like to stop our climb at 5000 and we would probably be heading back to ZZZ. ATC gave us a 280 heading to put us on a downwind for runway XXL and began giving us a descent to 4000 feet. As we leveled at 4000 feet we received an Off Schedule Descent light.I pulled the QRC down from the glare shield and looked at the immediate action items for Smoke/Fire/Fumes. I saw that we had already accomplished the steps of donning our oxygen masks and establishing crew communications. I pulled out the QRH from my side of the pedestal and was about to go to the fire protection section as it was the next step from the QRC but was distracted by the purser calling up from the back. She confirmed that the smoke was coming from the oven. She told me that she didn't want to open the door of the oven. She was afraid that it would make it worse. She told me that she shut the ovens off but there was still a lot of smoke coming out.  I instructed her to pull the circuit breakers for both ovens in the forward galley. We continued to receive transmissions from ATC. They wanted to know what the issue was; souls and fuel onboard. it was at this time that we received priority handling with ATC.At the captains direction; I began setting up the FMC for the ILS XXL at ZZZ. I loaded the approach; set the ILS frequencies and minimums. I also loaded VREF and target speeds for landing. The purser called up front again. I answered and was told that the smoke was starting to dissipate. I told them we were heading back to ZZZ and we would be on the ground shortly. I told the captain that the smoke was dissipating in the back. We noticed that we did not have the acrid odor or smoke in the cockpit anymore either. We decided it was safe to remove our oxygen masks. We had some issues communicating with each other. I remembered to close the oxygen mask door and test it on my side to return the audio to normal. I failed to remind the captain of this and they continued to have some issues with communication that I wasn't aware of at the time. I pulled up the divert page on the ACARS portion of the FMC and told the captain that I was going to send a divert notice to dispatch. I glanced over the page briefly and thought that I pressed the send button. I later found out that dispatch didn't know about the divert. So I either didn't press the button hard enough or it didn't go through. I began going into the ACARS section to get landing data as I knew we were overweight landing back at ZZZ. I typed in 161.0 for our landing weight and XXL for the runway and pressed send. I didn't see until we were on short final that I received an error for our landing data. I believe that I didn't enter ZZZ as our landing airport. The landing data page defaulted to ZZZ1 for the landing airport and the error was because there isn't a XXL runway at ZZZ1. At this point we were on downwind for XXL. The captain transferred the controls to me and they briefed the approach. I believe at this time the captain also made an announcement to the passengers. I transferred the controls back to the captain. ATC began turning us on a base leg and descending us further. The captain began to call for flaps and the gear down. We were given one more turn and then cleared for the ILS XXL. I pulled out the checklist and accomplished the descent checklist and after we were fully configured for landing I accomplished the landing checklist. When we were on short final I received the error for the landing data. I showed it to the captain. I can't remember if the captain acknowledged it or not. The captain later told me that they felt we had plenty of runway for landing considering the headwind and dry runway conditions.The landing was normal and uneventful. We cleared the runway to the right at taxiway 1. There was ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting ) equipment that was waiting for us as we cleared the runway. They followed us to the gate. I spoke to them on the frequency at one point and they told me that they would be on the jet bridge as we pulled in to make sure the fire in the oven was contained. There was about a 5 minute delay holding short of the gate as we waited for a ramp crew to guide us in. Parking and shutdown was normal. The captain called the fight attendants and instructed them to disarm the L1 door and allow the firefighter on the aircraft to look at the oven. We deplaned the passengers and our maintenance crew came out to look at the write-up for the smoke coming out of the oven as well as the overweight landing. Maintenance determined that there was a lot of grease all over the top of the foil on many of the meals. They think that the grease dripping off of the foil on our takeoff roll and climb out caused the smoke event.
column123: Climbing through 3000 the purser called reporting smoke in the cabin. She said it was either coming from the oven or behind the oven. Looking at the flight deck door camera we could only see solid white since the smoke was rising to cover the camera. At this point smoke began entering the flight deck so I commanded oxygen masks on and had the FO requested priority handling with ATC. I requested an immediate return to the airport. We were given a left downwind vector and subsequent turn to base. The flaps were already at 1 and I began configuring. Brakes were selected to 3 and an abbreviated descent check was completed to include speeds and gust factor. The purser at some point in this called to say the smoke was slowing down after they had turned the oven off and pulled the circuit breaker. I made the decision to continue our quick return rather than diving deeper into the smoke checklist. I made a quick announcement to the pax (Passengers) as to the plan of action and what to expect when we landed. My concern was that there was a fire that couldn't be seen and could reignite. Rescue vehicles were dispatched and followed us to the gate where fire personnel boarded the aircraft and used thermal imaging to make sure all was okay. The oven was taken out of service and an overweight landing inspection was completed. We departed again about 2 hours late with an uneventful flight to ZZZ1. As for TEM (Threat and Error Management) during the air return; VVM (Verbalize; Verify; Monitor) was done to the best we could with the challenge of oxygen mask use. Someone was always flying the plane. If I had the event to do over once I heard the smoke was decreasing I would have asked for a delay on the approach to readdress the smoke checklist. Everything was conducted safely but was more rushed than it ultimately needed to be with the smoke decreasing. I think total flight time was 12 minutes. It was a definite learning experience and has put additional tools in my 'toolkit'.

column121: Be advised; the crew got to the aircraft and it was extremely Hot. The station indicated that the jet bridge air was hooked up and turned on WIDEBODY. This will not help IF THE battery switch is OFF AND NO ground power is established on the aircraft. I got 2nd secondary screened and my luggage was run through the scanner TWICE and so by the time I got to the gate it was 5 minutes past board. The First officer halted boarding because it was too hot and we needed to cool the cabin off. They remarked the Battery switch was OFF; no Ground power and it was hot. They told the flight attendants that I would be down in a minute to assist. We were negative APU; NO ground power; NO battery ON and Maintenance deferred it that night; meaning they knew. OBVIOUSLY NO COMMUNICATION at all at this station. I had the flight attendants open doors to start circulation and RADIO coordinated with ops (Operations) and the ground handlers to get the AIR START AIR hooked up so I could cool off the cabin using the aircraft PACKS and begin loading. I performed the walk-around; the first officer handled the inside of the aircraft. I was met by an ops supervisor and I explained what I needed as we walked around the aircraft; I asked if he understood; he said yes. While downstairs under the aircraft I briefed the LEAD ground handler as well as the supervisor that we would require the air start cart for Starting ENGINE #1 on this Aircraft. And cooling the aircraft. I went so far to walk over the LEAD and showed him on the AIR START CART the various switch positions; ONE for PACKS usage and one for ENGINE START. I asked him if he understood; he said yes. I continued my walk around and noticed the lead hooked up the air start hose with a major kink in the hose. As they started air; the air cart relief valve kept popping air the air was blocked from entering the aircraft and the packs. (This will play out again) The lead untangled it slightly and the PACKS received air and were used for cooling. I got back upstairs; the purser thanked me for the help and remarked it was already cooling. I asked her to shut the open doors 1R and 2L and we began boarding at XA:40 for an XB:00 departure; not good. AS we were loading up another ground handler asked if he could disconnect power several times; I called OPS again requested that a supervisor intervene and talk to ALL the guys below the wing and I AGAIN explained to her (OPS AGENT) that we have to leave the POWER connected; start #1 ENGINE;  disconnect the power and pull off the jetway. I told her to send a supervisor out to brief everyone AGAIN; I was falling behind in MY DUTIES.I used communication and coordinated with everyone in the operation and I received ZERO support from OPS; LEADS; Supervisors and baggage handlers and I repeated myself several times. We need to look at this incident and make adjustments. Early flights are not just the FLIGHT crews responsibility; it's everyone's. As we attempted to start the #1 ENGINE; the ground handler switch to engine start mode; we attempted an ENGINE start and not enough air pressure; I told the guy in the head set that the engine will not start with a kink in the hose; he finally untangled it ALL THE WAY; and we got the pressure we needed for an engine start.We pushed @ XB:12 and arrived to LAX 5 minutes late after I bumped up the CI (Cost Index); and reported everything to dispatch. After departing AUS and getting established in level flight I read up on gate notes at LAX for gate XX and noted a larger than 90 degree turn to get aligned with gate from taxiway C. Meaning both engines running to limit engine blast in the turn. I then contacted dispatch and ask if they would advise LAX that we were coming with NO APU and we would need Ground power and an AIR START cart. I even stated in the note ENGINE #1 will be running until we get ground power hooked up. Then I sent a station note indicating the same thing. I got acknowledgments back from both parties In level flight; the FO and I reviewed what occurred in AUSTIN before departure and talked it through. I had an uneasy feeling about LAX but pressed on; SURELY everyone communicated with everyone; RIGHT?We arrived in LAX and received taxi instructions to the gate via B C5 C which meant a right turn beyond 90 degrees for gate line up. I made another announcement to the passengers to REMAIN SEATED until the seat belt sign was extinguished. As I began the turn BOTH ENGINES were running to minimize jet blast for this maneuver. I got the aircraft aligned began a slow taxi in; approximately 40' from the gate stop. I instructed to FO to shutdown engine #2. Again I had a weird feeling. They did; I continued my approach and came to a stop.I set the brakes and looked around at the ground crew; mass confusion was occurring below the wing; the ground handler would not allow the jetway to approach the aircraft because #1 ENGINE was still running. NO ONE KNEW WHY IT WAS STILL RUNNING. I opened the window and explained to the ground handler that we had NO APU and need ground power before I shut down the engine. The engine noise was too loud. I indicated he needed to get on a headset and called OPS again. JUST THEN I NOTICED A FWD CARGO light went on. They were opening doors before the engine was shutdown and the aircraft secured. Surely this is a mistake I used priority communication behavior... RIGHT? The lead ground handler ran over and told the baggage handler to close the door again. I called OPS and explained that I coordinated this with several folks before my arrival; the OPS folks said they communicated it to ramp; and they acted like it's OPS NORMAL. NOT GOOD!!A portable ground power cart was used on the right side of the aircraft; normally the jetway pulls up; the ground guys hook up ground power and I shut the engine down. I have done well over 100 NO APU OPERATIONS. This was by far the worst! DANGEROUS!! After some confusion; the guys hooked up the portable ground power and we finally shut the engine down 10 minutes later!! This was very dangerous; in fact my messages to DISPATCH and LAX STATION utilized that word. Prior I have never used that word; I had a feeling this was poor communication from the start. I extinguish the SEAT BELT sign made an announcement to the passengers and thanked them for their patience. I deplaned; talk to the gate agent and asked why he didn't drive the jetway up to the aircraft; he explained the ground lead told him NOT too. Because the number 1 engine was running. Again; I could have killed that baggage handler. Let's be very clear about that...  After all checklists were done; I sent  the dispatcher a note and indicated LAX... WAS NOT READY FOR US... MESS AND DANGEROUS". His reply... "THATS NOT GOOD AT ALL MAYBE WORTH FILING SOMETHING"Because the door was OPENED BY RAMP before the engine was shutdown; the OOOI (Out-Off-On-In) time are incorrect."

column121: Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1. Normal boarding and pre-departure checks. Pushback and started engine 2 at XA:08. Due to flow metering into ZZZ1; waited to start engine 1 at XA:27. No abnormal engine indications on startup or during taxi. Both engines had 8 minutes of warmup time and oil pressure/temperature/vibrations within limits before taking the runway. Flight OFF at XA:35. No abnormal indications during climb phase or cruise phase until approx XB:12 at FL340. At XB:12; an audible bang could be heard from the flight deck and cabin; followed by vibrations and a left yawing moment. EICAS indicated N1 decreasing to approx 22% with ENG1 OUT caution message. After confirming with the PM/CA verbally that I would be the Pilot Flying and that I had controls; the PM/CA immediately began consulting ENGINE 1(2) out QRH. To start the APU in accordance with this procedure; PM/CA requested priority handling and requested a descent to FL280. Once below FL300; the APU was started. An engine restart was considered. An additional descent to FL240 was requested and the APU-assisted engine restart procedure according to the QRH  was attempted once below FL250. The engine restart was unsuccessful. After coordination with dispatch via ACARS and air traffic control; a decision was made to turn right direct to ZZZ2 for diversion and continue descent. The flight attendant was briefed on special procedures according to company SOP and PM/CA turned the fasten seatbelt sign on and provided an announcement to the passengers regarding the requirement to divert to ZZZ2. Inflight Engine Shutdown QRH was completed for Engine 1. One Engine Inoperative Approach and Landing Procedure QRH was completed. Landing speeds and landing distances were calculated for ZZZ2 XXL according to QRH. We confirmed that the aircraft would be under max landing weight. A single engine approach briefing was given by the PM/CA. ATC provided delay vectors for an extended right downwind for a visual to ZZZ2 XXL to coordinate airport services to follow the aircraft after landing and for us to complete the approach checklist and one engine inoperative go around procedure. We then requested a right turn to join the ILS XXL (in lieu of a visual approach). ATC cleared us for ILS XXL approximately 9nm beyond the FAF for the approach. At 3nm from the FAF; the QRH landing checklist was completed to fully configure the aircraft. The autopilot was disconnected approximately 1nm from the FAF and the ILS XXL was hand flown to a normal landing. The after landing checklist was completed. We taxied to the gate; shut down the aircraft; and completed the parking checklist. We consulted airport services and airport operations and began appropriate company reports regarding the incident. A post flight walk around was conducted and found no obvious damage to the aircraft exterior; nor the cowlings; intake fan blades; or exhaust section of Engine 1.
column123: The flight began as normal. Pushed back in ZZZ; started engine number 2 and then engine number 1 about 10-15 minutes later. No abnormal indications during either engine start. We took off normally and climbed up to our cruising altitude of FL340 as normally. During cruise at FL340; about 45 minutes after starting the number 1 engine (based on a timer started at engine start); we heard a loud thud and felt a large jolt and then immediate pull to left. We looked at the EICAS and saw that engine number 1's N1; N2; and Fuel flow were all decreasing rapidly. The N1 stabilized at approx. 25%. N2 and fuel flow dropped to 0% and 0PPH. Followed shortly after was the EICAS caution msg 'E1 OUT' add some associated msgs like shed busses off bus. It was verbalized by both of us that the number 1 engine had failed and rolled back. I then pulled out the QRH and started turning to E1 OUT QRH. The FO was the pilot flying and I restated verbally that he had the controls and he acknowledged. I then began running the ENGINE OUT QRH. ''The QRH directed us to start the APU. At this point; we needed to descend so I called ATC on the radio and requested priority handling and requested a descent to FL280 in order to be low enough for an APU start. After passing below FL300; I continued with the QRH by starting the APU. When reaching the section that asks us to consider a restart; we both looked closely at the MFD systems pages and the EICAS engine instruments to determine if there was any obvious reason for the failure. We could find no indication that was abnormal or expected. The oil quantity was showing 10 qts and all other indications were normal. (the E1 fuel flow and oil pressure were 0 due to the failed engine and I considered them expected). We decide that we would attempt a restart and then followed the QRH reference to the Inflight Restart Procedure. Before attempting the restart; we descended to FL 240. We followed Engine Airstart for an APU assisted start. Engine failed to start with no N2 rotation. We then finished the QRH and then decided to divert to ZZZ2 (as we were nearby). This decision was confirmed with Dispatch via to ACARS and they agreed. ATC was informed and we were given vectors towards the airport. We then continued with the Engine Failure/Shutdown normally. I then informed the flight attendant and gave her a special procedures briefing informing her of the issue and plan to divert. We then set up and briefed the ILS XXL at ZZZ2 and I ran performance numbers for the landing. We made sure the aircraft was under max landing weight. After Setting up and briefing the approach; we then ran the One Engine inoperative approach and landing procedure. At this point the flight was mostly uneventful. I asked ATC to have the emergency equipment ready for us just in case. The FO performed the landing and we then taxied to the gate.  A post flight walk around was accomplished and we found no obvious signs of damage to the aircraft or engine.

column121: On Day 0 Aircraft X had a Main and a Back up trim failure during the initial climb out. Flight crew got to the aircraft at the scheduled time of XA:30 in the morning. A GPU was not available for the initial start up of the APU. Started the APU soon arriving at the aircraft. Had PAXs and cockpit ready to go at XB:10. Was given a EDT time of XB:45 local. I chose to stay at the gate and only run the APU. At XB:35 I gave the order for a push back. Now running 20 minutes late. Started both engines and was at the RWY XXL at XB:40. At XB:46ish was given clearance to take off. Gave the control to the first officer for his takeoff. Takeoff was normal and uneventful. Climb check was complete and was handed off to departure. Climb through 4;000ft we got an EICAS message of PTRIM Main INOP fallowed by PTRIM Backup INOP. ATC had just cleared us to FL230. I said the FO let stop the climb and go down to 4;000ft. FO said we have to go back to the field. I agreed and said maintain 4;000Ft and will get radar vectors (RV) and set up for the ZZZ ILS XXR approach. I called approach and said we have an issue and will need to stay at 4;000ft and RV for the ILS XXR approach. Dispatch ACARS us asking us if we were OK. I ignored the message. I had to keep it simple and Aviate; Navigate and Communicate.ZZZ1 Approach was very helpful and wanted to give us RV directly right to the ILS XXR. I requested delay RVs to burn gas; run through a check list (QRH) and set up for the approach.  Approach gave us 3-4 more RV as I figured the weight of the AC; got Vspeed numbers; set up the approach in the FMS and on the flight panel. I quickly briefed the approach. All during this time Dispatch was trying to get a hold of me via ACARS. I gave back to two quick replies about my intentions. The 2 replies to dispatch came in between a call to the FA and announcement to the passengers. Due to time and  the quickness of situation I did not use the full special procedures. Basically; I said we were returning to ZZZ due to mechanical issues. The landing will be normal.For the final RV to final I took the controls and had the FO give me back pressure on the yoke. I brief the FO he would be my trim by providing back pressure on the yoke as needed by my verbal commands. This worked out well and I have to commend my FO. He did a great job. The approach was good and straight down the pipe. Landing was smooth as butter. Touchdown at 1200-1400FT down the RWY. I got the AC stopped and turned off the RWY by taxi way 1". Received a taxi clearance from tower to cross RWY XXR and taxi via taxiway "2" and Taxiway 3 to the gate.  Passed by the fire truck that had been rolled for us and gave them a thumbs up and a friendly wave.Upon reaching the gate the rampers guided us in to a stop. Did the nominal parking flow. The rampers said there was no gate agents at the gate. So I made announcement to the passengers "to please remain seated until we can get a gate agents. " 10 minutes later the gate agents showed up. Then were able to deplane all of the PAXs normally. I stood by the cockpit door said to each passenger thank you for your patience and sorry for the inconvenience.After once the passengers were off of the airplane and were working with the gate agent on rebooking. I started making phone calls. I called dispatch and then maintenance for the write up of the Main and Backup pitch trim.  Also called the Chief Pilot to cover all my bases."

column121: On initial climbout from ZZZ RWYXXC at approximately 3;000 FT MSL the purser called the flight deck to alert the Captain that there was a 'large amount' of black smoke coming from the oven at a flight station. For the duration of the entire event I was not in communication with the back of the aircraft. At this time the Captain was hand flying the aircraft to 5;000 feet and I was PM. ATC gave us an initial vector and a climb to 15;000 feet; I read back the clearance but delayed input into the control panel for concurrence with the Captain. We decided to call back and request priority handling and request vectors to land back at ZZZ. At this time we split duties with the FO flying the aircraft and handling ATC; Captain ran the Fire Protection checklist. Received short vectors back to land RWYXXL. The Captain loaded the ILS XXL into the FMC for a back up to the visual and then continued to run the non normal checklist. I called the airfield in sight at approximately 9 miles. A faster than normal airspeed was flown while turning onto final due to the unknown status of the galley fire. No ILS frequencies were tuned and the FMC was not re-cruised to our current altitude. Flight directors were ignored and the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) was referenced for runway alignment verification. Gear and flaps were dropped to 30 on speed to be configured at approximately 700 feet AGL. Normal flare and touchdown was made for an overweight landing; on landing rollout is when I noticed that we had not selected an autobrake setting. Manual braking was used to slow down and vacate the runway at the last high speed taxiway. Crash Fire Rescue met the aircraft right after vacating the active runway and we taxied on Taxiway 1 to hold short of runway XYR.  At this time we slowed down and verified all appropriate checklist were completed and passengers were seated. We communicated with operations for a gate and taxied back to gate XX with no further issues.
column123: I was PF and my FO was PM. Shortly after takeoff and climbing through approximately 3000MSL; we received a call from the cabin. I took the call while my FO answered a call from departure to continue the climb. The lead FA said black smoke was emanating from one of the forward galley ovens. We noticed a burning smell in the flight deck and executed immediate action items. We did not observe smoke in the flight deck and did not don O2 masks. Instead of continuing the climb; we leveled off at 5000 while my FO referenced the QRC. Departure queried us about the climb and instead we requested priority handling. My FO supplied departure with Souls on Board and fuel. I failed to remind him to include information about the hazmat we had on board. After referencing the QRC; I gave flying pilot and normal ATC duties to my FO while I referenced the QRH for Smoke; Fire or Fumes. I began running that checklist and in the process called the lead FA back to brief her; as well as send a message to dispatch. The lead FA said she would make a PA to the passengers. ZZZ approach asked us if we had a runway preference; and considering that we did not have any aircraft performance issues; I suggested any runway; not thinking about the fact that we were over maximum structural landing weight. As we were vectored onto final for rwy XXL; I was only about half way done with the Smoke Fire Fumes QRH and decided I didn't have the time to finish prior to landing. To this point; my FO had masterfully piloted the aircraft and communicated with approach back to the airport. I abandoned the QRH and began setting up the FMC for the approach. I entered the ILS for runway XXL and sequenced the box; but failed to re-cruise it. I selected V ref and target for flaps 30; but failed to select an autobrakes setting. By this point my FO was hand flying on final and calling for appropriate flaps. Unable to select approach mode or vnav; my FO verified the correct runway from the magenta line and continued the approach entirely visually without vertical guidance. In the compressed time; we got on short final before final configuration. I suggested to my FO to level off to bleed off speed in order to fully configure prior to continuing the descent. I don't know if we were configured prior to 1000 AGL; but we were stable prior to 500 AGL. The flair; touchdown and rollout were textbook excellent; as my FO applied manual brakes to exit the runway. We taxied off the runway with Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) following; and stopped to assess; coordinate with the FA and call ops. The lead FA notified us that the smoke had stopped and the fumes were dissipating. We received a gate assignment and taxied with ARFF following us to the gate uneventfully.

column121: During climb; the #1 [FA] called and said that they smelled an electrical odor in the forward galley; near the R1 door. I sent the FO back to check. He returned and said that he wasn't certain; but the floor near the door felt hot. I was about to call back to ask the FAs if that was normal when they called up again to say that the floor material was melting. We were just about to level at FL350 approaching ZZZ [VOR]. I asked the FO to request priority and ask for a return to ZZZ. While he had been in the cabin; I looked for nearest airports and determined that the closest large airport was ZZZ. If the FAs had said that there was smoke; I would have dropped into ZZZ1 as I know they do have airline service and a long enough runway to stop. Gave the plane to the FO and he got the plane going to ZZZ at a high speed. About halfway back I called back to see how things were going; the #1 said that the area was growing but still no smoke. I discussed that we were going to stop on the runway to be checked out and that I hoped we wouldn't need to evacuate but to listen if I called for that. She agreed that we didn't want to evacuate but would be ready and would let me know if she saw any reason to do so. ATC gave us as direct of a routing as they could with the mountains and we proceeded to XXR. Informed ATC that we would be stopping on the runway. After we stopped; ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) came to check us out; they saw a heat signature in the R1 door area- not blistering paint or any sign of an active fire so they asked us to proceed to the gate so they could check from inside. Coming inside; the burn area was still showing about 107 degrees. They looked inside the cargo compartment and the E&E (Electronics and Equipment bay) area and saw no damage. The circles over the right side of the floor heating pad had disappeared by the time we landed. We deplaned using the L1 door after we determined that it was safe to do so.Cause: Don't know why the pad decided to overheat. There is NO circuit breaker information. I was fairly certain that it was the heating pad overheating but I could not find someway to turn off the power to the unit. With an electric jet I don't want to be pulling breakers without any information as to what they control. However; after the turn to ZZZ; if a fire had broken out I think I would have started to pull anything that sounded like galley power. A little more info about things that can catch on fire in the plane would be nice.

Approximately 5 miles outside of the FAF; ATC asked us to look for traffic on final for runway XX and cleared us for a visual approach to runway XYR. At the time we were still at 5000 ft. In an effort to avoid and TCAS message we decreased our intercept angle slightly which then had us intercepting after the FAF. We selected a lower altitude of 1000ft to assist in descending and intercepting the glide slope. We were configured prior to the 1000ft callout. However due to task saturation and fatigue (simply from the time of day) both pilots missed that the aircraft had now descended below the glide slope; in an effort to regain the glide slope autopilot was turned off; we leveled off to reintercept the appropriate glide slope The aircraft continued on a visual approach however multiple glide slope advisory's were issued as we had decended to full scale deflection of the glide slope. Glide slope was eventually captured and the approach continued to a landing. Given the tight vectors and high altitude with the parallel traffic the work load got very high very quickly; a go around; even a soft go around when we knew we were just too high would have been appropriate to mitigate the risks associated with getting below glide slope.

column121: The entire length of the flight was 10 minutes in duration. Shortly after engaging the autopilot after takeoff from ZZZ; the yoke rapidly began violently pitching the plane forward and back suddenly. We previously had been experiencing unexplained issues with the autopilot including but not limited to: failure to capture localizer course; flight directors disappearing; red elevator trim annunciations necessitating the disconnecting of autopilot and trimming manually. I disconnected the autopilot; and the uncommanded pitch ceased. Minutes later; ZZZ [TRACON] control instructed me to fly direct ZZZZZ descend and maintain 2000 for the RNAV XX into ZZZ1. The autopilot at this time was engaged in Nav/Vnav mode and 2000 was preselected in the altitude selector. What had occurred was the autopilot did not capture the altitude; instead descending below it. Rather than disconnecting immediately and maintaining my assigned altitude manually like I should have; I was late to react appropriately to the error and attempted to rectify the issue using the abnormally behaving automation; all the while the aircraft continued its rapid descent. We were several hundred feet below our assigned altitude before I disconnected and began climbing back to 2000. I then hand-flew the rest of the approach; landing on runway XX. There were no terrain or traffic alerts. I understand had the circumstances been different this could have been a fatal mistake; and I regret the actions I took. I should have taken control immediately upon discovering the deviation instead of trying to diagnose the problem. I am thankful that no other aircraft were affected.
column123: The entire length of the flight was 10 min in duration from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Shortly after takeoff from ZZZ; the yoke rapidly began violently pitching the plane forward and back suddenly. We previously had been experiencing unusual issues with the autopilot including but not limited to: failure to capture localizer course; flight director disappearing; red elevator trim annunciations necessitating the disconnecting of autopilot and trimming manually. As pilot not flying on this flight; I was managing the radios and the FMS programming. My FMS keyboard backlight was not working too well; making it extremely difficult to see and type inputs correctly in the darkness of the night. We were cleared to cross ZZZZZ at 2000 for the ZZZ1 RNAV XX. 2000 was set in the altitude preselector and the autopilot was engaged in Nav/Vnav mode. I executed direct ZZZZZ on the FMS and remained heads down working on the approach performance for the aircraft using ATIS information. When I looked back up; the aircraft had continued its descent below 2000 prior to ZZZZZ. The pilot flying disconnected the autopilot; regained the missing altitude; and the rest of the approach and landing was completed without the use of autopilot

column121: We cancelled IFR with ZZZ approach; about 5 NM from RWYXX. Flew offset to north of runway XX; followed the local entry procedure; intending to enter the traffic pattern (left traffic) for RWYXX. We turned crosswind and flew above the DER at 2200ft MSL; 500ft above the traffic pattern altitude; intending to make the teardrop entry at 45-degree angle (given the existence of multiple airplanes in the pattern/vicinity of the airport; we avoided a direct entry). After the frequency change approval from ZZZ approach; we have been announcing our location and intention via CTAF when off-setting to north; turning crosswind; starting the teardrop; joining downwind; base; and final at CTAF frequency. We are sure that we tuned into the correct frequency as we heard the preceding aircraft (Barron) communicating over CTAF as well. When we were descending while in the tear drop; and joining to the downwind at 45-degree angle; we noticed an aircraft turning into the downwind; in our ADSB; about 100 feet below us; which made no radio call. At that time; it was about 500ft horizontal distance; I think. I asked my student; who is flying; to maintain the altitude and even slightly climb; to ensure we won't descend to the same altitude; and asked him if he could visually see the aircraft. He saw it below and behind us (abut 7 o'clock direction; in line with our ADSB screen). We flew the downwind faster at around 100knots; to ensure we have enough distance horizontally before descending for the base turn. We confirmed that we have made enough distance and turned/descended to base; final turns; and landed safely. We have been monitoring the distance with the aircraft behind us that seems to have slowed down to secure the distance as well. We did not check the tail number for that aircraft but noticed that it seems an old; vintage aircraft (single-engine); and also noticed that their radio calls after we took the above evasive actions. Their ADSB seemed sporadic and not consistently shown in our screen; unlike other aircraft that have been shown continually. We assume they might have had an incorrect CTAF frequency at the beginning.

column121: While holding short of Runway XXR at Taxiway 1 at ZZZ Airport; I received a transmission that included flight following information (remain clear of Class B airspace; a departure frequency; and a discrete transponder code). At the time; I believed I was on the appropriate frequency for departure. Due to the high traffic volume; extended delay prior to taxi; and my position at the hold short line ready for departure; I misinterpreted this transmission and believed it was a takeoff clearance.I read back: 'cleared for takeoff Runway XXR; remain clear of the ZZZ1 Class Bravo; departure frequency; and squawk code.' The controller responded with 'readback correct.' I interpreted this as confirmation and believed it was a takeoff clearance. Believing I was cleared; I visually checked final approach and did not observe any traffic on final; and observed a Cirrus holding short at Taxiway 2 (full length); which I believed was the aircraft I had heard waiting for an IFR clearance to ZZZ2. I then entered Runway XXR from Taxiway 1. An aircraft was still on the runway but in the process of exiting; and after it cleared the runway; I started my takeoff roll.Sometime during the takeoff roll; I heard 'monitor tower;' which led me to recognize that I may not have been on the correct frequency or had not received a valid takeoff clearance. Around liftoff; I attempted to contact tower on the assigned frequency (XXX.X) but did not receive a response and then switched to the other tower frequency (XXX.XX) to establish communication. During this time; I heard another aircraft execute a go-around. I adjusted my climb profile by shallowing the climb to reduce the risk of conflict but still maintain a safe distance above the ground.The problem arose from a misinterpretation of flight following information as a takeoff clearance. I believe some of the contributing factors included high workload due to traffic volume; frequency congestion; extended ground delay leading to expectation bias; and the similarity in cadence between the transmission and a takeoff clearance. Receiving the flight following information while holding short of the runway; in a position normally associated with an imminent departure clearance; likely increased expectation bias and contributed to the misinterpretation. Additionally; in busy environments it is common for flight following to be delayed or unavailable; and because no earlier indication was given that flight following would be issued later; I did not anticipate receiving it at that point; which likely contributed to the confusion. My perception that I was on the appropriate frequency and ready for departure influenced my judgment and decision-making. The issue was discovered when I heard 'monitor tower' during the takeoff roll; which prompted immediate recognition of a discrepancy.Corrective actions included attempting to establish communication with tower; switching frequencies when necessary; and modifying my climb profile to maintain safe separation from other aircraft. No further conflict developed.To prevent recurrence; I will ensure I'm on the correct frequency prior to departure and will positively verify that an explicit takeoff clearance has been received from tower before entering the runway. I will also deliberately pause at the hold short line; particularly in high workload environments; to confirm clearance and reduce the effects of expectation bias.

After establishing radar contact; Aircraft Y reported a scary close call with another aircraft approximately 400 feet from his position. I didn't see a primary anywhere in close proximity to Aircraft Y. I issued traffic advisories for the only aircraft observed in the area but both were well above Aircraft Y and on my frequency. Aircraft Y indicated the conflicting aircraft was talking with ZZZ [Tower]. I advised that we would coordinate with ZZZ [Tower] to see what was out there.Shortly thereafter; Aircraft X contacted me just outside ZZZs Class D airspace. I issued a discrete code. The pilot reported a position southwest of ZZZ and stated he did not have a transponder. I instructed the aircraft to remain clear of the ZZZ1 Class B airspace.Based on the pilots position; timing; and degraded radio quality; I suspected Aircraft X may have been the aircraft referenced by Aircraft Y. I did not ever call him radar contact due to the lack of a transponder and only an intermittent primary target. I told Aircraft X to exit the ZZZ1 Class B Mode C veil due to operating without a transponder. The pilot objected; stating he had a right to be there because he doesn't have a generator. I asked for his altitude and relayed that information to the next sector for traffic awareness. He flew NW bound through the veil until NW of ZZZ2 field when I briefed the next controller.After being relieved from position; I reviewed the AIM regarding operations within the Mode C veil with the supervisor. The AIM notes that certain older aircraft not originally equipped with certain equipment may be permitted to operate without one but it also indicates that aircraft intending to operate within the Mode C veil without a transponder are expected to coordinate with ATC in advance to ensure situational awareness and safety. Further review of 14 CFR  91.215 says that operations within the Mode C veil generally require an operable transponder; with limited exceptions outlined in  91.215(b)(3) for certain aircraft not originally equipped with the required systems. Additionally;  91.215(d) requires prior ATC authorization for deviations from transponder requirements when applicable.Regardless if the exception applies to him; the lack of coordination reduced our ability to provide traffic advisories and maintain situational awareness. I believe that operations within the Mode C veil without a transponder and without prior coordination increases the risk of potential unsafe situations.  Aircraft intending to operate in the Mode C veil without a transponder should coordinate with ATC in advance to prevent unsafe situations EVEN IF they are allowed to be there due to equipment limitations.  ZZZ [Tower] could have coordinated with us about the aircraft with equipment issues or no transponder.  Somehow; we need to reinforce pilot understanding about how potentially unsafe this would be operating in the veil without coordination.

Winds were variable according to the ATIS. At approximately 700 ft I disengaged the autopilot once I believe the managed thrust had properly adjusted for the winds. At approximately 650 ft I observed a tailwind on the display. I adjusted to a more nose down attitude in order to keep the aircraft from landing long with the tailwind. At 500 ft the aircraft and PM announced '500 Feet' and I responded 'stable' referencing my airspeed on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). When I referenced the PFD at 500 ft for speed; I noticed the wind had shifted from a tailwind to a crosswind. In order to correct my previous tailwind inputs; I shallowed my pitch inputs inside of 500 ft to maintain my aim point.At the 50 ft automated callout I remembered I had previously briefed I would keep the thrust in longer than normal due to the high; hot; heavy conditions. However; I do not remember exactly when I began my thrust reduction. At 30 feet I started my flare but noticed the controls were not as responsive as I was accustomed to on other landings because the airspeed had slowly decayed prior to my flare input. The following events happened in very quick succession. The aircraft bounced; I heard an automated 'pitch' annunciation; the PM said 'continue' ( or something similar); and I flew the nose wheel to the ground and simultaneously engaged the thrust reversers. It was definitely a startle event because of the firm bounce and by the time the thought of 'go-around' entered my mind I was already flying the nose wheel to the ground.We exited the runway and pulled into a de-ice pad while we waited for parking. After providing the flights attendants and passengers an update on our gate; the PM told me what he saw and experienced. We taxied to the gate and conducted a more thorough debrief using the crew debrief card. The Captain conducted a walk around of the aircraft after we pulled into the gate and I began preparing for the following flight. After the box was prepared for the following flight; I conducted a walk around to visually inspect the aircraft before the following flight.

A decision was made to proceed directly to ZZZ1 and execute a straight-in approach to the nearest suitable runway equipped with PAPI for visual glide path guidance. Runway XX was selected based on prior departure earlier that day and availability of PAPI.Due to the lack of airspeed; altitude; and other flight instruments; entering the traffic pattern was deemed higher risk because of the potential for unsafe altitude or airspeed conditions. Additionally; given the electrically dependent ignition system; engine reliability was uncertain. A straight-in approach minimized maneuvering and time to landing.A no-flap landing was executed on Runway XX.
