column121: During pushback I notified the push crew first to standby;" then when cleared by ramp I said "cleared to push tail north". I did not release the brake and I failed to say "brakes released."  An unusual sound was heard and I immediately realized that the brake was still set.  The push crew stopped the push and investigated for any damage - I informed him that the brake had not been released. They advised that tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. I released the brake and the push continued. About 50 yards into the push the crew stopped and had me set brakes. Something was not right with the tow bar and they had to swap it out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push.  Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as I waited for the driver to advise me to "set brakes." Just then the tug and the aircraft began to roll forward and the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  I immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes and stated "brakes set; cleared to disconnect inter phone."  I had assumed the aircraft was still being positioned by the tug driver; but perhaps we had been disconnected without brakes being set.  On taxiout we entered the hardstand. The FO researched tow bar pin shear (FOM requires inspection) as we both began to wonder if that may have occurred. Since we were off gate we contacted Dispatch and were patched through to Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control did great work to coordinate with ZZZ Maintenance and OPs to find out if there was a shear.  While we waited in the hardstand the FO and I decided it best to taxi back to gate and get the nose gear inspected just in case there was a pin shear. We taxied back to Gate XX; shutdown and entered an logbook entry.  There was notably good collaboration at the gate from our Maintenance team including the original ground crew providing their inputs so that the inspection could be done properly. With the inspection complete we departed without further issue.Cause: Causal was my failure to release the parking brake prior to authorizing the push.  My normal habit is to say "standby" after receiving the guide person's "all secure below" advisory; which I did.  But when I reviewed the ECAM just prior to clearing the pushback I only noted the NW STRG DISC memo and failed to note the Park Brake memo. And I didn't state "Brakes released" nor did I release the brakes. I am going to add a technique of pointing to the parking brake handle and then to the ECAM prior to stating "brakes released; cleared to push."  This was suggested by the FO who has seen other CAs using this technique.  And while I didn't feel rushed; I think making this process a slower and more deliberate execution will do me well in the future. I'm certain that the drop point rolling issue was part of this cascade from the non standard pushback. The guide person was very quick to catch the issue and call for brakes."
column123: We were given the brief from the pushback crew but had not completed our Before Start Checklist and had not received our pushback clearance from ramp.  The Captain told the push crew to standby."  Then once we were cleared by ramp to push he informed the ramp crew  "cleared to push tail north".  At that point the parking brake was still set. (Normal call "brakes released; cleared to push (tail north)").  When the ramp crew went to push we heard an unusual noise.  Then we realized that the parking brake had not been released. The Captain then notified the ramp crew to stop the push and investigate for any damage.  Additionally; he informed him that the parking brake had not been released. After the ramp crew investigated; they advised us that the tow bar and plane looked ok and were ready to continue the push. The captain released the brake and the push continued. After about 50 yards; the push the crew stopped and had us set brakes. They informed us that there was an issue with the tow bar and it needed to be swapped out. Once the new tow bar was attached we continued the push. Nearing the desired drop point; the aircraft was stopped by the push crew and the left wing walker gave a hold brakes signal with his wands as the captain waited for the driver to advise "set brakes." We then noticed the tug driving away and the aircraft appeared to be rolling forward.   Shortly after this the driver said "Captain brakes brakes."  The Captain immediately stopped the aircraft from rolling and set brakes.  Then he notified them that the brakes were set and they were cleared to disconnect the interphone.  To us what had appeared to have happened was the aircraft was still being pulled by the tug driver; but other indications made us question what was happening.  I believe the tug driver was a little shaken from the previous events that had occurred but the error had been trapped and damage/injury was prevented..On taxiout; I researched the publications for tow bar issues and discovered we may have sheared a tow pin and needed an inspection.  We coordinated with ramp to hold in the hard stand and worked with Dispatch; Maintenance Control; ZZZ Ops; ZZZ maintenance; and ramp to setup an inspection.  We proceeded to a new gate for the inspection.  The Captain made an logbook entry and maintenance performed the inspection.  We then proceed with the flight with no further issues and as a crew talked about what had happened and ways to prevent such a miscommunication in the future.Cause: The cause of the event was a miscommunication between the Captain and the push crew.  He did inform them that we were cleared to push but never said that the brakes were released.   I can see why this was confusing for the push crew.  Depending on the situation; Captains sometimes release the parking brake immediately after the brief is received from the push crew but tells the push crew to standby for the push clearance.   Also I'm curious how often the push crews ensure the light is out prior to initiating the push.  If the push crew would have referenced the light this would have been trapped and no error would have occurred."

column123: Taking off on runway XX I increased power to 50 percent to sync engines and then started to bring power to toga. After landing ARFF inspected the aircraft and told us there was hydraulic fluid on the right landing gear. I decided to have ARFF follow us to the gate for safety and to avoid a possible similar situation as a recent incident. column123: On descent into ZZZ we had an ECAM indicating the yellow hydraulic system reservoir was low. I continued flying and the CA ran the ECAM. The fluid level was mostly empty and the ECAM had us turn off the yellow pump and PTU (Power Transfer Unit). Since we were down a hydraulic system we decided to advise ATC. Due to where we were; we also decided that ZZZ was still the best option to land. The CA informed the FAs and passengers. Out of caution we also requested XXL as it was a longer runway. Also; for safety we requested to stop on the runway and get inspected. On final approach; we turned on the yellow engine pump according to the ECAM procedure. The remaining fluid leaked out in less than a minute. The CA had me continue to fly and land the plane. Upon landing; we stopped on the runway. I talked with Fire and Rescue and they reported that our right main landing gear had some fluid on it and was smoking. I assumed it was caused by the hydraulic fluid on the brakes. Fire and Rescue reported the right brakes were showing hot. Our wheels page didn't show any high temperatures on the brakes. We took the airplane off the runway and began taxiing to the gate. During our taxi; Fire and Rescue reported our right brake temperatures were decreasing pretty steadily and there was no more evidence of any smoke coming from the main landing gear. We pulled into the gate with no more events.Cause: Training really kicked in and everything happened in a way both of us expected; as far as who did what and when. It really helped to keep the stress levels low. We did use a procedure to help with the precautionary landing and they also helped to make sure we didn't miss anything.

column121: We were cleared from the DISNEE arrival onto the final for runway 20R and subsequently cleared for the visual approach after calling the airport in sight. I was on the ILS to back us up with automation fully on. Somewhere around 1000 feet I visual saw Aircraft Y; wing up turning final onto 20L. We both dont recall having this traffic pointed out to us. I saw that it appeared they had joined the final. It startled the FO at first as at first glance it was not clear to him that the aircraft was turning onto final; although I could tell his wing was 'up' and joining. We were dealing with turbulent conditions and a tailwind that at somepoint was supposed to shift to a slight headwind for a landing on a very short runway for us. We quickly overtook the aircraft that was on our wingtip and it became a non factor. We received one TCAS TA for the aircraft at some altitude and possibly too low for an RA to take place. The speed of aircraft vs a small single engine airplane that it would be really difficult to measure closure rates and to avoid abruptly. We proceeded to have a normal landing. Perhaps that one of the most troubling things of all; this was a normal day at SNA with an experienced crew that has been to the airport before. We had briefed these multiple threats; were ready for them; and everything went uneventfully. However; It is honestly shocking to me that this is SOP at the airport. We are running large aircraft at 160knots on a final to a challenging runway; while very close on our wingtip we have student pilots doing multiple approaches in VFR traffic patterns. If Aircraft Y had misaligned for final approach; I would have had little time to avoid.Cause: I understand that this airport has been operating this way for a long time and to my knowledge mostly uneventful. However; under 'see something; say something' I feel compelled to file this report after having similar experiences in my recent trips to the airport; including at night. With recent revocation of the side by side approaches at SFO; SNA to me; is a far bigger safety risk than SFO. We are now reliant on low experience pilots to join onto final in front of aircraft traveling twice their speed. We are putting to much trust in a private pilot to not overshoot the final. Student activity and traffic pattern work should not be permitted at the airport. I do not even think 20L should be operational when 20R approaches are being conducted. We have some mentions of the GA activity along coastline in the company pages; but that really does little to express what the first time pilot could expect flying to SNA as the traffic isn't isolated to the coastline; it is joining up on your wing.

column121: After aircraft shut down and parking checklist accomplished; the FO and I had begun disembarking the aircraft.While the FO was exiting the aircraft during deplaning; and I stood with my bags at the flightdeck door; I heard 4 (or more) chimes which could be either the FAs calling the front or the ground crew.  I did not see any indication of a call from the FA's; and noticed the ground crew trying to get my attention on the right side of the aircraft.  The FO must have heard these chimes as well as he managed to make his way back to the flightdeck.I opened FO's side window to talk to ground crew from the flight deck.  After about 20 seconds I realized they were indicating a fire in the right engine.  Looking back toward the #2 engine there was no indication of any fire.  No smoke was noted and no flames were visible.  Routinely; the ground crew will see something and think it is a problem when in fact it is not.  The FO left to investigate from the ground.I saw the FO return to the right side of the aircraft where I was still located and he indicated there was a fire back there.  I still could see no visible smoke or fire from my viewpoint.  I queried if he thought fire trucks should be called.  The FO indicated that he believed it would be a good idea to call them out and assess the situation.I immediately grabbed the hand Mic (as all our belongings had been stowed and some were on the jetbridge) to call ground and ask them to send the trucks out due to a fire that the ground crew had told us about.  I also advised it was the #2 engine that was in question.  Ground asked a passing by jet if they saw any fire from our #2 engine.  The jet confirmed they did see some fire located at the 6 O'clock position of the back of the motor.With still zero visual evidence from the flightdeck of smoke or fire; I proceeded to call the Air Carrier X maintenance Control office to let them know of a possible fire and give them a heads up" of an upcoming Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) entry.  By this time; while on the phone with maintenance; my FO returned to show me a picture he had taken of the fire.  It was; in my opinion; not anything major; but had been now burning for approximately 10 minutes.  I described the fire to the mechanic through the phone as being between the exhaust nozzle and the rear blades.  The mechanic indicated he thought it was a "candle flame".  Right about the same time; I herd the FO say; "They're foaming the engine".  A quick glance out the window; and I could see foam flying by the FO's side window.  When I indicated this to the Mechanic he said that the action of foaming was a big problem and that I needed to find out what type was used for my AML entry. At this point we were nearly deplaned.  I did not make any special PA's to the passengers since most the people were already off and all remaining passengers were in the aisle with their bags in hand.  The two forward FA's were made aware of the situation by the FO.  The cleaning crew that had tried to come onto the aircraft were told; by me; to leave the aircraft.  I had contemplated making a PA but feared at our current point in the deplaning process; the PA could create some unnecessary panic and do more harm than good.  I allowed the deplaning to continue normally which took another couple of minutes.After the passengers were off; I got word from the FO; that the fire chief wanted the APU shut down.  All the passengers were off the aircraft at this time and the FA's were gathering their belongings for their layover.  We did not have any ground power attached; the APU was shut down as if it was the last flight of the day.The FO and I went down to the aircraft to talk with the firefighters.  We ended up talking to the firefighter that sprayed the aircraft.  He mentioned that he had never seen that type of fire and did attempt to spray it with water first; this did not yield the desired result.  I assume this to mean that the fire would not extinguishby water alone.  He then resorted to the foam and mentioned he also foamed the wing as an extra precaution.  When asked the type of foam used for my AML entry; he said it was the "latest and greatest F-3 foam".  Later he indicated the new foam being used was non-corrosive.Having the information we needed and the AML entry complete; the FO and I grabbed our already packed bags and proceeded to the hotel for our scheduled layover.  While walking up the jetbridge I contacted our assigned dispatch at Air Carrier X to make them aware of the aircraft state and that maintenance had been contacted.Cause: During the event a tailpipe fire never entered the conversation.  On our return flight we discussed about the potential being there and that neither of us had really witnessed a persistent tailpipe fire; if one exists.  Myself; I've flown for decades and a majority of that has been in jets.  Pictures of tailpipe fires and possible expansion of QRC to include all steps if this occurs well after engine shutdown."

column121: While near the end of the ZZZZZX arrival; RWY XX transition; we experienced two uncommanded roll events to the left while autopilot B was engaged. The aircraft was below 10;000' on the segment of the ZZZZZX before the slight left turn at ZZZZZ; on the straight-ahead sequence of fixes between ZZZZZ1 and ZZZZZ when both of these uncommanded roll events occurred. Neither event could be attributed to any change in aircraft configuration; input; or other factor that I can identify; both happened without any identifiable cause. Before the first uncommanded roll event; we were descending via the arrival in LNAV and VNAV with autopilot B engaged. Without warning or identifiable reason; the aircraft suddenly began rolling to the left. The autopilot initially stayed connected; and the autopilot system turned the yoke significantly to the right in an attempt to counter the roll. However; the autopilot was unable to stop the roll; the aircraft continued rolling; an amber 'ROLL AUTHORITY' displayed on the attitude indicator; and an aural alert sounded (this all happened very quickly--I cannot clearly remember what the aural alert was; since at that point I was already reaching for the disconnect to take recovery actions. My captain later said that he recalled it being a 'BANK ANGLE' aural alert). I called out 'my aircraft;' disconnected the autopilot; and applied right aileron and some right rudder to stop the roll and return the aircraft to level flight. Since the aircraft was notifying us that the autopilot's aileron authority alone was insufficient to keep control of the aircraft's bank angle ('ROLL AUTHORITY' annunciation); I determined that some amount of rudder was necessary to ensure we could overcome whatever unusual force was causing this uncommanded roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron alone. My inputs successfully stopped the roll; and I returned the aircraft to level flight and re-established the aircraft on the flight path. Feeling that the aircraft was now under control; my captain and I searched for any reason why that might have happened and couldn't identify anything. For that reason; we initially suspected wake turbulence. The captain asked ATC if we were following a heavy aircraft on the arrival; but ATC responded that we were following another 737 MAX. We did not think that a fellow MAX miles ahead would cause such an aggressive effect on our aircraft. Since the aircraft was stable and showing no further signs of control issues; we elected to re-engage autopilot B to monitor its response. Shortly thereafter; the same thing happened: an uncommanded continuous roll to the left that the autopilot could not counter with aileron input. I was already prepared to disconnect the autopilot quickly at the first sign of a recurrence; so I did so; applying the necessary inputs to stop the roll and re-stabilize the aircraft. In both instances of this uncommanded roll; it felt as if the autopilot had been commanding some sort of continuous control input that then released when I disengaged the autopilot; because the aircraft was responsive to my control inputs and recovered without difficulty after the autopilot was disengaged each time. Since the aircraft annunciated 'ROLL AUTHORITY' on the attitude indicator; indicating that 100% of the autopilot's roll authority was insufficient to control the aircraft's roll; I wondered if perhaps the aircraft had experienced an uncommanded rudder deflection that the autopilot was unable to overcome with ailerons; which then released when the autopilot was disconnected. However; that is just a possibility that crossed my mind; we could not identify any cause; nor did I feel any sort of yawing or rudder pedal movement prior to each event. After two uncommanded roll events in a row on autopilot B; we were convinced that we had a genuine problem with something in the autopilot system; as two events in a row like that did not seem like a wake turbulence encounter with anaircraft of the same type that was miles ahead. At that point; we were about to make the turn to ZZZZZ2 to join the ILS course to runway XX; so I continued to hand-fly the aircraft to a safe and otherwise uneventful landing. I experienced no control issues while hand-flying the aircraft. The captain made a logbook entry and notified dispatch after gate arrival; in accordance with company SOP.Cause: Causal factors unknown. Recommend thorough maintenance investigation.

column121: After clearing RWY22L after landing; we were giving taxi instructions to proceed down RWY 31L to hold short of MB. Approaching taxiway KE which goes across runway 31L; we observed Aircraft Y proceeding across runway 31L in front of us; not slowing down. I braked to a stop; and we asked ATC if we should give way to Aircraft Y; the response was 'uhh; yessssss' We were not told to give way to any aircraft. We did not hear Aircraft Y receive clearance to cross  or to give way to us. Until we observed the aircraft cross in front of us we had not situational awareness there would be an aircraft crossing our runway in front of us.Cause: This is the third time in 8 weeks that JFK ATC has lost track of either my aircraft or others that impede traffic flow until ATC is queried for clarification. We have had a mid-air collision and a runway fatal accident due to ATC losing situational awareness. What I often hear is 'well; it's JFK'; 'it's JFK; that the way it is'. The pilots and ATC at JFK are operating under an extreme setting of a systematic normalization of deviation of safe practices; policies; and procedures. It is a daily occurrence to hear colloquial language; American slang; incomplete clearances where the pilot is expected to interpolate what ground control is wanting them to do and were to go; and losing track of aircraft completely. This is not new. Reports for years have been filed by pilots. It is time to act. It is time for industry; FAA; and ATC to make the needed changes.

column121: Took off of XXL at ZZZ assigned a 080 heading. Right after takeoff; around 2500 feet; we recieved a L PITOT HEAT caution message on Engine Display 1. The captain flew the airplane while I ran the QRC and QRH. The QRH lead us to the source selector panel and changing the air data source to 2; which created a plethora of red Xs on the captain side Primary Flight Display (PFD). The plane briefly climbed through our assigned altitude of 10;000 feet at this point (reaching 10;400) so the captain disconnected the autopilot and hand flew the plane back down to 10;000 and stayed at 250 knots. I asked air traffic control for present heading and present altitude while we troubleshoot an issue. The captain handed me the airplane; transferred flight directors; and ran the QRH themself; leading to the same issue. The end of that checklist led us to the air data failure QRH which led us to the unreliable air speed QRH. It was at this point that we decided it would be best to return to the field. The captain notified dispatch; and then flew the airplane while I briefed the flight attendant on the brief items. We asked ATC for vectors back to ZZZ airport. In my recollection; ATC didn't tell us what runway to expect; so the CA directed me to load the RNAV for XXL in. I started working on setting up the approach and getting landing performance. As we received further vectors; ATC informed us that we can expect runway XXR; so I reloaded the correct approach. At this point; the captain handed me the aircraft while they double checked my work; double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH to make sure there were no signs of discrepancies; and I was given instructions to intercept the approach and a clearance for the visual approach to XXR. Instead of clicking approach mode; I accidentally clicked the speed mode button. This prompted the captain to take controls; disconnect the auto pilot; and hand fly the intercept. It initially looked like the captain was lining up for runway XXL; so I clarified with them; and we corrected to the correct runway; XXR. The captain kept a buffer above Vref as a precaution for unreliable air speed. Once we landed safely and got off the runway; I called operations to get us a gate. Once we were stopped with the parking brake set; the captain delivered a PA to the passengers. A taxi to the gate without issue and had maintenance meet us there.Cause: I believe the lightning strike that the aircraft suffered the day prior may have affected certain systems that led to this failure. However; I'm not certain.'Suggestion: I should've discussed with the captain about declaring an emergency; and taking a little bit more time up in the air to set up the aircraft properly and calmly before commencing the approach. I should've also flown the airplane the entire time while the captain managed the aircraft and the situation. Tunnel vision and adrenaline were running high in this situation and I failed to speak up and instead deferred to the captain for decision-making.
column123: Got a Left Caution Pitot message at 3;000 I had the First Officer run the QRC and the QRH while I continued the climb. He did and it led us to turning the ADC to 2; when we did it killed everything on my side and disconnected the autopilot. We blew through 10;000; I corrected manually and notified ATC we needed present heading and 10;000 ft we needed to trouble shoot and that I was correcting back to 10;000. We ran the Left PITOT caution QRH again and it did the same thing;  I had coupled everything to the First Officer's side so it would knock the Auto Pilot off. We ran the next QRH for ADC failure which then lead us to the unreliable airspeed QRH. At this time I told the First Officer to notify the Flight attendants that we would be returning to the field for a small flight control issue and to remain seated no emergency. I told ATC I wanted Vectors back to ZZZ airport. We were not an emergency at this time but we were returning to field. We got vectors for the approach; we had XXL loaded got switched to XXR reloaded that as we were being vectored. We double checked the unreliable airspeed QRH and we didn't see any signs of unreliable airspeed with the pitch but I flew cross panel off the first officers side and the standby for reference and kept us 10 kts faster from VREF just to make sure I had a buffer. On intercept of course the First Officer accidentally hit my speed mode. This caused my side to black out and clear everything and I clicked off Autopilot and deselected both Flight Directors then hand flew the approach. The First Officer made sure we were lined up with the correct runway XXR since we never really intercepted the course so we corrected to XXR and landed safely. I delivered a PA once we exited the runway and were stopped to inform passengers we had a small flight control issue and needed to have Maintenance check it out and I would be getting a new aircraft to continue to our destination and to remain seated everything was fine.Cause: Electrical damage to systems from the lightening strike the night before.Suggestion: This plane was struck by lightening the night before; it needs to have all of its wiring replaced. I believe quite a few items got fried which lead to our situation.

column121: While operations were ongoing on the ramp; two baggage carts that were staged on Gate XX became mobile due to strong wind conditions. The carts were not properly secured and had no functioning braking systems. As a result; both carts rolled from Gate XX toward Gate XY.Ramp personnel responded immediately and ran to intercept the carts; successfully stopping them before they entered the Non-Movement Area (NMA). No aircraft were parked on Gate XY at the time. Had an aircraft been present; the situation could have resulted in significant aircraft damage and potential personnel injury.Upon inspection; both carts were found to have no operational brakes whatsoever. It is currently unclear whether these carts have been properly serviced or inspected; however; their condition indicates they were not compliant with ramp equipment safety standards.This incident highlights a serious safety gap regarding staged ground equipment on the ramp. SOP requires all ramp equipment to be serviceable; secured; and routinely inspected to prevent uncontrolled movement; accidents; or injuries. Failure to comply puts all ramp personnel; aircraft; and partner operations at risk.It is imperative that all staged ramp equipmentregardless of vendor or partnerundergo periodic servicing and brake inspections in accordance with SOP. Additionally; equipment must be properly parked and secured at all times; especially under adverse weather conditions.This event underscores the need for consistent SOP enforcement across all vendors and partners operating on the ramp. A lack of compliance by one party creates unsafe conditions for everyone and increases the risk of serious incidents or injuries.

column121: We planned a time building flight from ZZZ to ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1 to ZZZ1 to ZZZZZ1 to ZZZZZ to ZZZ. This flight took place around XA:00 and was the second flight of the evening; the first went well with no issues. On the return trip around 20 minutes from ZZZ we decided to proceed to ZZZ2 and do a practice approach before continuing on to ZZZ. We decided on this course of action after verifying with the fuel gauge that we still had roughly 9 gallons of fuel (estimate of around 2.5 hours of flight). After completing an approach at ZZZ2 we then planned and flew directly towards ZZZ. However; on the flight at about 10 nm from ZZZ at 8000 Msl we experienced engine failure. Over the course of less then a minute our engine became very rough and had a large drop in RPM; we increased throttle and had no change; and then the engine fully died. We verified that the gauge still read 4 gallons of fuel; the battery still had 13.1v but the oil pressure read 0. The PIC for this flight contacted ATC and landed in a field close to ZZZ when it became clear we would not make it to the runway. After landing we verified that we were both unharmed and then contacted emergency services. The main factors that contributed to these events were unfamiliarity with the plane and over reliance on fuel gauges rather than our planning. Both the PIC and I had flown this plane before but neither of us were 'experienced' in it and while we had both read the POH neither of us were knowledgeable in it. Additionally; we should have trusted the flight plan and calculated fuel burn and trusted it rather then our instruments mid flight. What can be done in the future is ensure that pre flight planning is the number one source of planning information and that it is stuck to unless forced to change.

column121: I was piloting a hot air balloon on a passenger flight. We launched from a field just west of ZZZ; and our flight path took us approximately 8 miles to the northwest.I was flying a Cameron Z105 with passengers.Weather was clear with visibility greater than 10 miles. Surface winds were 7 mph at launch and approximately 6 mph at landing; both from the southeast.The takeoff and flight were uneventful. I approached a large open grass field (approximately 7 acres) to land near the driveway leading from the road to the house. I was approximately 5 to 10 feet above ground level; moving about 6 mph toward the driveway. The passengers and I scanned the area for power lines and poles but did not see any in the field. We did see and discuss the power lines along the road; and we agreed the area between us and the driveway was clear.As we approached the driveway; a passenger and I noticed two single-strand power lines running from the road on our left to another pole north of the house. The lines were about 80 feet in front of us.  This occurred at about XA:40 PM; sunset was XB:43 PM.  Factors affecting the visibility of the power lines would have been background clutter with the background field and trees.   The balloon chase crew was also turning onto the driveway at the same time and called out the power lines over the radio.  This occurred just seconds after the pilot and passenger noticed the power lines.  I immediately opened the parachute valve to put the basket on the ground short of the power lines and allow the balloon envelope to lay over the lines. This is considered a 'rip out' situation as described in the flight manual and the FAA Balloon Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-11B). This is the safest maneuver to perform when contact with power lines is inevitable. If not performed; the basket could have contacted the power lines and injuries; or further damage could have occurred.There were three electrical arcs with two power lines. On the third arc; the fuse on the street power pole opened. The basket came to rest on its side; and all occupants were uninjured. We were able to exit the basket on our own. The balloon remained draped over the power line. There were no injuries to the pilot or passengers.A power company removed the balloon envelope.  The power was restored to one residential property.   The balloon and equipment were packed and transported to our storage facility. The next morning; I inspected the aircraft.  Four panels within the first 10 feet of nylon fabric had burns and holes. No load tapes or structural members of the aircraft were damaged. Per the Continued Airworthiness Manual; the holes were not required to be repaired because they were below the first 10 feet of nylon fabric.I plan to develop a near-miss presentation to share with fellow pilots and balloon crew members.The envelope has been repaired by an authorized repairman and returned to service.   The event arose from late identification of two single-strand power lines along the intended landing path. The balloon was already very low and moving toward the driveway when the lines were recognized; leaving limited time and distance to fully avoid contact.Contributing factors-	Low-visibility hazard: The wires were single-strand and therefore harder to see.-	Background clutter: Trees and the field behind the wires reduced contrast/visibility.-	Operating environment: Landing near a road/driveway/house increases the likelihood of utility spans and service runs that are not as obvious as roadside distribution lines.-	Expectation/attention: Attention was drawn to and discussion occurred about the roadside power lines; reinforcing the assessment that the area between the balloon and driveway was clear.-	Time/distance constraints: Wires were detected at close range (~80 ft) during a low-altitude; high-workload phase of flight.The wires were discovered visually on short final when the pilot and a passenger noticed two single-strand lines spanning from the road to a pole north of the house; approximately 80 feet ahead. The chase crew also called out the lines over the road seconds later as they turned onto the driveway.Corrective actions-	Immediate operational action: Pilot opened the parachute valve to execute a stop-short landing ('rip out' procedure) intended to keep the basket short of the lines and reduce occupant risk.-	Utility coordination: Local power company responded; removed the envelope from the lines; and restored power to one residential property.-	Recovery and inspection: With permission; balloon and equipment were packed and transported to storage.-	Maintenance disposition: Damage assessed; envelope repaired by an authorized repairman and returned.-	Lessons learned dissemination: Plan to develop a near-miss presentation for pilots and crew members.Human performance considerations-	High-workload phase: Approach and landing require continuous control decisions while scanning for obstacles; time available to detect/confirm thin hazards can be limited.-	Attention management: Visual attention may narrow toward the touchdown zone; making small; low-contrast hazards (single-strand wires) easier to miss until close.-	Team scanning and shared assumptions: Having passengers assist with scanning can increase coverage; but agreement that the area was clear can also reduce continued challenge/verification.-	Lighting/angle considerations: Late-day conditions and low sun angle can reduce contrast and increase glare risk (sun angle noted in the report).

column121: On flight; to ZZZ I met my partner for the first time. Because she is more senior I asked her what position she would like to work and she said AFT. I didn't want to work FWD but I had no choice. Everything went as normally until during the taxi right before take-off I saw she was falling asleep in her jump seat. I watched for a little bit to see if she was okay but she opened her eyes looked at me for a while and continue to sleep again- on and off a few times. I continually looked to see maybe she was just on her phone but she wasn't. I'm 100% sure she was asleep. I had previously told her I didn't need her to do my announcement; so by the time we got into the air she stayed in the back. I had did snacks and the drink orders on the ground so once we could get up; I'd just have to do drinks. The flight was short; so I knew I didn't have much time. She did come to the galley once to grab a trash bag and gloves to do a trash walk then came back to put it in the bin. The flight completed as usual.The following flight from ZZZ is where the real issues started. The flight was now even shorter; so I did the same as the previous flight: snacks and drink orders on the ground. This time around I hadn't seen my partner fall asleep. Once we got into the air I began drinks and had only completely row 1; when the flight deck called. They told me that we didn't have any steering; would have to reset on the ground or be tugged away but didn't declare an emergency. In that moment I immediately began mentally preparing for an emergency while also completely the 2nd row of drinks. As I was pouring drinks; I pulled my flight attendant device and opened the Flight Attendant Manual to ensure my memory served me correctly in this potential emergency. Before I could take the second row of drinks to the passengers the flight deck called again and stated that ATC is providing priority handling. The flight deck had called back to back within 2 minutes- if that. In that time I looked to see if my partner was on the phone but she wasn't anywhere to be found. I finished up my drinks and immediately began to double check the galley and cabin to secure anything that wasn't secured. The flight deck called again third time to ask for specials and give me a time update. We hadn't had any listed specials so I just relayed that message where they then told me it was 15 minutes left. Once the flight deck told us the time; I finally then heard my partner respond okay into the receiver. I always keep my phone timer on so I can also be aware of time just incase. My time was aligned with their time. Less than a minute later my partner came to the galley and asked me to repeat what was going on. I relayed the information to her and told her it's priority handling; so be prepared if it turns into something more. She shook her head as if she understood. She told me she missed the first two calls because she was in the bathroom but knowing that I've seen her asleep in the jumpseat and the bathroom sign NOT illuminated; I don't think she was telling the truth. A few minutes later the double chime sounded and I began to secure the passengers and fulfilling all my duties. She made her way back to her seat from the galley after collecting trash. Before the gear could come out and the sit-down chime went off; I had locked the bathroom and was seated. She was not in her brace position but very relaxed in her seat. As we landed I did a partial announcement by stating to remain seated with the seatbelts on and personal items stowed. I didn't want to give the standard announcement because I knew the captain would make an announcement almost immediately being as though we wouldn't turn off the runway. They then told the passengers what was going on. Making the taxi a bit longer than usual. Once we got to the gate is when I could finally breath. I didn't want to work as FWD but I'm really glad and blessed that I did because I don't trust my partner even with her seniority to handle this situation in the manner it needs to be; let alone to be awake. I am okay just shaken up but with the events of today; I do NOT feel comfortable flying with her. We only have one leg tomorrow but I do not feel safe knowing how she disregards safety standards regardless of what did or did not occur.

column121: My student and I planned to conduct a pattern flight at ZZZ. The taxi was uneventful and runup was successful with indications within limits of the POH. We took off of runway XXL; and as soon as we were airborne; my student and I smelt burning plastic/insulation. I told my student to continue to fly while I troubleshot. My first thought was an electrical fire; so I checked the avionics and lights for heat/smoke; and I checked the CO2 indicator which was turning brown. We landed after the first lap in the pattern; to where my student noticed a very small amount of smoke in the cockpit. I let tower know that we wanted a full stop to taxi back to the ramp; and that we did not need any assistance since I could not see any smoke. About 5 seconds later; thick white smoke entered the cockpit through the dash; and at that point I knew there was an engine fire; so I told the tower we would shut down the plane. At this point; we had not declared an emergency; but tower provided priority handling at their discretion. I shut the engine down; and my student and I exited the plane. After about 20 seconds; I went to the front of the plane and saw an orange fire burning from inside the engine cowling. I grabbed the fire extinguisher from the aircraft and put the fire out. After successfully putting out the fire; maintenance personnel towed the aircraft back to the hangar to inspect the aircraft. During inspection; it was discovered that a rag was the cause of the fire.To prevent this situation from happening again; although a thorough pre-flight was conducted by the student and the instructor; both parties could have looked inside the cowling for any FOD.

column121: I approached ZZZ for a full stop landing. While 10 and 7 miles south; I announced my position and intent on the CTAF. As I arrived in the terminal area; there was another high wing Cessna in the pattern on the left downwind leg for XX. I coordinated with this pilot to enter the downwind behind them and continue for landing in the number two position. I acquired the plane's position visually and announced that as I entered the downwind behind them. I then began to configure my plane for landing and go through my checklist. At this time; the other plane must have begun its descent because when I looked back up from my checklist; I had lost visual on the plane. It's possible that the hazy air conditions may have also contributed to me losing visual. When the other plane reported that I had passed above them; I immediately re-acquired them visually; making a right turn out of the pattern and announcing my intentions. I then returned to the downwind and landed without issue. I had no further contact with the other pilot. I think the most critical issues were the haze and the difference in airspeed between the two planes with mine being faster and closing the gap between us.

column121: The flight began as normal and uneventful. Both engine starts along with taxi for takeoff were all normal with no abnormal indications. During the takeoff roll we didn't notice or feel any abnormalities beside the runway being very rough and bumpy (which is normal for ZZZ). After rotation and during climb out I noticed that I could feel a slight vibration from the airplane engine and looked at the VIB indicator and notice it was sitting around 3.9. We initially followed immediate action items (non involved); then I called for the QRC; then captain assigned me to continue PF duties while he conducted the QRH. While we ran the checklist I asked ATC to level off at 12;000 feet and stay there while we were troubleshooting. Once I brought the thrust levers back to a normal 250kt cruise speed the engine vibs returned to a normal green range; we continued with the checklist and it directed us to continue with the flight while monitoring the engine vibes. We both agreed that declaring an emergency didn't seem appropriate since the engine was operating normally at lower thrust settings. We communicated with dispatch and came to the agreement to return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight we asked ATC for 'speed our discretion'. We flew back to ZZZ without any other abnormalities. During the landing we didn't feel anything abnormal and even during the taxi to the gate. When we arrived at the gate XX we heard a ramp truck report to ramp control that the aircraft he was looking at had a blown tire. We asked ramp to confirm if it was our aircraft he was talking about; and he confirmed it. During the walk around I saw that the inboard left main tire had blown; I also noticed dents and tire marks on the underside of the wing and flap. The engine showed indications that tire debris had entered the engine. We then notified ground control of potential FOD on runway XXL and XXR.Would have been helpful if someone had noticed our tire blow out during departure. We had no indications that a tire had blown.
column123: Tail swapped into Aircraft X for unknown reason. Push back; engine starts; taxi all normal. During takeoff we assumed runway was poorly textured. During rotation FO called out N1 fan vib at 3.9; he called for QRC and QRH. After completing necessary immediate action items we followed QRC and QRH procedures. I instructed him to continue flying while also maintaining radios as I completed the procedures in QRH; coordinated with dispatch; and the FAs. Sometime below 10;000 (I believe around 6;000) the aft FA called and was unable to communicate with the flight deck. The aft FA had to communicate using the fwd fa telephone in order to tell us that he heard a loud bang and vibrations from the left side of the aircraft. After we decided to return to field; dispatch also got in contact with Mx (Maintenance) who agreed that we should return. We determined that we could safely contain the vibration in CRZ setting and deemed that declaring an emergency was not necessary; however had priority to the field. I communicated with FAs; dispatch; then made a PA to the passengers telling them that due to the 'loud vibrational noises from Aircraft left; we would be returning to ZZZ out of precaution'. Completed the rest of the flight as routine standard; landed safely; coordinated gates and specials with operations. We fully taxied to the gate before a ground person told ramp that our left main inboard tire was completely blown and it was communicated to us. We deplaned; contacted maintenance; dispatch coordinators; scheduling; and the chiefs. This resulted in 3 write ups from us directly. We did notify ATC about the tire issue for possible FOD on the runway (either on takeoff or landing); ground called us back to say yes; FOD was found on XXR.Would have been nice to know we had tire damage before parking; but it seems like nobody was around to see it and we didn't believe to have had any indications stating otherwise.

column121: Flight purpose was to regain proficiency after not flying for several months. Checked fuel quantity using sight gauges and found 2 gallons in the right tank and 5 gallons in the left tank. I expected to use about 4 gallons during the flight. Other aircraft were parked at the fuel pump; so I decided to fill up after the flight.After some airwork and practice landings at another airfield; I headed home. As I was initiating the descent from 3000 MSL (about 2000 AGL); I got a fuel pressure warning from the Dynon system. The fuel pressure indication was fluctuating widely. I decided to stay at my present altitude until within easy gliding distance of my home airport. Roughly a minute later; the Dynon system gave me an engine speed warning and the engine stopped.I glanced at the glide ring on the Dynon system and my home airport was right on the edge. Knowing that the glide ring was based on conservative glide data; I was tempted to continue to my home airport. Then I thought about the reason that I had used conservative glide data (because I might encounter sinking air) and decided that a farm field nearby was a better option. After an uneventful landing in the field; I contacted a neighbor and had him bring fuel to the field. We added five gallons to each tank and I made an uneventful flight home.After getting home; I reviewed the POH. It states that the pilot should alternate between the left and right tank. I had been in the habit of setting both fuel valves to open assuming that; if one tank became empty; fuel would flow from the other one. The POH stated that is not guaranteed with both valves open. In the future; I will follow the POH recommended practice for setting the fuel valves.

column121: During arrival into Boca Raton Airport; while being vectored for the RNAV (GPS) RWY 5 approach by Miami TRACON; the aircraft was descending through approximately 2;000 feet in compliance with an assigned altitude restriction to maintain 2;000 feet until established on the approach. The First Officer (FO) was Pilot Flying (PF); and the Captain was Pilot Monitoring (PM) handling communications. At approximately XA:53-XA:55; Miami TRACON issued a traffic advisory indicating traffic below the aircraft. The Captain acknowledged the call and initiated a visual search for the reported traffic. Shortly thereafter; the aircraft's TCAS generated a Traffic Advisory (TA); which escalated almost immediately to a Resolution Advisory (RA) with the command 'CLIMB; CLIMB.' In response to the RA; and consistent with standard operating procedures and regulatory guidance; the flight crew immediately complied with the TCAS command. Control inputs were made to establish the commanded climb; maximum available thrust was applied; and vertical guidance provided by TCAS was followed. The aircraft climbed to approximately 3;100 feet (+/- 100 feet) before the TCAS annunciated 'Clear of Conflict.' The maneuver was executed in a controlled manner; with no injuries or damage. The conflicting traffic was not visually acquired during the maneuver. Subsequent post-flight review of ADS-B data indicated that Aircraft Y was operating in the vicinity at approximately 2;500 feet. Based on available information; that aircraft appeared to be operating under VFR and not in communication with Miami TRACON. This information is observational only and not intended to assign causation. Due to the time-critical nature of the event and associated workload; the TCAS RA was not communicated to ATC during the maneuver. ATC was notified via telephone after landing.

column121: This incident happened on Day 0; XA:15. It was a cloudy day with a very low 300ft ceiling. I arrived at my friend's house at around XA:10; and I decided to take my drone out while I was waiting. There is an open field in front of his house; and it is a clear-to-fly airspace for drones under 400ft; but a little close to the nearby airport's controlled airspace. After I got my Potensic Atom 2 drone out; a teenager approached me and asked to fly my drone; and stated he owned a DJI Mini series before. As I just got two newer model DJI drones; I feel I no longer value this drone that much. I have altered the maximum distance to around 500m(1640ft) horizontally; and did not change the maximum altitude at 120m(400ft) before handing it to him. I saw he started the motor without any problem; and started climbing; clearing nearby objects. I turned around and went inside my friend's house to use his restroom.After 5 or 6 minutes; when I went out; I saw the drone was descending below the cloud. After he returned the drone to me; I found it was slightly wet on the hull. I checked the drone; and I found the altitude limit was lifted to the max at 800m(2625ft); and the flight log indicated a 798m(2618ft) maximum flight altitude and probably busted B airspace at my location; which was where I realized it is a clear violation for both losing VLOS and busting altitude.I do understand the risks of flying UAS above 400ft; especially into B airspace; and now I also know the risk of putting drones into the hands of someone you do not know. I truly regret letting an unfamiliar person operate my drone; and the lack of continuous supervision. In the future; I will not allow others to operate the aircraft without direct supervision and will never let incidents like this happen again.

column121: Staffing started a dramatic decline in the area. Weather had been forecast for the OKC area up to the Northwest all shift long. The weather had built enough to make one gap for most trans-continental traffic east to west to funnel through a gap over IRW. Aircraft were diverting southwesterly around to IRW and then points west and northwest. The UKW area had sectors all split off; with DSides on Sector XX; XY; and XZ. A handoff was put on Sector XX which left 0 people in the break list for such a high stress; high volume situation. Holdover overtime was used where possible; but eventually staffing declined more; with 7 positions open with 7 controllers available. This includes 2 of the mid workers that came in. We could no longer support a handoff on Sector XX which absolutely needed one. The controller on Sector XZ asked and said he needed to have a DSide; but we had no staffing to provide one. The controller on Sector XY also said he needed help; but we did not have help to offer him. We had 2 RSide's that were trainees; and 1 DSide trainee that could not work Sector XZ Dside as we had to combine Sector XZ with XA because of the lack of bodies. The traffic volume was some of the highest I have seen; especially that late in the evening. I was later informed that the Command Center had gone home and left us all to fend for ourselves with no outside help besides controllers to controllers. This is an insanely unacceptable situation and one of the more dangerous I've witnessed in my career. There was a lack of experience in the area. A lack of anything being done by Command Center. A lack of adequate staffing. Extremely high and complex workload while controllers are forced to suck it up and deal with it for hours on end without breaks. Controllers were put in an extremely risk heavy and dangerous position; asking and voicing their need for help and D Sides; and yet we are unable to provide them with any help what so ever. The controller on Sector XA; being slow but necessary to have been split off; was essentially acting as a 'handoff' or 3rd set of eyes for the sectors above them. This is TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE. The FAA is constantly knowingly putting it's controllers in harms way and throwing them to the fire. Late last night we entered a situation that was forecast well in advance. Command Center did nothing to alleviate or spread traffic out effectively and left to essentially put the entire workload on controllers that are perpetually over worked. Controllers needed DSides and Handoffs and yet due to staffing it wasn't possible. I am not aware of a staffing trigger that evening. We were hung out to dry last night by an administration that fully knows about these issues that occur all the time; and nothing is being done. This was a total failure of outside leadership.We cannot work hours on end sectors that have 40+ aircraft for hours on end. This was a forecast situation in which Command Center had en entire shift to come up with a plan better than 'Let them all go through one gap and let the controllers figure it out'. Any aircraft transiting the airspace down over IRW heading up to the north west should've come through that gap.Any aircraft diverting around the weather going to points out west or southwest; should have been routed down over ADM and out into Sector XZ. This would even out the workload between multiple airspaces; instead of having every single east-west transcon going through one spot and intersecting 2 different Centers; and 4+ sectors of airspace. Then; right as we're in the thick of it; Command Center decides to go home. We had multiple controllers in the Center here go over 10 hours last night; and almost everyone was held over and working without a break in sight. Command Center can stay and help try to figure something out.

column121: While I was providing training; my trainee cleared Aircraft X for takeoff on RWY XXL with Aircraft Y on short final for RWY XXL. I did not catch it as my attention was focused on the aircraft on extended downwind as I was worried one might turn base early and cut off someone on final. Aircraft X crossed the hold bars and then stopped short of the runway edge line and asked again if they were cleared for takeoff because they just saw an aircraft land in front of them.  That is when I realized that my trainee most likely forgot about the aircraft or didn't see the aircraft short final thinking he had a hole to get a departure out when he did not. The traffic was very busy especially because local 1 and 2 where combined. They were combined because we recently got new radios and there have been a lot of issues with them.  The Local 2 frequency was XXX.XX and out of service. With it being out of service; we did not have the option to have local 2 split off from local 1. Under normal circumstances; we definitely would have had split locals during this time and had the locals been split I doubt my trainee would have made this mistake.Frequency outage leading to locals being combined; when there definitely should have been split; is the biggest contributing factor to this event. My recommendations are make fixing frequencies; especially local frequencies; a much higher priority so we don't continue to keep working combined locals at a busy airport when they should be split.  Another recommendation is give us a 3rd tower frequency that we can use as a backup frequency if one of the tower frequencies is OTS (Out of Service). That way one frequency outage doesn't lead us to unsafely combining locals.

column121: I was working a combined feeder and satellite sector for ZZZ.  VA (Visual Approach) RWY XXL/ ILS RWY XXR was in use.  With almost no notice we lost the use of RWY XXR because of a tall vessel in the RWY XXR approach area at approx XA:00z.  This forced all AC to use RWY XXL.  I was vectoring all of the ZZZZZ arrivals to blend flows with the other feeder sectors; working arrivals into a satellite and working overflight AC.  This is not uncommon; but it does create a heavier workload.  Once RWY XXR reopened there was a bit of a scramble to reassign AC to the appropriate runways.  I had a lot of things to do and I had released an IFR from ZZZ1 Aircraft X.  I am not trying to assign any blame; but things were busy and the situation was just bad in general and a lot was happening. At approx XA:35Z Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z had a Conflict Alert (CA) in the final box.  Same altitude and closing; and I was honestly kind of in shock.  They were same altitude and the targets were nearly merged.  It was extremely distracting to say the least.  Aircraft X had departed ZZZ1 and was nearing the edge of the class D. He never checked in; so I had to call ZZZ1 to have them switch him.  I got him; radar ID'd him and put him on a heading away from the final box.  I couldn't climb him yet; so I assigned a 270 and went on to the next task.  Aircraft A was seeking flight following to ZZZ2 and was nearby so I gave him info about pattern traffic and changed his frequency.  He never read this back; then called me after to change his destination.  I was having an issue with his data tag and he them went to a vfr tag on his own.  He was leaving my airspace so I quickly assigned him a tag to try and get a handoff to ZZZ3.  At the same time Aircraft B was looking for flight following and for some reason his tag had been terminated.  I had basically 4 things going on in different corners of my airspace.  I couldn't get Aircraft B  to tag up because of a STARS flaw.  Aircraft A was pulling my attention away and messing with his transponder; and I was trying to sequence AC in a complicated RWY config.  Aircraft X called my to ask for higher about 10 miles into ZZZ4 airspace.  He was at 2000 in a 3000 foot MVA for approximately 5 miles.  I immediately coordinated with ZZZ4 and turned him back into my airspace.  I then climbed him and transferred him to the appropriate sector.Recommendation: This was honestly such a tense moment; and a high workload that you can pick your poison.  The supervisors were helping coordinate; but stupid things were drastically making my life harder.  Sequencing in these instances is typically the priority; but having to call a tower to talk to the IFR they just departed; 2 separate automation issues; and an honestly terrifying proximity of 2 AC made for the right blend of distractions.  The action was not on the left side of the scope; and I let an IFR get away from me to fix radar tags on 2 VFR AC and sequence jets to ZZZ.  I guess it was the straw that broke the camels back.  I think the biggest problem is that we get these tall ships in the harbor and they throw the operation into disarray.  There was no notice except; hey this is the last AC to XXR; make it work.

column121: We departed the gate and had a quick taxi to XXL @ Taxiway 1.  The takeoff was a normal with a strong crosswind from the south.  After takeoff (Approx. 1000ft) an ECAM appeared.  HYD Y RSVR LO LVL followed by I believe a PTU (Power Transfer Unit) Fault and a low pressure.  We told departure that we needed to stop the climb and take care of an issue.  At this time we had not declared an emergency.  We leveled at 5000ft; maintained 220 kts; on a heading of 270; and the autopilot was ON. The ECAM was announce and we decided that I would continue flying and the PM would run the ECAM.    The PM went through the items instructed by the ECAM.  I was flying and working the radios; but I believe the PTU was turned off and possibly the yellow engine pump.  After the ECAM was completed and the screens were normal; the PM contacted dispatch via ACARS and was given a frequency so that we could have verbal communication.  According to the PM communication was difficult due to poor reception.  After we discussed the situation; we decided that returning to ZZZ was the best option.  We discussed requesting priority handling and decide to do so because of the spoilers 2 and 4 being inop.  After our plans were settled I requested priority handling and notified ATC of our intentions; souls; and fuel on board.  ATC began vectoring us for an ILS to XYC.  The PM informed the FA of the situation and gave them a briefing.  Dispatch sent us landing distance numbers approx; 8900 feet which was well within the 10800 feet for XYC.  The PM ran through the Overweight Landing Checklist.  I configured early and dropped the gear early to burn more fuel to reduce the overweight landing issue; and the flaps would be moving slower than normal.  The autopilot came off at about 1000 feet.  The flight controls felt spongier than normal but not so much that aircraft was difficult to control.  The strong crosswind remained present.  I would consider the touchdown to be smooth. The Capt took the controls at 80 knots and taxied off the runway at Taxiway 2 and held on taxiway 3 short of 4.  Emergency vehicles were behind us.  We went to frequency XXX.XX where ground and emergency services were accessible.  Emergency service circled the aircraft and found no evidence of damage or fire.  The brakes topped out at 505C on the number 1 caliper.  The other were 380 to 425.  We discussed our ability to taxi in but were hesitant due to the brake temp and we had been made aware that a fluid was now leaking from the belly of the aircraft.  A tug arrived and we decided out of an abundance of caution that we would be towed in.  This took a while.  Mx (Maintenance) arrived and asked for the gear pins.  We had trouble locating the gear pins. They asked if the aircraft taxied fine. We stated yes and since the brakes had cooled significantly; we decided to taxi it back to the gate.  The aircraft was choked at the gate and the maintenance requests were sent in.
column123: Departing ZZZ on our third flight to ZZZ1; climbing out of 1000 feet we had yellow hydraulic reservoir low ECAM. Additional messages came up with that failure. I was the pilot monitoring; and I informed ATC that we needed too level off at 5000 feet to work a problem. I asked the FO if he was comfortable flying and working  the radios so I could run the checklist; and he was. He turned on the autopilot and continue to fly and work the radios. We ran through the procedure together; verifying everything was done correctly. At that point I tried a call me message for a frequency with dispatch and Maintenance Control. Since we were at 5000 feet; we had a hard time hearing dispatch and I've ended up telling them our plan was to return to ZZZ; the dispatcher was phenomenal and getting us landing data and information we needed for landing.  We advised ATC. We set up for a return to ZZZ and briefed the plan. I then called the flight attendants and advised them of the situation as well as notified the passengers. We were aware of the possibility of an overweight landing and had a discussion on burning the fuel or just going into land. We elected to land as we were down one hydraulic system. The landing was incredibly smooth and uneventful. Being that we were overweight and heavy; we had the fire trucks meet the airplane as a precautionary measure. Once off the runway; the fire trucks notified us that we did have hydraulic fluid leaking out of the belly; it was described as a slow drip. I communicated with dispatch and Maintenance Control on the ground for the safest course of action with hot brakes. I'm not sure who; but somebody sent us a tug so we thought we would use the tug to get back to the gate. Unfortunately; in the midst of the chaos; I could not find the gear pins in the flight deck as that back closet was dark and the gear pin holder was a dark color. This is no way in excuse that I could not find them; just telling you the real time situation as I was trying to communicate with everybody and find gear pins for the tug in. At this point; the brakes had cooled down enough that we discussed with maintenance and they thought it would be better if we could just taxi in so that's what we elected to do. (once maintenance arrived at the airplane. We did shut the engines down in preparation for being towed in). We started the engines back up and order a taxi back to the gate uneventfully. We coordinated with operations to chock us ASAP as the checklist says that the brake accumulator may not hold the aircraft in position. Maintenance personnel met us at the gate where we continued the discussion of what happened.

column121: Abnormal Aileron Control Feel. During preflight; the First Officer and I reviewed the logbook and noted a previously closed write-up stating: 'Noticed excessive yoke movement up to 2 units without aileron response.' The write-up was discussed during the departure brief. Control checks after start were normal. During departure from ZZZ; during departure while hand flying in moderate turbulence; the First Officer noticed an abnormal aileron control feel. During right aileron input; resistance was sometimes normal; sometimes significantly lighter than normal; and at times initially normal before abruptly becoming very light. Left aileron inputs were initially normal. The First Officer advised me of the condition and elected to continue hand flying while we discussed what he was experiencing. I subsequently hand flew the aircraft and immediately experienced the same abnormal and inconsistent aileron control feel the First Officer had described.Throughout this period; the aircraft responded appropriately to all control wheel inputs. However; the feel or resistance of the ailerons was highly variable; at times heavier than normal; at times lighter; and occasionally transitioning from heavy to very light during a single control input. We elected not to use the autopilot and to continue the climb to FL300 (planned FL370) to evaluate the condition; and coordinate with Dispatch and Maintenance before making further decisions and determining the safest course of action. There is no published QRH procedure that directly addressed the abnormal aileron control feel. The Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls QRH was reviewed as the closest reference; although it did not precisely match the condition observed. In accordance with our plan strategy; I transferred aircraft control and radios to the First Officer; who is very experienced and had a good feel for the aircraft. I contacted Dispatch and Maintenance Control via Crew Phone. Maintenance Control stated they were not aware of known issues with the aileron system that would produce the symptoms described and advised that the aileron system does not share characteristics with elevator systems that typically experience bearing-related feel issues. No additional guidance was provided. The abnormal aileron feel persisted; remaining variable.After further discussion; and considering the current condition in combination with the recent prior closed aileron write-up; we determined that although the aircraft remained controllable; we could not ensure an adequate margin of safety to continue to destination; nor could we be confident the condition would not worsen. We notified ATC and elected to divert to ZZZ1 which was previously coordinated with Dispatch. ZZZ1 was chosen to allow sufficient fuel burn to reach landing weight with minimal maneuvering; favorable weather; long runways; and crew familiarity. We started the APU; and initially remained at FL300/275 KIAS and did not change airspeed. To continue assessing controllability while burning fuel; we later descended to FL260 and further slowed to 250 KIAS to stay in smooth air and then later descended slowly to 16;000. Airspeed changes were then made in 5 knot increments; closely monitoring control feel with each change. The abnormal aileron feel remained variable throughout all speeds. We extended the landing gear and began configuring early to assist with fuel burn and continue evaluating controlabillity. As a precaution; we elected to limit bank angle to 15 degrees and elected to land Flaps 15 to maintain higher approach speed and roll margin. The aircraft was hand flown for the remainder of the flight; as we were unsure how the autopilot might respond given the abnormal aileron control feel.Below 10;000 feet; continuous light turbulence required frequent control inputs. The aileron feel remained abnormal and variable; however; aircraft control remained effective. The Non Routine Landing Considerations QRH was completed. We requested theILS Runway XXC at ZZZ1 and requested ARFF to observe the aircraft after landing. Descent and before landing checklists were completed; with continuous updates provided to the flight attendants and passengers. The landing was normal. We remained on the runway for a post landing Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) inspection; no abnormalities were observed. ARFF accompanied us during a normal taxi to the gate. The shutdown was normal. Passengers were reaccommodated onto another aircraft. After completion of the flight; both pilots discussed that we did not feel fit to continue flying. The ZZZ1 Chief Pilot assisted in removing us from further duty.  Threat and Error Management (TEM) was used throughout the event; including the decisions to notify ATC; divert to ZZZ1; restrict bank angle; slow and configure gradually; and land Flaps 15 to preserve controllability and safety margin.Cause: The following day I noticed a maintenance write up for this aircraft that air was suspected in the hydraulic lines. That would be a condition I believe would be consistent with what was felt on the controls.  However; that was not something considered during the flight as our attention was more about safe recovery of the aircraft.

column121: On flight XXXX at XA16; approximately 25 miles south of airport 1M9 while on frequency 124.27.   We were at cruise at flight level 340 and smooth air. There was an aircraft ahead of us approximately 12 miles at the time at 360. That aircraft started to descend into our flight path as we were both apparently heading to Memphis.  it seemed to be getting closer as it descended down and it was approximately 8 miles or so in lateral distance ahead of us. It was less than 1000 feet above us and continued Its descent to the same altitude of 340. Not knowing what type of aircraft or its call sign standing out to us. I didn't think much about it; I did make comment that it was not a Company A or same type aircraft due to its strobe lights not being the same. As a descended down to about 350 or less; we got a little light chop; and I thought that that would be it as we passed through its wake or as I assumed. Everything seem normal until it happened.Soon after we experienced a moderate chop and then successive small rolls to the left and right; followed by a heavier role to the right greater than 30° less than 45° as we did not get a bank angle; but the auto pilot disconnected. At this time; I told the first officer to manage it and then to climb to 350 immediately and which he did.  I responded to ATC telling them we are responding to a wake turbulence encounter and leveling at 350. The first officer over shot during the process and then descended back down to 350. We were then in smooth air at 350.I believe at this time ATC tells me that the traffic was a heavy airbus ahead of us about 7 miles or so leading to that situation. I contacted the flight attendants to check on their conditions and of the cabin.  They responded no issues no injuries. As we continue to Memphis following this aircraft; ATC allow us to descend with discretion so we maintained higher altitude throughout this flight all the way to landing to avoid getting in the wake turbulence.  Although we did experience just a little bit; but not bad on short final.Once at gate and debriefed Fo; I called Operations about clarification if write up is required in AFML (Aircraft Flight Maintenance Log) ( it is not explicit but vaguely assumed via 'severe turbulence ') I did write it up regardless. I then contacted dispatch and Maintenance Control and followed through the severe turbulence process with Maintenance Control. They stated the AP (Autopilot) disconnected due to slat or aileron miscomp or something when they remotely pinged the aircraft.
column123: We were flight XXXX ZZZ-MEM; level at cruise FL340. Conditions were smooth and clear. We were near the fix RAMRD when we started to get some turbulence that we didn't realize was wake turbulence from a HEAVY that ATC had started descending out in front of us. They had been at FL360 on the same route as us going into MEM. During their decent; we gained some distance on them and were at one point 6 nm in trail without warning from ATC. That wake turbulence very quickly turned into severe that kicked off the autopilot. I was the PF and grabbed the controls to correct back to level. The Captain suggested we climb to FL350 to avoid encountering any more wake. So we climbed and leveled at FL350 and the Captain notified ATC.After getting settled at FL350; the captain called the FA's to check on them and to see if there were any injuries.
