column121: The First Officer was flying a normal approach to Runway XXR. As the aircraft settled on to the runway; FO said that the braking felt a little weird and that the aircraft was not decelerating correctly. FO disconnected the AUTOBRAKES via brake pressure; and I said let's go to the next high speed [exit taxiway] 1 because I did not want to try and stress the brake system more. I took control of the aircraft and finished the rollout to 1; made a left turn and the aircraft brakes appeared to be grabbing; and letting go. I then made another left on to taxiway 2 and began taxing EAST on 2. I slowed for a second to gain a better understanding of what was going on. FO asked if I wanted him to tell ATC that we were having brake problems; I asked him to hold off until we got EAST of the next turn off taxiway 3 going eastbound because that was a NORMAL turn off and I wanted to get EAST of it before the next aircraft landed. After I past [taxiway] 3; we called ATC and told them we may need to taxi slowly because of brake problems. As the ground speed dropped below ANTISKID engagement speed; 27 MPH; the aircraft began to roll normally. NO more wobble; no more grabbing; so we continued.The tower asked if wanted different taxi routing because of the brake problem. I told them NO; I then explained to FO that I did want to heat the brakes up any longer on the longer route. I then said; FO; I'm not sure what is going on so we will leave both engines running for idle speed; control and avoid braking.ATC immediately cleared us across RWY XXL so we didn't have to stop; then taxied to 4; 5 and ramp on the bridge. I asked FO to input an ELB (Electronic Log Book) for the anomaly and he did. As I turned on 5; FO then got a clearance for parking via 5; 6 to the alley for gate X. I asked FO to contact maintenance because we need to have a discussion with them and because it was an international flight; I needed them to catch us before we went on to customs. On initial contact with Maintenance; they informed us we had a wheel FIRE; we notified RAMP to dispatch ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) to our location. FO asked if I wanted to evacuate and I said no we simply did not have enough information to that. I stopped the aircraft and made an announcement to the passengers and crew and told them we were not on the gate yet; and Fire rescue will be inspecting the rear tires. After a few minutes; I engaged with MX (Maintenance) Control and Ramp to find out where the ARFF was on the field and an ETA. Numerous employees gathered and took pictures from afar; but no one could tell me if it was getting worse. I made another announcement to the pax reassuring them that we were safe and the ARFF would be pulling up shortly.  Each announcement had to be translated for our passengers by the flight attendants. I made announcements every 5-7 minutes.ARFF arrived and got on the RAMP frequency; asked us to shut down the RIGHT engine; so they could inspect the right wheels; we complied. The Left  Engine was still running; the APU was running. FO asked about shutting down the LEFT engine; we did; and now the packs were running off the APU bleed air. We spoke with ARFF on ramp frequency for a minute and no one said an ACTIVE FIRE was present. As we sat there for about 5 minutes; no communication with ARFF; they elected to spray fire retardant on the brakes; 1st the RIGHT SIDE; then the LEFT side brakes. This forced Smoke and fumes into the cabin because the retardant struck the hot brakes; formed a smoke and the South wind blew it right into the PACK INTAKE system. As soon as it happened I reached up and turned off the packs; and made an announcement to the passengers and crew to remain seated. I later found out the Flight Attendants were getting ready to evacuate until they heard my announcement. This whole sequence of events took less than 20 seconds.I called MX on radio one and notified them I was no longer communicating with ARFF and that they just created a problem with smoke in the cabin. Poor communications between ARFF and the crew.Then ARFF told me to taxi into the gate; I told FO to tell them MX would be towing us; both engines were shut off. After a few minutes; I elected to turn the PACKS back on; made an announcement and asked the passengers to be patient.Numerous vehicles airport ops; MX; baggage handlers; police; etc.; were around the aircraft; but NO ONE was telling me about an active fire. Then MX showed up and requested that I through down the gear pins. RIght then I knew we were NOT on fire; and MX was going to set the gear pins for pull in to the gate. Again; no verbal confirmation from anyone.Ground personnel finally showed up; some frequency communication problems with them; then they pulled us into the gate about :40 total time from the fire notification by MX (Camera - not sure how they knew) and in at the gate. The passenger deplaned; I contacted MX again and requested a face-to-face with someone so I could give them a quick debrief. Someone came up; took my statement. I was informed right then… for the 1st time by the MX guy that we DID NOT HAVE a fire; only the hub cap melted. Good thing we didn't evacuate on just a report of a fire and not confirmation. I wanted to go down to the ramp but Customs had not released the aircraft yet. FO and I proceeded to customs; cleared customs got on the bus and called the Chief Pilot from the employee parking lot.

column121: When we were assigned the VUNOX1A arrival; ATC gave us further direct points on the arrival. Near GR259; we were cleared direct to the SAMPA intersection. Before reaching SAMPA; we were cleared direct to LOMEN (the final fix on the arrival) and assigned 6;000 feet as the final altitude.During the arrival; when ATC issued a clearance; they used the word 'VIA' for direct SAMPA. This led to some confusion on the flight deck. I verified with the controller what he meant; and he clarified that he wanted us at SAMPA at 6;000 feet. We rectified the situation; though the phrasing was non-standard.Before reaching LOMEN; ATC cleared us for the ILS 10L approach. At this point; we were slightly higher than the glideslope; and I noticed that the FO had not armed approach mode on the Mode Control Panel (MCP). I informed him that we were cleared for the approach and prompted him to arm the Approach button.By the time this was completed; he became preoccupied with the high altitude; he selected FLCH and dialed 3;000 feet in the MCP altitude window. Before I could warn him; he disconnected the autopilot and decided to follow the flight director (FD); which was providing incorrect guidance at that moment.Consequently; we received a GPWS 'GLIDESLOPE' alert. I told him; 'You need to go up; you need to capture that glideslope;' as I noticed he was below the slope and continuing to pitch the nose down.We were stabilized by 800 feet RA and completed the landing checklist. The weather was VMC; the field was in sight; and the glideslope was captured. Despite the instability prior to the 1;000-foot AGL stable approach gate; I decided not to call for a go-around; as I felt it would have caused further confusion in the cockpit. We landed without further issues and discussed the event during the van ride.Cause: One of the contributing factors to this event was the fatigue. Even though we all felt fine at the beginning of the flight; with rolling delays for a couple days; ever changing departure times and multiple long delay made things a bit harder on us.Suggestions: We were delayed due to aircraft maintenance; which caused rolling delays. I woke up on my own for the early departure; but there was no wake-up call.When I called dispatch; they told me they were having customs issues. Nobody updated the departure time until we were on the plane. Once we boarded; there was no ground crew available to load the aircraft; which caused further delays. Eventually; we were delayed by almost four hours; which contributed to our fatigue.

column121: After departing runway 07 on the LITRA1D departure climbing through 2500' we were alerted to traffic by Goldson Radar. Traffic was reported to be at our 11:00 position and 3;000 feet. At the time the traffic was reported we were IMC in a cloud.  Shortly after the report Aircraft Y showed up as a primary target at +200 feet and course converging.  About one second after that; we were clear of the cloud; I got visual contact with the converging aircraft and simultaneously we received an RA to descend.   The proper RA maneuver was performed by the First Officer with appropriate very aggressive flight control pressure to initiate the descent and avoid the collision.  We recovered from the maneuver at approximately 1900 feet.  Negative G forces were felt in the cabin as reported by the cabin crewCause:  Goldson Radar should not have cleared Aircraft Y to cross the RNAV departure course at an altitude that conflicted with the charted altitudes on the departure
column123: At the gate in BZE during the departure briefing we again discussed the threat of the number of small aircraft traffic and would mitigate that with looking outside and using caution on taxi and takeoff.  We were given push clearance from stand XX onto 'B' taxiway which meant we were pushed almost directly straight back.  As we were clear of our stand two smaller aircraft rapidly taxied through our vacated spot; joining taxiway 'A' towards runway 07.  Shortly thereafter we requested taxi clearance. As we reached the holding point for runway 07; the second of the smaller aircraft was given takeoff clearance and a turn to the north.  We watched them takeoff and start their turn north; well clear of our initial departure path to the east.  Tower asked if we had the traffic in sight; which we did.  We were given takeoff clearance; had a normal takeoff; and switched to Goldson Approach.  Following the LNAV; reaching BZ910 we started the turn to the north. Shortly thereafter we entered the clouds.  Sometime while we were in the clouds Goldson Approach pointed out traffic which we did not have in sight due to IMC. We then saw the target on TCAS to our left (west of us). We agreed it was probably the traffic that took off ahead of us; presuming they were continuing northbound as we didn't hear otherwise.  We were not in the clouds long when we climbed above them becoming VMC again.  It was at that time the captain (PM) visually acquired the traffic; TCAS target turned amber then immediately red with a commanded descend RA.  I aggressively pushed the nose down and realizing that wasn't enough pushed again as I pulled power back.  Once clear of the conflict; I resumed the climb and departure.  ATC was notified of the TCAS RA response by us.After getting our bearings again; the captain called the FAs to make sure they and the passengers were okay.  They did comment on the perceived negative G's but that everyone was ok.  We initially attempted to contact dispatch however neither of us could get the desk numbers to populate.  The captain then notified dispatch using ACARS. As Maintenance Control could not immediately see if the aircraft had been overstressed in the maneuver; we elected to continue to destination as any diversion short of destination would result in an overweight landing and potentially further overstress the aircraft. A logbook entry was made regarding the event.Cause:  The high volume of smaller light aircraft; the fast pace they operate (ie short approaches; short landing and takeoff roll; fast taxi speed); and the sometimes indecipherable communications from those pilots sometimes make it harder to keep situational awareness of where everyone is. We were asked if the traffic was in sight and it was until after takeoff and climbing through the clouds.  We had no way of knowing though what their intentions/clearances were after proceeding northbound and if being complied with. Ultimately ATC should have kept both aircraft well clear of the other either by extending our upwind off the departure path or not allowing the other aircraft to turn east across our path until we were further north. Also; as per the Jeppesen page; the stated IFR departure information was not followed assuming the proceeding aircraft was IFR as they climbed through a cloud layer.We practice responding to TCAS RAs every recurrent. After this experience I feel those are very benign and perhaps a more aggressive and faster paced scenario would be better served. We weren't afforded the luxury of time to watch the scenario build. Add to it that we were in an initial climb profile with pitch and power and when the event started below 3000 feet AGL. Aggressively transitioning from a high pitch and power to nose down; pointed down to the ground still initially with climb power causes a secondary startle effect in the 'float' feeling from the dramatic pitch change.  We can't replicate that part in a sim but the aggressiveness required to respond could be possible; decreasing that startle factor.

column121: Enroute to ABQ I had the Colter4 arrival loaded and the RNAV (RNP) 26 approach loaded into the FMS. ABQ ATIS was calling winds 260/08 and RNAV 26 in use.  We checked in with ZABQ and were not given any other information other than got you check in".  Several other aircraft checked in with ZABQ and then center stared letting people know "Whites Sand is testing GPS and ADS-B jamming." As we started setting up for the arrival and RNAV I noted we had high accuracy on the prog page; however we had zero satellites and no GPS signal.   We asked ZABQ how people are doing the RNAV app road into ABQ with no GPS and he said to do the RNAV visual.  We said we're not doing a night visual around mountains.  We asked for an early switch to ABQ approach to see what other people are doing.  Switching to ABQ approach two aircraft were in the same predicament we were in.  One aircraft elected to do the ILS runway 8.  They noted a 30kt tailwind until 300 feet AGL then a 5 kt tailwind at touch down.  At this point we only had about 7;000 of fuel and no listed divert.  The second aircraft did the same ILS 8 approach and reported them same.  I elected to do the same. We briefed the approach and I briefed the FO.  We flew the approach as advertised at 300 get the tail wind died off.  This caused our indicated airspeed to jump about 10kts at 300 for a brief moment the. Quickly captured back to on speed.  Landed and taxi in was uneventful.Cause: WSMR (White Sands Missile Range) regularly conducts jamming.  If this is known ahead of time we should add fuel and an alternate for a situation where the only approach to the runway in GPS.  Center and approach control need to communicate better to each other and aircraft inbound.  Center seemed to not think this was a big deal; approach was overworked with four inbound aircraft all unable to shoot the approach do to jamming; weather and all other runways beside 08/26 being closed."
column123: Immediately prior to top of descent into ABQ as we were setting up the cockpit for the RNAV (RNP) Z Rwy 26 approach we discovered that that our GPS was being jammed and operating in a greatly reduced capacity only receiving between 3-5 satellites at any given time with an operating mode of AIDED instead of NAV. This completely precluded us from preforming the approach to runway 26 which was the only runway open at the time with winds being reported as 270/8 kts and winds aloft being out of the west at approximately 30 knots until 300 feet above the ground. This put added pressure into preforming a tailwind approach in challenging conditions at night using the only available approach. As we crossed the mountains just east of the airfield I observed GPS 1 receiving only a single satellite and GPS 2 receiving no satellites. Multiple aircraft were adversely affected by this GPS jamming at and around our arrival time. This is a major safety of flight issue in ABQ when the winds are out of the west as this completely inhibits us from using any approach to runways 26 or 21. If the winds would have been above our max tailwind component we would not have been able to legally land anywhere as we were not filed with an alternate and did not have the fuel to make any airport without dipping significantly into our fuel reserves. We assessed after the fact that the closest company airport to us would have been ZZZ and at 200 miles away would have used up a significant portion of our remaining fuel. In my estimation if we would have had to divert there we would have arrived with around 30 minutes of fuel remaining onboard the aircraft given we arrived with around 70 mins of fuel in ABQ and assuming the approx 40 minutes of flight time to cover the 200 miles down to ZZZ. In the end we conducted a tailwind approach within limits to runway 8 however there is in my opinion a significant risk of aircraft flying to ABQ with jamming in progress not carrying the fuel for an alternate and not being able to land in ABQ because of tailwinds on the only useable approach as we were only between 2 and 7 knots of wind; depending on the exact aircraft; away from being unable to legally land in ABQ without using emergency authority.Cause: White sands missile range GPS jamming creating a significant threat to aircraft approaching ABQ with no filled alternate under clear weather in particular at night. It is my belief that as long as GPS jamming is underway at white sands every aircraft arriving at ABQ should have a filed alternate and carry sufficient fuel to reach it. In particular aircraft operating at night when winds are forecast to be out of the west.

column121: We were cleared for the RNAV XX approach to ZZZ by ZZZ center. The tower was closed. After passing fix ZZZZZ began descent from 3200 to 2000 as published. I was slowing and configuring per non-precision profile. I was fully configured by 3mi from FAF(ZZZZZ1). I chose to set the missed approach altitude but did not notice we had not Altitude Select (ALTS) capped 2000. We continued descending approximately 800fpm. The captain saw the deviation about 1700ft and called ALTITUDE; I said CORRECTING. We climbed back to the 2000ft published altitude prior to the FAF and then began normal descent to the runway. No further problems. The cause was my setting the missed approach altitude prior to ALTS capping the published altitude and not recognizing. Due to terrain the altitude change between segments on the approach is larger than no terrain areas and my feel for elapsed time was off for the altitude change compared to other non-precisions I have done. I did not verify the ALTS cap. From the start of the approach thing had progressed nicely and I got lulled into a complacency after we got fully configured.Suggestions: This is a sobering lesson knowing we were so close to the ground and I put us into a premature descent unknowingly. And only the captain recognized it. This will stay with me for a long time. I know to make sure we have captured an altitude before spinning the knob. Take a moment to be sure it's the correct timing for the input.
column123: On the RNAV Rwy XX approach in VMC; after crossing ZZZZZ at 3200' my first officer began descending to 2000' at ZZZZZ1. Shortly thereafter he called for the Flaps 45 & before landing check; so I went head down to run the checklist. As I was running the checklist; he set the go around altitude of 5600'; and as soon as I finished he stated go around altitude set since we were in visual conditions. I confirmed the altitude selection. However; I did not immediately notice that he did not let the plane reach Altitude Selection (ALTS) CAP; so we unintentionally descended below the altitude on prescribed on the chart roughly 4 miles before the final approach fix. As I began to scan I realized the mistake and called Altitude"; to which he immediately began a climb back up to 2000'. We continued the flight and landed uneventfully. We debriefed the event at the gate.Cause: Mismanagement of automation systems is the primary factor; but in talking to my first officer we also agreed that fatigue played a large role on his part- He had been awake for a long time. On my part; I needed to verify the Flight Mode Annunciator (FMA) right after returning from the checklist. Additionally; complacency could have had a part to play in it too; as it was visual conditions and an overall simple approach.Suggestions: In debrief I mentioned the dangers of creating unintentional; unlimited descents and how important it is to allow the plane to level off at assigned altitude on approaches; especially when low to the ground as the ALTS CAP mode is a safety feature installed for this exact reason."

Due to the potential fire hazard; we elected to stop the aircraft on the ramp rather than proceed to the gate.I immediately requested Fire and Rescue. There was a delay in their arrival; estimated at approximately 5-10 minutes. During this time; we maintained communication with ground personnel; the flight attendants; and passengers.Both engines were shut down at the request of Fire and Rescue personnel. Fire and Rescue approached the aircraft and initially reported no visible fire. Shortly thereafter; they began applying fire retardant to the brake area without prior coordination. As a result; fumes entered the cabin. Upon recognizing this; we promptly shut down both packs to mitigate further cabin contamination.Throughout the event; there appeared to be a lack of coordinated communication between Operations; Ramp; and Maintenance; which contributed to confusion and increased workload in an already time-critical situation.A tug was eventually dispatched; and the aircraft was towed to the gate without further incident.

Our GPS reception was restored about 10 miles east of waypoint JOKIM; the final waypoint on the assigned ZONNA STAR. As the result of restored GPS capability; we were able to execute a safe approach. My concern is GPS jamming by our government with no advance notice unnecessarily reduces the safety margin. With mountainous terrain and Davis Monthan airbase nearby; which can and has been mistaken for TUS; having to conduct a visual approach at night to an unfamiliar airfield unnecessarily complex. If we experienced a non normal requiring a divert to an area being jammed; the GPS jamming may have precluded a safe approach from being made. Is disabling commercial aircraft GPS capability necessary and wise?Cause: The causal factor was our aircraft GPS capability being jammed by White Sands. My recommendation is don't jam commercial aircraft GPS capability. If our government must jam GPS signal; duration must be the shortest possible timeframe and commercial aircraft should be routed so as their flight path will not be impacted by the jamming.

Our flight was completed normally without any need for maintenance action; calls; nor any other required report. This report is being submitted for informational purposes only.I'm not an engineer; however; I understand the difficulties that even the roadway engineering departments experience due to our extreme heat and moisture swings (one year drought; followed by torrential rains). It is my educated guess that the runway TDZ on 17L is somehow warping or that the concrete has become / is becoming deformed due to environmental conditions. I think that this requires action to prevent further degradation of the concrete and to avoid safety of flight issues for all aircraft."

Then tower called us to let us know that Aircraft Y would cross above us and to continue on course. I believe this event could have been prevented with better communication. I think tower could have instructed Aircraft Y to look for us sooner; or that he would call their turn to heading 320. I was tuned in to the local UNICOM frequency for the area; but we did not hear any calls from the other pilot about positioning. We definitely would have been within 500 feet from each other and at the same altitude; my best guess would be around 300/400ft. Once I entered the Delta airspace of our home airport and was set up in the left downwind; my instructor visibly noticed that that same plane was on final approach; and once I looked again at my plane's MFD it was at that point we saw them appearing on our radar. So it looks like they have ADS-B capabilities; but it may not be functioning correctly all the time. They landed a lot quicker than we did as I had to extend my downwind for traffic; but I wish I had found that pilot and gotten their contact information after the fact.

column121: During a landing rollout on Runway XX at ZZZ; the aircraft encountered a localized; quartering tailwind gust that was not reflected in the previous AWOS report. Despite following established traffic; the aircraft experienced significant directional instability shortly after touchdown.The combination of the high groundspeed from the tailwind and the LSA's free-castering nosewheel led to a diverging yaw that could not be corrected with full rudder deflection or differential braking. Recognizing that a high-energy ground loop on the asphalt was imminent; I utilized my PIC authority to make a deliberate; proactive transition off the pavement and onto the wide; level grass adjacent to the runway. This choice utilized the grass's lower lateral friction and higher rolling resistance to stabilize the aircraft. The aircraft was brought to a safe; controlled stop on the grass with no damage or injuries.Human Factors & Contributing Factors:Environmental: Rapidly deteriorating surface conditions were confirmed by METARs showing a 70-degree wind shift in just 20 minutes (from 130° at 08KT to 200° at 11KT); transitioning the runway from a headwind to a quartering tailwind while I was in the pattern.Herd Mentality: I initially deferred to the 'de facto' runway in use by other aircraft (two landed just before me) rather than independently verifying the current windsock indication during the final approach.Aircraft Design: The light wing loading and free-castering nosewheel make it sensitive to 'tripping' or pivoting on high-friction pavement during a tailwind-induced swerve.Corrective Actions & Lessons Learned:Personal Minimums: I have established a new personal minimum of a zero-tailwind component for this aircraft due to the narrow safety margins it provides during rollout in such conditions.Checklist Revision: I have modified my short-final flow to include a mandatory visual verification of the windsock to ensure surface conditions match my expectations; regardless of radio traffic; 'runway in use'; or AWOS.Safety Training: My previous tailwheel transition training was critical in recognizing the point of 'no return' on the pavement and choosing the more forgiving grass surface to dissipate energy safely.Systemic Recommendation:It is recommended that LSA manufacturers and flight/transition training providers include specific warnings in the Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) and Flight Training Supplements regarding the hazards of tailwind landings in these aircraft. Documentation should explicitly address how light wing loading and castering nosewheels can lead to rapid loss of directional control on pavement; which may not be intuitive to pilots transitioning from heavier GA aircraft.

Aircraft X was about 15 miles from the airport; he was issued traffic on Aircraft Y; who was turning for the right base.  Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight and was instructed to maintain visual separation. Aircraft Y was told that traffic landing RWY XXL had him in sight and was maintaining visual separation. While this was unfolding; we were in the process of opening a seond position so it was a stand alone scope. The second position was opened as Aircraft Y was given the base turn.  I was coordinating with the second position the sequence offline and who would be their first aircraft and the general sequence for XXL/R. An aircraft; 25 miles south of the airport on a right base; that we had determined was going be worked by the second position checked in on my frequency. I immediately gave them second position frequency.  At that time I realized that I was late turning Aircraft Y and he would overshoot the XXR final.  I gave Aircraft Y a 070 heading to try and salvage the situation.  I informed Aircraft X that the Aircraft Y traffic would be through their approach course and gave them the option to continue or climb. They opted to continue; reiterating that they had the traffic in sight.  I then saw that Aircraft Y must have gotten a TCAS-RA because they started to climb.  I never heard them report that they were responding to an RA.  I canceled the approach clearance and issued a 040 heading and climbed Aircraft Y to 4000.  I re-sequenced Aircraft Y back around and they landed without further incident. I feel that I should have held the Aircraft X at 4000 until I completed the vector to have Aircraft Y join the final. As soon as Aircraft X reported the traffic in sight I gave them the visual approach clearance.

column121: During takeoff roll started to have popping in ears at high speed.  After rotation it got worse and heard wind noise until gear retraction.  Ears get having to be popped multiple times.  I knew something was not normal so I asked to level at 3000 feet so we could check things out.  Once leveled off we asked for vectors around.  We noticed that the cabin pressure matched altitude which indicated no pressurization.  We looked for checklists.  We had no annunciations on the overhead nor on the recall.  After running the cabin depressurization checklist we noticed that everything was normal and the pressurization panel was in the normal operating position.  I contacted dispatch and got Maintenance Control on the line and we exhausted everything.  Told dispatch that we will be going back to ZZZ and would be landing overweight.  I burned as much fuel as I could before heading back and we had tower roll trucks for precaution.  We never declared an emergency.  Went over the overweight landing section and used the guidance to come in and land on XXR.  As soon as we put the gear down the noise intensified beyond normal which further indicated something was wrong.  We shot the ILS down and had a smooth landing.  We taxied off the runway and had the fire department check the brakes.  No hot brakes so we taxied to the gate.  Wrote up the aircraft pressurization and the overweight landing. At the gate MX (Maintenance) came aboard and asked if we had the equip door light on.  Which we told them we had not seen that light on the entire operation including no door annunciations on recall.  They told us that the e/e (Electronics/Equipment bay) door was open.  They then determined that the door annunciation switch was not working and that they needed to replace it.

ATC immediately gave me vectors and an altitude to avoid the aircraft; which I attempted; but aircraft continued to converge on me. Tried climbing and turning; but aircraft began climbing and following me too. With less than 100' indicated of vertical separation; I reduced power and began a descending right turn per guidelines that converging aircraft shall yield to the right. Mindful of not getting too close to the terrain; I leveled out and worked with ATC to travel out to the West to avoid any additional encounters with this traffic. In retrospect; I will be a lot more aggressive with modifying my travel direction to avoid non-communicative traffic. Instead of making a slight adjustment to my flight path; I plan to more intentionally alter my direction of flight to avoid any close encounters with such aircraft. Additionally; I will be more intentional with planning lessons to try to avoid being near untowered airports that may have a greater preponderance of non-communicative traffic.

column121: A student and I were on a post solo flight to check their work regarding maneuvers and pattern work at an uncontrolled field. We had already completed the maneuvers being evaluated at this point and picked ZZZ as the uncontrolled field to use for today's lesson. The student executed a pattern entry recommended by the FAA in which they overflew the field by 500' AGL and enter on a 45 degree to the downwind. The student and I proceeded to continue in the pattern making appropriate radio calls and normal landings/takeoffs while in the pattern. After our first full trip in the pattern another aircraft I noticed had shown up on ADSB; Aircraft Y. I proceeded to have visual contact with the other aircraft as they were cutting through the approach corridor for the runway the winds were favoring and we were using. The current winds at the time were 070 9kts from the ZZZ1 ATIS and the wind sock at the field confirmed this. We had quite a bit of lateral separation from this aircraft due to us being mid-field downwind for RWY XX at this point and elected to have the student side-step to provide additional separation just in case. I watched the aircraft turn Southbound and was 200' above pattern altitude. This led me to believe it was transient and it was transitioning through the airspace. I lost visual contact with the other aircraft after we turned final and they did not make any radio calls on the CTAF frequency for ZZZ. Focusing on the remainder of the pattern the student and I turned base and final completing a successful landing. Upon powering up the aircraft to initiate our takeoff I noticed Aircraft Y was short-final committing to their landing. The student and I exchanged flight controls. We were already close to our rotation speed roughly 3/4ths down the runway to which I took off and side-stepped to the left to de-conflict with the traffic. There was no ADSB traffic indication on our end showing this traffic and no conflict advisory. Given this situation I would likely believe if we had tried to stop it would've created a runway excursion or accident as the other aircraft continued to land behind us giving no indication of a go-around on their part.

column121: In cruise at FL400 light chop. Heavy thunderstorm activity 56 nm to west of our position; with tops estimated at 45;000.Position was south of nav point OHLAA off coast of Florida. Heading 210 due to 56 kts wind from 287/52kts.Experiences what felt like a mountain wave which I assumed was due to the the upper level winds caused by the ++THR [severe thunderstorm] activity 56nm to the west of us.In anticipation of an increase in speed I informed the PM I was selecting manual speed; and reduced our Mach # from M.85 to M.83. There was a 39 kt spread between our IAS and the BARBER POLE. Airspeed continued to increase and auto throttles slowly started to reduce. As it was evident that the speed was increasing faster than the auto throttles were responding I again informed PM I WAS disengaging the auto throttles and manually reduced the power back further and then to idle!. Within a second the airspeed increased into red line activating the aural OVERSPEED warning.I extended the AIR BRAKES AB1; and the speed stopped increasing but was still within overspeed regime by 10 kts. I decided not to disengage the autopilot but rather press the Touch Control Steering (TCS) button to raise the nose as the only option to reduce the speed out of the overspeed envelope. This did reduced the speed to below the BARBER POLE causing the aural OVERSPEED to cease.I released the TCS button allowing the Autopilot to immediately engage selected VS MODE on the guidance panel  to descend back to our assigned Flight Level; and manually took command of the throttles manually. I instructed the PM (Second in Command) to inform MIAMI CENTER what had happened and explained why.Miami asked if it was due to severe turbulence; to which we replied NO; it was type of mountain wave or rather severe thunderstorm wind turbulence wave that caused uncontrolled speed deviation most likely caused from the severe thunderstorm 56 nm west of our position.Other aircraft were also experiencing the same type of effects after our encounter.Once things had settled down and I felt we were away from any possible reoccurrence; I engaged the auto throttles keeping the M.83 (our turbulence penetration speed) set to manual.  We then verily reviewed the automation confirming we would keep the autothrottles (AT) / manual M.83 set until we both felt we were away for the area of concern. Miami ATC  seemed fine with our immediate explanation and we were not asked to call anyone; nor have we been asked to explain further to anyone.Suggestions: I have experienced mountain waves around the world many times as well as thunderstorm rotor turbulence. However after many hours I have never encountered such a rapid uncontrolled  speed increase (within seconds) as I experienced with this one. On reviewing our actions to control the rapid speed increase; I don't think we could have done anything different. Hindsight is always 20/20 and one could say had we waited with power at idle and AB1 (Air Brakes) extended; the speed would eventually certainly started to reduce.Although on reflection this might very well have been so; yet I could not be sure that the speed might not have continued to increased into a very critical regime where structural damage might have been encountered. Therefore utilizing the TCS and using pitch as a last resort to control the speed was;  I think the best cause of action.56 miles away from a ++THR is generally considered ample distance.

column121: CA PM FO PFWe were cleared for the visual approach XX backed up with the ILS. The FO had briefed me that he was just off low-time hours in type. We had done one leg together which I flew. On the approach we identified the traffic to follow and proceeded inbound. The FO was delayed in calling for configuration as we became established on the LOC. I am not the type of CA to micromanage speed reductions and flap configurations as long as it does not affect stabilized approach criteria. However; I prompted that we need to begin configuring as we are getting close to the aircraft ahead and do not know their ground speed. I believe we were at flaps 3 gear down when ATC notified us of a 60kt overtake and that S-turns to the right were approved. We slowed to final landing configuration and were stabilized at 1000'. I told the FO to perform S-turns and he proceeded; reaching 1000 fpm momentarily and getting low - hitting 3 red lights on the PAPI before he rejoined the course and corrected - but otherwise we continued to remain stable through 500'. ATC told us at about 200-300' to go around and the FO hit the TOGA button but I did not hear him make the call-out as he was a very soft-spoken individual. I looked down to make sure the throttles were in TOGA detent and made the call-out myself then retracted the flaps to position 2. We performed the gear retraction properly and at that time ATC told us to climb 2000' and turn heading (I believe) 270. I bugged the panel and selected Heading and was monitoring the FO hand flying when I prompted him to take the Autopilot (AP) to reduce our workload; which we engaged. It is hard to remember the exact sequence of events that followed because of the momentary stress but after I engaged the AP; we received another instruction to climb 3000' and turn heading (I believe) 330. It was at this time I noticed our speed reducing and realized we missed the FLCH 210 call out and were still bugged at our Vap of 131. I noticed the speed around 140kts approaching 131 quickly and because we were in a turn; the low speed tape was higher; buffering Vap speed. I called out Speed 210 Speed 210" as the speed turned amber and instead of spinning the speed bug the FO disconnected the AP and pushed the nose down; which threw me off since I was not expecting the action and now I was back to manipulating the control panel. We did not receive a stick shaker. I spun the speed to 210 and at the same time I saw we were in a nearly 40-45 degree bank and approaching 3000' with a high rate of climb. I told the FO "altitude" "bank". I pressed forward on the controls and we managed to level and the FO reduced the bank angle. I engaged the AP once more and we continued to speed up and clean up the aircraft. We came back for a second approach without incident and landed uneventfully. We parked and debriefed the event. It was the FO's first go-around. We discussed fixation which led to the omission of speed on both our ends and the importance of aviate-navigate-communicate. We discussed the speed tape and how at higher bank angles it can lead to accelerated stalls and that there was no need to turn to the heading so aggressively. I also encouraged him to call for AP early in order to reduce workload."

column121: Preflighted the aircraft normally and performed initial start up and run up checklists as usual. No unusual readouts or abnormalities. On takeoff and climb out all indications were normal. Outside of the airport environment I had my student put on the goggles and directed us to a gps fix for some simulated IMC practice. Upon leveling out at cruise I took controls and had my student remove the foggles; handed control back and had him run through his initial checklist for maneuvers. We loaded in the nearest fields frequency and made a call that we would be maneuvering 15nm NW of the field at 5;700. I demonstrated a set of steep turns and then we went over the importance of running our cruise checklist and scanning all instruments every time in between. Student attempted a set of steep turns and requested to practice another set. We ran through the cruise and instrument scan and noted no abnormalities. We went over the importance of finding good visual reference points; and he attempted a steep turn to the left. After completing and leveling back off; I re-scanned the instruments and noted the Ammeter read out was low (around 2 or 3). I looked to the annunciator panel and noticed there was no illumination and the engine instruments digital screen was flickering and dim. Upon noticing this I took controls and had my student get his checklist to check the alternator low / inop checklist. At this time the Primary Flight Display (PFD) gave an AHRS failure notification and inop readouts for our attitude indicator and heading. Simultaneously both of our G430s went black and our PFD /Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) flashed off and back on. We ran the troubleshoot checklist and verified circuit breakers had not popped; they hadn't; attempted to reduce the load by shutting off the fan; shutting off lights; tried turning battery master and alternator off and back on; turned on the power for the standby attitude indicator and it worked alright for a couple minutes before flagging that it was inop. Nothing worked; and at this time we were a little over what looked like 10nm from the closest airport ZZZ. I made the decision to head to ZZZ and as it was an untoward field and G430s were black screened; I squawked 7600 for loss of comms and attempted to transmit in the blind. Called that we were approximately 10nm NW of the field and inbound for a landing with no electrical power. ZZZ center responded asking if we could hear them; if we needed assistance; and informing us we were transmitting on guard. I responded with our location and intentions and that was when we lost our standby attitude and our PFD / MFD went black. ZZZ center asked if we were able to swap and transmit on the local CTAF. I responded unable as we still did not have the 430s. A nearby aircraft also on guard called center and offered to transmit on our behalf on the local CTAF. Center agreed and we continued inbound to ZZZ prior to landing we lost all electrical. We landed; taxied to the ramp; secured and post flight inspected the aircraft. The only abnormality we found was a significant drop in oil level. In pre-flight it was 6.5 and in post flight it was 5.5 at most

As a former Chief Pilot and Check Airman and former Chief Flight instructor; I have never seen anything so dangerous; unprofessional and poorly run as the facility at ZZZ; nor have I seen such a wrong allocation of Class D Airspace when quite clearly; Class C Airspace as a bare minimum should be applied.There is no flow for departures and arrivals by sector; no reporting points; no entry or exit altitudes. column121: I was on short final at ZZZ for runway XX. It was sunset. The entire runway was in shadow. The sun was in my eyes from the sunset at my right. I had repeatedly tried to activate the PAPI using 5 clicks on the radio; but it was not activating and was discussing with my pilot/passenger in the right seat why it was not activating. I did not realize that I was on the wrong frequency and not on ZZZ CTAF. I made a call that I was on final runway XX at ZZZ about 3 miles out. I did not see any other aircraft on ADSB north of the field; and I'm not sure I looked south of the field on the map to see if there was anyone on ADSB. The wind was calm; so either runway was a candidate for takeoffs and landings. At about 500 feet AGL/MSL my right-seater and I both noticed at the same time an aircraft's landing lights on the runway. I was doing a short field landing; so was slow; and so I carefully broke off to the left without adding G loading; adding full power; and gently entered a climb with full flaps; gradually working the flaps out. The aircraft must have just landed on runway XY without me hearing them on the radio because I was on the wrong frequency; and without realizing I was on final for XX because they didn't hear my transmission; and they probably didn't notice me on ADSB; if they even have it. Once I was in a stable climb; I realized I wasn't on frequency and changed to CTAF and heard the other pilot calling me. I replied explaining it was entirely my fault because I had been on the wrong frequency; and the other pilot was gracious about the situation. I'm assuming the other plane must have taxied off the runway and to the ramp because I didn't see them after that. We set up for another landing; which was uneventful.The problem was that I don't have a correct-frequency check as a checklist item; and skipped verifying that I was on the correct CTAF. This was compounded by the runway being entirely in shadow and the sun in my eyes. The PAPI not turning on should have alerted me to the fact that I was on the wrong frequency. The short field landing I was doing also had me in a nose-high attitude behind the power curve; which made it slightly harder to see down the runway. I was also focused on maintaining the plane at a low airspeed; lined up for landing; during the slow approach; which is a bit more demanding and may have been an additional distraction from the issue unfolding. The plane that had just landed on XX may have turned on their landing lights on the runway to alert me of their presence; because neither my right seat pilot/passenger or I noticed them until the plane appeared halfway down the runway. To avoid this in future I plan to add a frequency check to my checklists; make sure I run my checklists every time; make sure my landing lights are on for takeoffs and landings; and consider what else may be wrong when I notice something 'weird' like a PAPI not activating.

column121: The Captain and I were doing a leg of a multiple day trip. It was a flight to ZZZ. Captain was the PF and I was the PM. We were setting up for the ILS XXR into ZZZ. Weather was about 4sm and overcast around 1500'. We were vectored for the approach around ZZZZZ at 2500' and cleared for the approach. Captain armed the approach. The MAX9 captured the LOC and GS roughly at the same time causing the airplane to aggressively pitch down attempting to catch the glideslope. Airspeed was increasing rapidly toward the barber pole; decent rate was increasing rapidly and Captain attempted to override the autopilot by pulling back on the yoke. He did not disconnect the autopilot. As he saw the airspeed increasing he extended the speed brakes. Airspeed is at the barber pole; aircraft pitching down aggressively and we hear Sink Rate; Sink Rate." Captain disconnects the autopilot (AP); pitches up very slightly and banks right. I said "roll wings level" he rolled wings level momentarily; still high on the GS and turned to the right again; ignoring the flight directors. I said again; "wings level" and put a little pressure on the yoke to get the airplane level. Captain said "UPSET!" We were not in an upset condition and I was afraid Captain was going to pitch the aircraft down; I said "my controls". I took control of the aircraft and executed a go around procedure at 1200 Agl in IMC. We got runway heading up to 4000'; cleaned up the airplane and I asked the Captain if he wanted the controls back; he said "yes". I gave him the controls and requested vectors for the approach again with an extended final. Once on the ground we debriefed the situation. The Captain admitted he was disoriented and was very confused about what had happened. We talked in depth about what happened and I made it clear how scary the situation was. The Captain just came off the 777 and just completed 737 IOE."
column123: Uneventful leg from ZZZ1 to arrival on the ZZZZZX arrival.  We briefed by the card and identified a possible short vector as well as the weather as potential threats.  I was vectored off of the arrival to a 300 heading to intercept XXR ILS's final; turned to 280 and maintain 4000 feet.  I was then turned to an ILS intercept heading; don't remember it; and cleared to descend to 2500 feet.  The airplane was at flaps 5 and slowing to 180 knots.  We were then cleared to maintain 2500 feet and 170 knots till a 5 mile final.  I started slowing to 165 at about a 6.5 mile final. The vector brought us just inside of ZZZZZ at 2500 feet.   I called for gear down and flaps 15 then 25 a few seconds later.   The airplane intercepted the LOC and GS at the same time and I called to set TDZE.  The airplane was a a half dot high and still in a 20-30 degree turn intercepting Final Approach Course.  The airplane dumped the nose to get on the path and the speed rapidly increased to almost 190-195.  I recognized the speed increase and pulled the speed break out to control it.   It was not slowing and we got a sink rate; pull up call.  (lowest alt was 1000 feet) I clicked the autopilot (AP) off; pulled up and turned to the right; which was the wrong way.  My FO recognized that I was disoriented challenged me twice to roll wings level; which I though I was doing.  He took the controls and executed the go around (GA).  The GA was challenging due to the confusion; but he executed it.  I took the comms; we cleaned up the aircraft and completed the after takeoff checklist.  Tower directed  to fly runway heading and climb to 4000 feet and later boxed back around to the right to try again.  We resequenced the box for the ILSXXR.  I felt fine; so I retook the controls on the downwind while the FO did the descent checklist.  The FO asked for a longer vector and I flew the approach and landing uneventfully.  Once at the gate; we thoroughly debriefed the event and determined that between the short vector; intercepting the LOC/GS simultaneously; the steep decent (high airspeed) and disorentation led to the event.  We determined as well that the CRM skills of Situational Awareness; and monitor/cross-check by the FO fixed the situation.

column121: While operating flight from ZZZ1; we received a cabin altitude warning indication and associated master warning and horn. We were passing FL260 to our assigned cruising altitude of FL320. We performed the immediate action items (O2 masks; established communications; seatbelt sign on) and FO advised ATC that we had a pressurization issue and requested an immediate descent lower and then clarified 10;000 ft. The autopilot and auto throttles were disconnected and I requested LVL Change and 300 KIAS. The speed brake was utilized as well. While descending I observed that the cabin pressure was slightly above 10;000 ft and it didn't get much higher than that. It got very busy due to initial difficulty communicating (mask and volume issues); ATC requesting details and the FAs immediately trying to contact us multiple times as well. We didn't initially request priority handling since the focus was flying the airplane first and dealing with our issue; but we eventually did due to the fact that we were going to land overweight. When FO was performing the Cabin Altitude Warning or Rapid Depressurization/ Descent QRC he discovered that the pressurization switch was already in manual when he got to step 6. While he was performing the checklist; i was still hand flying in the descent to 10;000 ft. The FAs were concerned that we were concerned about our well being and tried to enter the Flight Deck (FD) utilizing the FD door EMERGENCY ENTRY button. This occurred after they attempted to call the flight deck a few times and knocking on the door as well. What they didn't know was that we were very busy dealing with the checklist and ATC concurrently. When we heard the DOOR DOOR DOOR audio; FO performed the immediate action item for the flight deck door and pressed the HARD LOCK switch. We were able to eventually advise them that we were very busy and that we'd contact them when we get a chance. After completing up to step 17 of the CABIN ALTITUDE Warning non-normal; we discussed diverting to ZZZ. We informed dispatch of our issue and our intentions to go to ZZZ. They eventually replied and asked if we requested priority handling and we informed them that we did. I slowed the aircraft to 250 KIAS at 10;000 ft as to not feel rushed dealing with our issue. The FAs were contacted and the brief was performed. The passengers were also briefed of our issue and our intentions to divert to ZZZ. Everyone was also informed about the emergency equipment on standby and they were going to be there as a precaution. The divert* function had been completed; aircraft re-cruised and set up for the arrival into ZZZ. Since we were landing overweight; we calculated our landing distance utilizing the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table. We were given vectors for ILS XXL and conducted a FLAPS 30/AUTO BRAKES 3 landing. After landing; we exited runway XXL and came to a complete stop so Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) could inspect the aircraft exterior for any damage. After none was noted; they departed the scene and returned to their base of operation. We eventually taxied to the gate. After we completed the parking checklist; we spoke to one of the maintenance technicians. They were debriefed. Afterwords; I contacted the Chief Pilot and advised him that we were ok to continue. Electronic Log Book entries were made for the cabin altitude (occurrence altitude and cabin altitude indication noted) and overweight landing (smooth landing and weight noted (…approximately 8200 lbs overweight). Outside the flight deck; we had to opportunity to conduct a thorough debrief. We discussed aspects of how we handled the situation (workload management and situational awareness) and the fact that we were able to cover all the steps dealing with our issue and safely divert to ZZZ. Communication is what could've gone better. We discussed how the warning horn was a distraction before cutout was selected; establishing communication with masks on; ATC callingus while we were doing checklists and the FAs immediately trying to contact us numerous times as well. The primary issue though was how we both missed the pressurization switch in the manual position. We discussed about the possibility of confirmation bias regarding the switch position; but we also discussed ways to prevent a repeat of undesired outcome of events.
column123: On climbout to FL320 at approximately FL270 the CABIN ALTITUDE warning light illuminated and warning horn started sounding.  We accomplished our immediate action items(O2 masks on; establish communications; and seatbelt sign on); and I asked ATC for a descent to 10000' stating we had a pressurization issue.  The CA; PF; initiated an immediate descent.  The CA called for the 'CABIN ALTITUDE Warning or Rapid Depressurization/Descent' QRC.  As I was accomplishing the QRC and got to item 6 I noticed the pressurization controller switch was already in manual and the MANUAL green light was illuminated.  I looked at the cabin altitude and saw approximately 11000'.  Also at this time the FAs began trying to call the cockpit. I attempted to establish communication with them but was unable initially; and was prioritizing the checklist and communication with ATC.  This quickly escalated to banging on the flight deck door and sounding of the 'door; door; door' alarm.  I pushed the hard lock button and attempted again to get in contact with the FAs.  I was able to very faintly hear them over the speaker and advised them we had a pressurization issue; we were descending to 10000' and to stand by. With the O2 masks on and with how busy we were I was unable to discern if they had heard me very well at this point.  I continued with the QRC and eventually the QRH.  We leveled at 10000'; took the O2 masks off and I established better communications with the FAs; restating the situation and asking if they passenger O2 masks had dropped; they had not. 	Level at 10000' at 250 kts and with the masks off and the QRH completed to the deferred items;  the CA spoke with the passengers about the situation and we discussed options between ourselves and with dispatch; eventually concluding to divert to ZZZ. ATC had already asked for souls and fuel onboard but we confirmed with them that we were a priority aircraft.  I then checked the LANDING DISTANCE NORMAL CONFIGURATION - FLAPS 30 (800) table in the Flight Manual (FM) for an overweight landing at 155.6lbs.  After confirming the runway length required we completed the deferred items checklists and the CA made an uneventful landing at ZZZ.  Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) was standing by and checked the aircraft out after we exited the runway with no findings.  We then taxied to gate XX. We debriefed the event as a crew thoroughly; the CA called the Chief Pilot and we put in Electronic Lob Book report for the CABIN ALTITUDE warning; and the overweight landing.   	On the descent while accomplishing the QRC was the first time that either of us noticed the pressurization switch to be in manual.  Both the CA and I remember verifying the pressurization panel was in the correct configuration during the initial flow; the preflight checklist; and the before takeoff checklist. Whether it was confirmation bias and the switch was in fact in the wrong position prior to takeoff or the switch was bumped during flight we are not entirely sure.

column121: Contacted MIA ground for taxi. Controller advised expect Rwy 8L for takeoff and to taxi via Txy K to holding point for Rwy 8L. As we crossed the hold short line for Rwy 8L; tower advised us to proceed onto hold for Rwy 8R.  I advised that we would need a few minutes to run checklists. I advised tower and he said to then expedite and hold short Rwy 8R; traffic on 2 mile final. CA advanced throttles; but we did not clear Rwy 8L in time and traffic on final was directed to Go Around.  Holding Short of Rwy 8R we completed all the runway change items one last time and rest of departure was uneventful.Cause: Change of Runway assignment followed by expedited instructions to cross and then on to the new runway and hold before crew could run required checklists.  I also should have been more vocal about our requirements before attempting to cross Rwy 8L; but with the hold short instructions initially provided for the other side; I thought we would have time while holding short of Rwy 8R.Suggestions: When workload is high and expedited instructions are received to cross an active runway; request hold short of that runway to ensure all requirements are completed to prevent conflicts.
column123: Our preflight was normal.  We had the aircraft set up for a departure off of runway 08R and also had the numbers for 08L.  We blocked out early.  Upon receiving initial Taxi clearance we were told to taxi via K to runway 08L and expect 08L for departure.  We immediately reconfigured the aircraft for 08L and had the runway change checklist completed before crossing taxiway K7.  Around approximately taxiway Z the ground controller had us switch to tower and monitor.  We were approximately abeam the beginning of taxiway K1 when the tower controller said 'Aircraft X; cross runway 08L hold short runway 08R traffic five miles out I need you to expedite.' We proceeded to cross 08L and were waiting to reconfigure for 08R until we were stopped and holding short of 08R.  All numbers and  power settings were exactly the same.  We had discussed and noted this before initial taxi. We just had to select runway 08R; reenter V speeds;  and repeat the runway change checklist. As we were crossing the runway 08L hold short line the tower controller said 'Aircraft X Line up and wait runway 08R.'  We responded we'd need a minute to change the numbers and run the checklist.  The controller then said 'Aircraft X hold short  runway 08L.' We responded 'Unable we have already crossed the hold short line.'  The tower controller then said 'Then I need you to expedite crossing 08L and hold short 08R traffic two mile final.' We had stopped when he initially told us to hold short and were now trying to expedite again. At that moment I immediately observed the aircraft on final begin their go around.Cause: When receiving our initial taxi clearance the controller initially gave us 08R then said 'hold on ….'  there was about a three to five second pause then he came back and said 'Taxi via K to runway 08L.'  I believe during that pause the ground controller likely checked with the tower controller or someone else and asked if it was ok to give us 08L. We did not ask for this however I think they were just trying to be accommodating. I think there was some sort of miscommunication between ground and tower and that translated into the tower controller giving us 08R when the ground controller had given us 08L.  In the moment the tower controller got audibly agitated with us as I felt he thought we weren't prepared.  In reality we were fully prepared for either runway and were set up for the runway given.  I just should have refused to cross runway 08L at the initial instruction until we were fully set up again.  In past experience I have also had them do almost the same thing previously to me. The previous time I stopped prior to 08L; reconfigured for 08R; then they eventually came back and reassigned us back to 08L prior to takeoff.Suggestions: In hindsight when the controller initially issued a runway different than we were expecting I should have just held short of runway 08L and told him we were going to have to change numbers and run the runway change checklist there.  I was trying to make it work in the wrong place.  Going forward I that's what I will do.

column121: I was flying aircraft x from EUL for solo training under part 91. I departed EUL and flew westbound in a continuous climb to 12500 MSL approximately 15 miles south of ONO. After maneuvering at 12500; I began a descent eastbound to 08500 MSL approximately 12 miles west-northwest of EUL; where I performed several standard maneuvers. Upon termination of those maneuvers; I began a descent on a 090 heading from 07500 MSL to a planned altitude of 03400 MSL with intent to join the 45 entry to the runway 30 right-downwind at EUL. During this descent I made standard radio calls on EUL CTAF MHZ including my callsign; type; location; altitude; heading and intentions. No radio calls were received which would have indicated conflicting traffic. At an altitude of 05700 MSL; I noticed a traffic alert on my EFB. The traffic was located at my one o'clock; 300 feet low; opposite direction; climbing; at approximately 1 NM range. I immediately applied full power; initiated a climb; and briskly rolled the aircraft into a 35 degree right-hand turn. Upon taking evasive action; I visually identified the conflicting traffic. The conflicting traffic was observed visually and via ads-b in an approximately 30 degree left-hand climbing turn. Observing the conflicting traffic in a left-hand turn; I increased my angle of bank to 45 degrees in the climbing turn. After observing traffic pass below me; I continued the right-hand turn to re-join my original course. During the evasive action; I climbed to a maximum altitude of 06200 MSL. The minimum observed vertical separation from ads-b data on my EFB was 200 feet.An attempt to raise the conflicting traffic was made on CAF and UNICOM MHZ after the conflict was resolved. No response was received.At the time of the incident; my aircraft was equipped with ads-b in and out; and I was utilizing an EFB with live ads-b traffic data from the aircraft superimposed over the sectional chart. At the time of the incident I was relying on visual traffic scanning and pilot-to-pilot radio communications to avoid other traffic. I was not actively scanning my EFB for traffic. If I had used my EFB more proactively during this descent; I likely would have noticed the conflict sooner and been able to avoid the conflict without aggressive maneuvers. During this incident; the conflicting traffic utilized non-standard collision avoidance technique by initiating a left-hand turn and continuing a climb to avoid opposite direction; higher altitude traffic. Because of this; a collision hazard existed throughout the evasive maneuvers; and altitude alone prevented a collision.During this incident; I do not recall hearing radio calls which would have indicated a collision hazard from the conflicting traffic. I was also unable to raise the conflicting traffic on the EUL CTAF after the incident. This serves as a reminder to actively listen to the CTAF when operating in the vicinity of an airport; and to make standard radio calls regarding your position; altitude and intentions.The conflicting traffic is owned and operated by a flight school. This raises questions of traffic awareness and avoidance while instructing; and ensuring that a competent person is actively looking for traffic.

column121: Returning to CXP after a discovery flight with multiple ac in the pattern and transiting the area north and south at CXP. we approached the field from the south to enter the 45 for runway 27. We entered the 45 with  Aircraft Y turning left downwind. we established and made frequent radio calls x 2 on the 45 at 3 miles and two miles; at left downwind midfield and abeam the numbers 27. sometime and almost 'stepping on another radio call I heard 'I'll be slow' assuming the call was associated/from Aircraft Y. not aware of what class or type Aircraft Y is; I interpreted ' I'll be slow' as I need to slow ourselves down or create space. I radioed that I would extend our down wind; I slowed ac further by lowering more flaps than normal and waited for Aircraft Y to pass my left wing (they were on final) and waited another 3-5 seconds to turn base. as I turned left base I also was slightly high. I then turned final to see comfortable spacing between our ac and Aircraft Y. We were about 0.5 to 1 mile from the numbers; Aircraft Y appeared almost halfway down the runway.  I was a bit high and utilized a slip to establish on glideslope; as soon as I saw pink(red) over white I removed the slip; maintained a stabilized approach.  with good spacing I felt we could continue to landing. Aircraft Y appeared to be at least if not more than half way down the runway and landed with what appeared slow to no movement. less than 5-10 seconds the spacing became uncomfortable and a go around was performed. full power with carb heat off nose pitched for increasing as. The ac didn't feel as thought it was increasing speed or climbing as it normally does; I performed a flow check and found the flaps still full. The flap setting was set to 10 degrees and the as and eventually the altitude increase. As the we climbed out two radio transmissions announced concern for the proximity of my ac. we performed the go-around in the pattern and landed without further events. I did attempt to find the Aircraft Y pilot  for  purposes of a debrief without success. I believe was ignorant to the type of Aircraft Y and how slow it really can be; and its normal taxi operation. I could have asked but the radio traffic was heavy enough I felt pressured to be short and succinct. I also believed I had enough spacing initially. I could have given more spacing than I thought I needed or performed a go around immediately. I felt I hesitated on my decision due to perceived spacing; the extended time needing to enter the traffic pattern. Possibly 'get there itis' was a factor due to another reservation behind ours; and we were running late due to the heavy traffic and maneuvering required. Last but not least having a goal of remaining minimum 500 feet from now landing aircraft and setting new personal minimums to 1500 feet horizontally with landing AC seems to be a good start; possibly increasing to 2000 feet. Also My muscle memory didn't automatically go to the flaps on the go around. I teach my students it verbally but I didn't automatically reach for flaps. So my going to go do go-around training with a flight instructor and build that muscle memory back into my routine.

column121: On descent into IXD we were given the option by ATC  to fly the ILS 36 approach or fly a visual approach. We had briefed the ILS prior; but having the field insight I elected for the visual. We were cleared for the visual and told to contact tower. We switched frequency and cleared to land. I glanced at the approach plate and saw the glide slope intercept at 1580. Being visual I asked for 1500 in the ALT select. I began my a gradual descent and adjusted my heading to intercept final. As we leveled at 1500 I noticed that we appeared much lower than anticipated and further away than I initially believed. I elected to stay at 1500 and intercept the glide slope as we got closer in.As we were looking outside at the field as we got closer; the terrain actually was beginning rise; triggering the aircraft to alert Landing gear; Landing gear. I asked for the gear. The gear was selected and I began requesting flaps. Flaps 1 and 2 were selected as we began to configure to land. As we were configuring I looked down at the PFD (Primary Flight Display) just in time to see the terrain turn yellow and get a terrain proximity alert then a pull up command.Cause: After shutdown; we debriefed the incident. After reviewing the approach plate I saw I had mistakenly seen and requested the altitude at ZIXAT not the altitude at the FAF SKINI. Complacency stemming from a nice early morning flying into a scenic area. Not reacting to multiple clues of rising terrain. No additional advisories from approach or tower to check altitude. Not excusing my mistakes or complacency; but may have triggered us to take action sooner.I pitched up adding power to climb. I leveled off still at roughly 2000 were I waited to intercept the glideslope before continuing descent on the approach. Once on the glideslope I continued the approach to land.Suggestions: Moving forward if an approach has been programmed and briefed; given the option to fly the approach or take a visual I will elect to continue on the approach as the difference would have been a few additional vectors to final. With regard to visual approaches I will continue to back them up with vertical guidance when available and be more cognizant of both information available to me on approach plates; airport information; and visual cues.

column121: At XA:30pm while conducting the visual approach into XXR at ZZZ I called for the landing gear down.  At that time we received a GEAR DISAGREE R CAS (Crew Alerting System) message and the right amber X on the gear indication for the right main.  I decided to go around when I saw the indications.  After the after takeoff checklist we asked for delay vectors to run the appropriate QRH checklist for the CAS message.  After running the checklist we still had an amber X for the right main gear indication and the CAS message. We then climbed to 10;000 ft where I was able to get a hold of the Chief Pilot who was Person A at the time. He confirmed with me that all of the items were done on the checklist.  He then stated we should request priority handling since we still had the amber X for the right main gear indication.  We did request priority handling.  We then discussed the landing and the threats associated with a potential unsafe gear and also an emergency evacuation if needed.  After the approach checklist I requested a low approach to see if the right main was out. It was dark but I thought I would try.  When the flaps were selected full; the amber X turned to a red X and we received the audible 'landing gear' warning that was very loud and continued which made it hard to communicate between us and tower.  The first attempt the emergency vehicles could not tell because of the runway light reflection.  They asked if we could do it again and they would aim spotlights at the landing gear.  On the second low approach they were able to see that the right main was down.   We then came back around and ran the approach checklist again and landed. The plane landed without incident but I elected to stop on the runway until emergency vehicles could inspect the airplane for any anomalies with the landing gear. They saw none so made a left turn on 1 and exited the runway and shut the plane down on 1 and was towed in from there.  Person A the Chief Pilot was helpful along with ZZZ tower and emergency vehicles.

column121: During takeoff from ZZZ in VMC conditions and LNAV deselected due to vectors from ATC; the CA nav display and Flight Director (FD) lost heading guidance. I (CA) was flying. Following completion of the After Takeoff checklist and once at a safe altitude; it was determined that the FO had full FD and NAV guidance; so controls were transferred and COMMAND B selected while I referred to the QRH. There were no FAULT indications on the overhead; and no procedures in the QRH to address the loss of heading guidance. No Circuit breakers were tripped. I assumed control of the aircraft to allow the FO to search the QRH for an applicable procedure with the same negative result.I transferred control back to the FO; did a thorough scan of the overhead and discovered that that the Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 selector switch was in ATT vice NAV. With concurrence from FO; decided to switch the IRS to NAV mode; which led to a complete loss of navigation data on both sides and autopilot disconnect. We had attitude guidance and altitude guidance from the FD; but were down to magnetic compass for heading. Notified ATC; and let them know we were trouble shooting the issue. There were no procedures in the QRH or AOM to restore the NAV. We coordinated through Dispatch with Maintenance Control (Crew Phone was down due to loss of WiFi); but Maintenance Control only asked if there were and circuit breakers tripped and had no alternative solutions. We decided that proceeding to our destination without navigation was a poor choice so requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ1; which was reporting VMC. With vectors from ATC; we hand flew the aircraft to an ILS/visual intercept where we regained FD guidance for the approach using raw data and landed without incident.Cause: The major factors that we identified as a crew that led to this were the inadvertent selection of ATT during preflight by the FO; not catching the lack of Flight Mode Annunciator 'HDG SEL' annunciation; lack of FD guidance at TOGA during the takeoff roll and selection of NAV inflight after the original issue was identified. There is a procedure in the AOM for inadvertent selection of ATT during pre-flight on the ground; but nothing for discovering the condition once airborne. In retrospect; without guidance we should have left the switch in the ATT position with the good data on the FO side; but it would be helpful if there were procedural guidance for this condition inflight.
column123: During takeoff from ZZZ; in VMC. LANV deselected; radar vectors on departure.CA PF; his Nav display lost heading guidance and Flight Director (FD). I FO PM; completed after takeoff checklist. Once at safe altitude. We determined FO side had all information; so aircraft control was switched to FO .CA was now PM and referred to QRH. There were no fault indications; no procedure addressing loss of heading guidance. No circuit breakers tripped. CA took aircraft back to be PF; and I also verified QRH for appropriate procedure. I agreed with CA not seeing an applicable procedure.CA transferred aircraft back to Fo to be PF again. CA did a review of overhead panel Inertial Reference System (IRS) 1 was on ATT not NAV. We agreed that was issue switched to NAV. Lost everything only had attitude and altitude; magnetic compass. CA advise ATC; dispatch and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control asked to verify circuit breakers. No reference in QRH to restore the NAV.  At that point requested priority handling and diverted to ZZZ1. CA took control again PF; I resumed PM duties. Landing in ZZZ1 without incident.Cause: Factors we identified; inadvertent switch position. Not trapping the error with before start checklist. Not recognizing missing information on Flight Mode Annunciator; lack of FD at TOGA. Without guidance we should have left the switch in the ATT position with good data on FO side.

column121: Near runway incident involving Aircraft X and a GA aircraft upon exiting runway. Aircraft X was exiting XXR onto the high speed taxiway 1 upon landing; and was advised to contact ground upon exiting. Nearing the hold short line; captain noticed first a GA aircraft taxing southwest on 2 and created a conflict with Aircraft X exiting the runway.
