Had Aircraft X been exiting onto the high speed at a higher energy state it would have likely been an incident.Cause: Probable cause related to ATC not notifying landing aircraft of potential conflicting traffic while exiting runway.High workload involved while exiting runway.Similar color of GA aircraft to taxiway made it challenging to spot.Suggestions: Suggest communication between tower and ground controllers of potential conflicting aircraft while aircraft are taxiing for departure and exiting runways; especially high speed exits.Suggest exiting runway as slowly as possible; even a high speed since the lower energy state of the exiting aircraft aided in the mitigation of the threat.
column123: Landing on runway XXR at ZZZ we were slowing and directed to exit on 1 and contact ground.  As I turned the aircraft onto taxiway 1. I saw a general aviation aircraft C-310R light twin right in my path of exit traveling west on taxiway 2.  I needed to aggressively brake the aircraft; bringing the aircraft to a complete stop to avoid a potential collision with the other aircraft.  Ground control did not appear to have noticed the potential conflict and issued us normal taxi instructions to follow the other aircraft.   We taxied to the gate without further incident.  As the passengers were exiting the aircraft several made mention of the other aircraft; noted my aggressive braking and thanked me for my quick action in avoiding a potential collision.Cause: ATC did not notify crew of opposing traffic taxing across our intended travel path.   High workload time right after landing where frequency switching would be happening; determining the taxi ways and directions to turn; not expecting another aircraft to be put in opposition to your ATC cleared travel path.Suggestions: ATC should warn exiting aircraft of a taxiing aircraft is going to be going through their intersection as the are maneuvering to exit runway.

column121: Crew briefing with Captain prior to boarding included expected turbulence 27-30 min after takeoff. However; FAs were good to get up at the audible signal. At the audible signal; 10;000 feet; there were some light bumps as we were still climbing; so we sat briefly for a few more minutes before prepping for service.Once we felt it safe to get up; we settled into normal service routine. Person A; my FWD galley; began to set up the galley while I worked on creating an order sheet for first class.While I was creating the order sheet; Person A and I both noticed an alarm sound that was continuously going off. At first we thought it was a pax (Passenger) phone alarm and I stuck my head out in the aisle to pinpoint the sound. That was when I realized the sound was coming from the flight deck. I listened in with my ear to the door; as this was an abnormal alarm sound that was constantly blaring. As I was listening; a few moments later; I heard what sounded like a release of oxygen followed by a loud air sound. Person A and I both looked to each other and confirmed we both heard the same thing. I could not hear the pilots--there was no sign nor indication of them moving or talking in the flight deck. I immediately called them. After a few minutes of no answer I called them again. While waiting on the phone for their contact; I noticed the plane descending back down. After several minutes of no contact with the pilots (5 minutes or more); no sounds or indications of them being conscious; paired with a continuous blaring alarm and air sounds coming from the cockpit; and the plane still descending… I began to be suspicious they could be unconscious and/or incapacitated whether it was due to a decompression or some other abnormality. At that point; my main priority was to make contact with the pilots. I kept calling; with no answer. Pressed for time; and aware of the incident surrounding the demise of another air carrier; I determined the best course of action was to use the emergency entrance system to enter the flight deck and wake them up/respond to any medical attention they may need in case of unconsciousness/incapacitation. I proceeded by calling the back galley; asking my senior co-worker; to come to the front immediately for assistance. When she came up I set up the cart barrier for normal flight deck entry/exit procedures. With the three of us now in the galley to assist in the emergency; I called the flight deck again. There was still no answer and all I could hear was a loud air noise in the background. This is when I proceeded to knock and attempt to enter the flight deck via emergency entrance system and the assistance of my coworkers.However; after thinking we knew how to enter the flight deck via emergency entrance system; the door would not open. I was a bit panicked by this because I couldn't understand what we were doing wrong. I banged on the door in hopes that; even if I couldn't enter the flight deck to check on them; maybe I could be loud enough to wake them up. However; I still could not hear anything on the other side--there was still no indication of them being conscious. At that point there was nothing more we could do other than me continuing to call and stay on the phone in hopes of making positive contact with the pilots. Eventually; after 15 minutes or so (from what I can recall) since the initial alarm and air sounds; we finally received contact from the pilots. All that was said was something like; 'hey sorry we've been busy up here; but we are ok. Just standby for more info and we will call back.' With positive contact from the pilots in the flight deck; I was so relieved and instructed my crew to put everything away and take their jumpseats while we stood by for an update.While waiting for the update; the cabin temperature dropped--we were very cold and our ears began to pop/hurt. I confirmed with my crew they were experiencing the same cold temperatures and ear popping. The next form of contact/update we received from the pilots was via PA. They notified the entire cabin that they had requested priority handling and we would be diverting to ZZZ. They confirmed we would be conducting an emergency landing and would have emergency equipment/authorities meeting us on the ground.Followed by the cabin PA; I received a call to the front from the pilots. Captain began by informing us that they had donned their oxygen masks and confirmed there was a depressurization. The captain asked me if our oxygen masks had deployed; I informed him they had not. Since they had advised ATC and we would be conducting an emergency landing; I proceeded with standard brief Information and procedures.After providing me with brief Information; the captain's tone seemed to be unalarmed and when I inquired about preparing the cabin; he said to prepare the cabin like normal. I inquired again; if he meant like a normal final/standard landing; and he confirmed yes. After receiving the update/information regarding our emergency landing and diversion to ZZZ; I proceeded by preparing the cabin like normal and did not perform emergency demonstrations. As I walked through the cabin for compliance; I made sure to talk to my exit rows and confirm they were aware of us landing and to be alert for further instructions. I also asked them to review their safety card again prior to landing. Despite cabin announcements; pax seemed to be unaware of the emergency landing and/or were incredibly calm by our updates. Our landing was incredibly smooth and did not cause alarm. Once we were on the ground; we could see emergency crews outside of the plane with sirens and lights. When we got to the gate and the seatbelt sign went off; I called the flight deck to confirm we were clear to disarm all doors (I had not received any instructions since being on the ground about what to expect). The pilot responded with 'we are at the gate aren't we?' I took his comment as a sign that it was clear for us to proceed with standard procedures and made the announcement instructing FAs to disarm doors for arrival and standby for all-call. We disarmed all of our doors; cross-checked; and all-called before the gate agent knocked like usual.Once the door was opened; all pax remained seated based on our instructions and supervisors boarded. With the help of staff; pax were instructed to deplane while I conducted a briefing with supervisor and her colleagues.There was no further conversation conducted between myself; my crew and the pilots beyond them apologizing for the lack of communication. I am still unaware of the circumstances surrounding the depressurization and what occurred in the flight deck.

column121: At about XA:0XX local time on Day 0 my son and I taxi to runway XX at ZZZ for a sight seeing flight. I heard a Sportsman in the pattern (multiple take offs and landings). I performed my run up at the ILS hold short line on taxi way 1/2. I thought I heard the sportsman call turning crosswind for XX and taxied to the runway. Before crossing the Movement/non-movement line for runway XX; I turned the plane toward the approach end to look for traffic. No traffic was seen and made the call I was departing runway XX. A second later I heard the sportsman say he was side stepping and asked if the Cessna departing would delay the take off for spacing. I pulled the throttle back to idle and confirmed I was delaying my take off roll. The Sportsman said he was just behind us about 200' above. I then saw him above and to the left as he performed his go around. I then commenced my take off and departed the area to the North. The problem: I did not see landing traffic and took runway XX for departure with landing traffic on final.Causes: 1. When I made my turn towards the approach end of runway XX; the sun was setting and right in line with any landing traffic; which probably obstructed my view of the landing traffic. 2. Perhaps the landing traffic calling crosswind when on base - which in my mind put him at the other end of the runway?3. I did not hear the call of the landing traffic of turning final. I may have missed it while explaining to my son what would happen on takeoff. Prevention:1. When checking for traffic before taking a runway and the sun is right in line with the approach end; wait a few more seconds while looking for traffic. 2.Verify/double check where known traffic is before taking the runway. Even a crosswind could be shorter than expected.3. When with passengers; have a sterile cockpit during pre-takeoff checklists.

column121: Enroute to ZZZ1; requested cruise climb from F340 to F360 per flight plan. At approximately F352 the number 2 engine EGT surged into caution range. Checklists were accomplished (autothrottle was disengaged and thrust lever retarded until back within normal EGT range). Red line was not exceeded. QRC and QRH were accomplished. Continued climb and leveled off at F360 and autothrottles were re-engaged. EGT was in normal range but was 100c greater than number 1 engine EGT. Radio was contacted and phone patch requested to dispatch and Maintenance Control. As we discussed options; number 2 engine EGT climbed up to 115c greater than number 1 engine. Due to warmer trending EGT; captain and I decided to request priority handling and divert to ZZZ. Preparations were made for an overweight landing (approximately 10;000 lbs over Maximum Landing Weight.) Emergency vehicles were asked to standby. Descent; approach and landing were normal and uneventful. Taxied to the gate under own power.
column123: While climbing to FL360 noticed Engine #2 surge into the caution range without any other abnormal indications.  Disconnected the autothrottles and reduced the thrust on the #2 Engine to get it out of the caution range. Accomplished the Checklists/QRH items.  Aircraft stable with the Number #2 engine running 100C degrees hotter than the left engine.  Consulted with maintenance and dispatch on the situation with the high EGT.  Maintenance was recommending on continuing to destination which was more than 2 hours away.  We agreed initially although after the phone patch was complete myself and the First Office continued to evaluate our situation and were formulating options as ZZZ1 was at least 2 hours away.  Shortly thereafter the EGT was increasing to 115 degrees C hotter in the wrong direction without any surging or vibrations or other abnormal anomalies.  At that point we made the decision to divert. Did not see any reason to continue away from close by airports or continue into high terrain and possibly have to shutdown #2 Engine.  Priority handling was requested and dispatch informed and a diversion to ZZZ the closest and smartest decision.  Decision to land overweight was executed as the status of the #2 engine was in question. Landing accomplished uneventful and aircraft taxied to the gate under its own power.

column121: The flight began with a normal and smooth pushback; taxi and take off. As we were climbing through 18;000 feet; Relief Pilot left for his rest break and as he closed the door behind him FO noticed a significant long spark on R2 window. At the time I was checking in with ZZZ [ARTCC] on a newly assigned frequency. FO brought into my attention about the spark on R2 and as we started to ascertain if that could have been St. Elmo's fire; EICAS suddenly displayed 'Window Heat (R)' message. I advised the FO to continue flying and I would do the Window Heat non-normal checklist procedure. The checklist directed us to check the window in question if it had any visible arcing or cracking. Since it was night time and the cockpit was too pitch dark; I advised the FO turn on the flash light and see if there was any damage to the window. On doing so we both discovered large arcing on left bottom side of the window. Checklist dictated to land at a nearest suitable airport if such damage was visible. I immediately decided to call Relief Pilot back and as he was stepping back into the flight deck he observed a large crack had also developed on right bottom side of the window. We decided to request priority handling and land back ASAP. Roles were delegated as per the SOP; FO was asked to continue flying while I and Relief Pilot completed the necessary checklists including diversion guidelines; obtaining weather and performances data. I advised the ATC of our intention; spoke to dispatch and Maintenance Control. We decided to return to ZZZ1 and ATC offered us Rw XXL for landing considering it was longer than XXR and we were going to make an overweight landing. I asked the purser to pull up his briefing card and briefed him accordingly. Made an announcement over the PA and apprised passengers of the safety concern and that we were returning to ZZZ1. Told them upon reaching the gate customer service would be there to arrange for their alternate travel. Also gave heads up to them they would be noticing emergency vehicles on the ground and they didn't need to worry about it as their presence was totally going to be out of abundance of caution. Due to heavy weight; high VREF approach and potential liability issues I decided to land the plane. An uneventful landing was conducted at the end. Briefed local maintenance and Chief Pilot thereafter.
column123: All was normal through takeoff. Upon climbing through FL180 the Relief Pilot was in the process of leaving the flight deck to go on break and I noticed a line of small electrical sparks coming from the lower left portion of the R2 window. Initially I thought it might be St Elmos fire but I could see it had left a crack where it was sparking. I brought the sparking up with the captain after he checked in with ZZZ [ARTCC]. About one minute after seeing the sparks; EICAS displayed 'R window Heat' message. I was PF so I continued flying while the captain worked the checklist. column121: After landing we taxied to our parking spot. We were pushed back into the spot and completed the secure checklist without further incident. column121: During a night visual approach to runway XXR in ZZZ with the first officer flying while I monitored; we received a low altitude alert from ATC and elected to abandon the approach and try again. We were initially expecting runway XXR; but when the ATIS was advertising that runway XYL was in use; we changed the approach in the FMS and briefed for runway XYL. Upon contacting approach control; the controller advised that the winds were from the south and gave us the option of XZ or XXR. We chose XXR; due to the runway being longer; and a runway assessment indicated we had adequate runway to land with a slight tailwind. As we descended to 2000 feet for the approach; we picked up the runway visually and were cleared for a visual approach. The final approach fix altitude was 1600 feet; and the first officer selected 1600 as the next altitude while arming the ILS XXR approach. However; when the autopilot captured the ILS signal; it turned away from the runway and paralleled the course instead. It was then that I realized that the ILS signal must have still been set to runway XYL. The ILS frequency for both XXR and XYL were the same; and I had not seen the IDENT displayed on the Primary Flight Display (PFD). The other issue was that the PAPI for that runway was out of service; so it was difficult to determine our glide path. The first officer disconnected the autopilot and tried to return the aircraft to the centerline while I disengaged the flight directors. While I was trying to find an RNAV approach to quickly load into the FMS; ATC alerted us to our low altitude; and I saw we were at 1000 feet and still outside the final approach fix. We attempted to regain altitude to salvage the approach; but ATC offered to vector us back for another approach; and we agreed. At this point; we had already been configuring for landing; and we had the gear down and the flaps were at config 3. As we continued to climb; we were slow to reconfigure; and the aircraft was still at approach speed (160-170 knots) when I instructed the first officer to select TOGA; and we were finally able to climb to 2000 feet and reconfigure the aircraft. On the next approach; I noted the correct IDENT on the PDF for runway XXR; and we were able to successfully land. In hindsight; I should have known something was wrong with the ILS signal when I did not see the IDENT displayed. I also should have been monitoring the approach better and corrected the altitude deviation sooner; or at least commanded a full go-around once ATC alerted us.Cause: It has been many years since I've seen a situation where the ILS frequency is the same for both runways. I did not consider that multiple runways changes might cause the wrong runway to be selected by ATC; and I should have confirmed the correct IDENT before allowing the FO to arm the approach.

column121: Our aircraft was parked at the FBO in TEB.  It had been towed into place and backed into a spot alongside other aircraft with our tail facing a hangar.  Aircraft Y; was parked slightly behind us and to our right.  We had a clear path in front of us to taxi out; and we discussed the nose of Aircraft Y being a little close but that we would keep an eye on the distance and taxi slow in case we needed a wing walker.With pax (Passengers) onboard; we cleared the area and started engines; ran the after start checklist; and got our taxi clearance.  Before we started moving; the captain announced 'Clear Left;' and when I looked to clear the right side; I was alarmed to see that Aircraft Y; parked with it's left wing behind our right wing; had begun to taxi forward.  I immediately notified my captain and threw up my arms to the window in an X signal to the other crew as it didn't look like they would clear.  My captain did the same.  The other crew appeared to see us motioning and stopped briefly; but then started moving again and subsequently struck our wing.  To our surprise they continued taxing out toward the runway and we called them on ground to inform them that they had hit us.  They said they didn't realize they had hit us; and we asked if they saw us motioning them to stop.  They said that they saw us motioning but their marshaler signaled them to go.  They aborted their taxi and returned to the ramp.We shut down our aircraft and tended to our passengers.  No one was injured.Suggestions: Suggest that the FBO use wider spacing with no overlap when positioning aircraft.  It is already a tight ramp with a high incidence of collisions.  Crew of Aircraft Y should use wing walkers when necessary and confirm wingtip clearance before moving.  It seems they were in a hurry; and I believe a slower pace could have helped them avoid this as well.
column123: Arriving at FBO X; we were tugged and placed in front of Aircraft Y. Loaded pax (Passengers); briefed and started engines. We gathered our taxi clearance; upon checking left and right; copilot brought Aircraft Y to my attention. From the cockpit it did appear fairly close and at an odd angle; nose pointing slightly towards us; more so than it did on my walk around; where I felt we should clear easily since they were parked behind us. We were discussing how to taxi; either immediately tillering to the left and slowly advancing or calling for extra wing walkers. During this brief discussion; Aircraft Y started moving and attempted to swing hard to their right to try and squeeze out from behind us. Copilot and I were shocked watching them attempt this though recovered and both threw our arms up in an X; universal sign to stop. The crew did stop momentarily; though continued to taxi while we continued to hold our arms in an X in an attempt to stop them. As their wing slid underneath ours; it lifted our wing slightly and dropped it back down as their wing slid clear. The owners saw the event unfold and were as shocked as we were; Person A (one of our passengers) called out the tail number to me as he had a clear view. I hailed Aircraft Y over ground frequency and told them not to take off; that they just struck our wing. They acted surprised. I asked them if they saw my partner and I yelling stop and folding our arms in an X; they replied that they did see us but that the marshaler waved them on so they continued. I believe I responded with 'ok' at that point; I was pretty stunned. I cut the engines; and went back to check on the owners and ensure them a recovery would be in the mix soon. Afterwards; met with authorities; gave a succinct written statement; a verbal statement to the police and met with the FAA shortly. After coordinating with the Chief Pilot and maintenance; applied the AOG and buttoned the jet down.Suggestions: One thing that struck out was the police telling us this happens far too often at TEB. I was unaware of that; at FBO Y south ground ops does a far better job of parking aircraft. FBO X should utilize more marshalers and should use wider spacing when parking aircraft. I can't speak for the crew of Aircraft Y but I would hope they are receiving additional training on spatial awareness and aeronautical decision making; this incident could have been avoided if they slowed their pace.

He found the speed and verbalized it. At that moment; we received a caution obstacle alert. I scanned the Primary Flight Display (PFD); and we were at 1080 MSL crossing ZZZZZ2. The crossing restriction was 1500. At the same time; tower called with a 'Low altitude alert; please check altimeter 29.76'. I responded '29.76; Aircraft X'. The captain disconnected the autopilot and initiated a climb. As soon as I finished responding to tower; I stated that we should be at 1500 ft. After climbing and reestablishing a stable approach; we continued the approach to landing uneventfully.
column123: As pilot flying we were landing GPS XX in ZZZ. When clear for the approach; I armed NAV and set Decision Descent Altitude (DDA) and started down to intercept the snow flake. Once I intercepted the snowflake I shallowed my descent and followed the snowflake and glide path down. We fully configured and completed the before landing checklist. One that was done I glanced outside and we looked low. At this point we were around ZZZZZ on the approach. I looked down and saw we were on the glide path. I decided to pull off the autopilot and level and further analyze what happened and get back on the visual glide path as I already had the runway in sight and was in VMC. As I pulled off the autopilot I ran the altitude we were at vs required altitude for the next fix and we were below it. As this happened all at once we for a too low Enhanced Ground Proximity Warning System (EGPWS) alert and ATC alerted of a low altitude alert and said check altitude. I also noticed the snowflake shot up and showed the glide path was above us and showed us low. I correct and flew the rest of the approach visually and off the PAPIs. column121: I was flying Aircraft X on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to IWS. My initial clearance was radar vectors/as filed (which was direct from ZZZ to IWS); and shortly after takeoff was cleared direct to West Houston Airport and climbed to my filed altitude of 9000 ft.; which was above the clouds. The ceilings were around 4000 - 5000 ft. for the entire flight; although the visibility was somewhat poor at IWS but still above 3 miles according to the unofficial AWOS that the airport has. The direct route from ZZZ to IWS puts traffic almost directly above 89TA. I used to tow and occasionally fly gliders; so I was familiar with their operations and local frequencies. On this particular day; IAH was landing east and therefore traffic had to be lower than the jets on the east finals. I was given a descent to lower altitudes and I had been hand flying these descents; but my ATP rated passenger (although not familiar with the Century 4 autopilot) stated the autopilot could do the descents. For some reason it kept keeping us around a 300 - 400 fpm descent rate. After struggling with the autopilot for the descents; ATC advised for us to pick up the rate of descent. We then tried to get the autopilot to expedite the descent; at which time I decided to hand fly the descent as I had almost every time flying this plane in the past. As we started coming down; ATC advised multiple targets (possibly gliders) in the area. I then switched to the local Soaring frequency; 123.3; on the secondary radio and made traffic reports for us. At around 4500 ft.; we went VMC through the clouds and immediately in front of us was a glider without ADS-B/transponder as it would normally show up on the display. I took evasive action by leveling off with a turn to the east; knowing that it was likely there were more gliders just below the clouds (likely the legal 500 ft. below; but still in the 3500 - 4000 ft. range). ATC then started getting on us about how we needed to descend. I told them I was leveling off due to glider traffic; and they started giving us vectors to the east and north to take us away from IAH finals while pushing us to descend. It was difficult to comply with the clearances while also trying to maintain visual contact with the gliders. Eventually we descended away from the glider field then landed safely at IWS.I believe the issue is that the glider field is right in the way of descending IFR traffic to IWS and SGR. I looked at procedures in the Houston area and the only arrival available to IWS/SGR is the SNDAY1 arrival that keeps traffic 15 NM west of the 89TA Soaring operation. Flying IFR traffic between 2000 - 4000 ft. within a 3 NM radius of 89TA is not safe due to the gliders being towed anywhere up to 4000 ft. in that area. I would therefore highly recommend not flying IFR traffic over the top of 89TA with altitudes below 5000 ft. on Saturdays and Sundays during daylight hours. I am filing this report for the information of ATC and also in the event that I did not comply with a clearance in the interest of flight safety.

Above 80 kts and approaching 100kts the airspeed indicators matched within 2 kts.   I elected to continue weather was CAVU and the airspeeds were within reasonable match to continue a normal takeoff.  We had no ICASS messages during takeoff roll.In cruise the Capt and  FO airspeeds stayed within 2-5 kts indicated.   In the descent airspeed indicators also stayed within 2kts   Approach and landing were normal.  During deceleration on landing again below 100kts the airspeed indicators began to separate between the Capt and FO up to 20 Kt difference as we slowed to turn off the runway.  The captains airspeed was again the lower airspeed indicator. Aircraft was written up in ZZZ1 after block in stating the discrepancy in speeds reference above.In ZZZ with the initial write up of HEAT P/S CAPT.   We observed the maintenance crew unbolting; cutting the seal and attempting to remove the Captains Pitot Static Tube.  Is it normal procedure to Defer the CAPT pitot under MEL 30-XX-X-X by just reattaching  the failed Pitot Tube and no further testing or action required?
column123: We pushed back and started normally. After engines were started; checklists complete; and aircraft began to move;  we received a EICAS message HEAT P/S CAPT .  Did the non normal; then called Dispatch and Maintenance Control; the conversation resulted in a Back to Base.Once in the blocks; maintenance ran tests and determined it was the Captains pitot static probe had failed.  They began to work on the airplane and said it would take anywhere from 1.5 to 5 hours.  We returned to the ready room to wait for word from Maintenance.   After an hour; they called and said they were going to defer the item. The deferral was under 30-XX-X-X; in addition to 35-XX-X-X-X.We blocked out again; this time the captain briefed we would watch closely for any anomalies.  On takeoff roll thrust was set. The Relief Pilot mentioned that the captains airspeed was not responding to the movement. As I looked over the captains airspeed jumped up to about 40 kts. At 80 kts the Captains airspeed was trailing the FO and Stby by about 20 knots. The captain said lets see what it looks like at 100 kts. I agreed .  At 100 kts the airspeed on Captain side was within 2-3 kts of FO and STBY.  The Captain elected to continue.In climb and cruise the Captains airspeed was within 1-2 kts.On arrival into ZZZ1 the speed was within 2 kts until touchdown.  After touchdown the airspeed on CAPT side began to deviate as much as 20 kts until we turned off the runway.  The captain decided to write up the deviant airspeed indicator.Unfortunately we could only put pieces together once airborne. Looking back; we all recalled that the Left Pitot tube was being unsealed and removed as we were leaving to go to the break room.  Somewhere in a that hour they decided to just defer the Aircraft. It is my belief that had they not touched the airplane; and just deferred it; that the airspeed would have been fine.

We agreed to that plan but once we had pushed back from the gate the smell was still present so we returned to the gate. After taxing out the FO and I both had a strange sensation of a metallic taste which later the #1 FA also commented she had. Upon return to the gate the #1 FA also said she felt slightly nauseous. I called the emergency line first who then directed me to call a medical advisory service. The medical advisory service asked about my symptoms during the event and that of the crew members which I explained in detail. Then the medical advisory service asked if any of us were still experiencing symptoms which none of us were. Then the medical advisory service said that in their professional opinion since no one was still having symptoms they would like to medically clear us to fly and continue on the sequence. I explained that we would still be seeking medical care. It took about 20 min with each crew member answering questions before they directed us to go to the Hospital. I was removed from the rest of the sequence and deadheaded home although my schedule does not reflect that at all. It simply shows me ending in ZZZ with no way home. I was told by my chief pilot that it was as if I were removed due to a family emergency. I explained that my schedule was altered due to a company failure to maintain its aircraft; not because I called in sick or with a family emergency. However; due to the lack of contractual language I learned I will not be getting paid for the extra day of the trip. Not only did I lose pay but my schedule for the purpose of FAR 117 work and rest schedules is completely inaccurate.Cause: Oil was found in APU inlet after the fact. This is a known problem with airbus and the mechanic should have recognized it and backed me up in writing it up. Instead he dissuaded me from writing it up and instead convinced me it had nothing to do with fumes coming from the aircraft. In the future I will immediately deboard if I smell anything even slightly abnormal.

Take-off procedures were normal; i.e.; brakes held until released and engines' indications in the green. Take off roll was normal with full RPM's; manifold pressures; and fuel flows. I extended my upwind flight along the runway center to 500' AGL; then entered a turn crosswind. That is a point at which I normally start another check of the engine instruments; starting with the EGT on the far right of the panel and working left across the RPM; throttle; and mixture in the middle of the panel; then to the lower left for the triple gauges and oil pressures; oil temperatures; and cylinder head temperatures; briefly before a normal RPM reduction to 2500 RPM at traffic pattern altitude or about 1000' AGL. That check showed the left engine EGT spiking to maximum temperature. I called ZZZ Tower for a return to the runway stating I had an instrument problem. The crosswind turn required additional right rudder to correct a slight roll; which keyed me to check the other indications for the left engine. They showed low RPM; low MP (Manifold Pressure); and zero fuel flow. I then automatically pushed all engine controls forward; which they mostly were anyway at that stage of flight. Because of the aircraft's known single-engine climb capability at ZZZ's elevation; I was able to obtain 800' AGL to 1000' AGL on downwind. After executing the emergency checklist; I adjusted the downwind-to base and base-to-dual turns to accommodate the critical engine out; extended the landing gear and flaps and landed on Runway XX; rolling out to Taxiway 1 and eventually taxiing to Taxiway 2 to exit the runway. The aircraft is undamaged and no one sustained an injury. Another aircraft on Taxiway 2 reversed and exited the taxiway as ZZZ personnel and the fire truck arrived. After shutting down both engines and securing the aircraft; I was handed paperwork by the ZZZ airport personnel; which I filled out. The maintenance shop was notified and came out to tow the aircraft back to the shop. Post event; the maintenance shop found a loose connection on a left engine fuel system hose which may have admitted air enough to disrupt normal mixture control. Further; after the event and after additional runups; the left engine boost pump was found to exhibit low pressure and is being replaced. Currently the aircraft is still in the shop awaiting the new left engine boost pump. An additional flight test upon return to service is anticipated. On the human performance considerations; a positive factor is my more than 1000 hours in this aircraft and regular participation in type; make and model specific re-currency training programs. These programs over the years made my responses to this event practically automatic.

column121: At approximately XA:00 in ZZZ. I was occupying the right seat of Aircraft X with my partner that day in the left seat. We have completed dual route verification and we doing our pre-departure briefing. We got up to the before start checklist. At that time ground control called us and told us one of our globals was returning to the ramp and they might need to switch airplanes with us. At that point we got out of the cockpit. The parking brake was inadvertently turned off during this process. Next we were standing in the back waiting for the company airplane to park. Then at or around this time Aircraft X started to roll forward down the sloped ramp. The airplane rolled approximately 30 to 50 feet where my partner reoccupied the left seat and applied the brakes. No damage to the aircraft or any other aircraft was done.Suggestions: This was classic case of task interruption. Our company has very specific procedures on the removal of chocks and the occupying of the pilot seats during the removal of chocks. Proper and immediate adherence to these procedures would've prevented this from happening. I would recommend in training we talk about the procedures we do every day and verify if we're actually doing procedures correctly. I would respectfully suggest covering procedures such as towing; jet blast on the ramp; chock removal; the discharging of coffee or ice and other liquids on the ramp. Also vehicle operations on the ramp around our airplanes; These but a few things that might be covered and reminded during training. I would further suggest some additional day to day operations that need covered include uncontrolled airport ops; standard instrument departures with an engine failure after the divergent point.I am not trying to shift blame from what was most probably my error. What I am suggesting is sometimes we need to reaffirm the day-to-day operation and make sure we're doing things correctly.

column121: Soon after takeoff from Rwy XX in ZZZ; the secondary eicas came on to show a partial compact engine indication.  Eng #1 oil quantity was down to 1.We were not surprised.  The previous crew had reported their engine oil quantity having dropped after heir takeoff from ZZZZ and maintenance in ZZZ had topped off the #1 oil by 11 QTS.The oil pressure was slowly decreasing; but without any eicas msgs I decided to continue climbing as much as we could because of the mountains ahead and below us.  We were very heavy; about 355 Tons.Some time later; the ENG 1 OIL PRESS advisory msg came on.  With oil P below the red line limit; the qrh directed us to shut the #1 engine down.  We continued to climb but only to 29;000 Ft to comply with the FMC engine out drift down guidance.15 or minutes later; I was in the process of telling the crew that I preferred not to return to ZZZ (RVRs reporting around 2000) and were about to call dispatch; when the HYD PRESS DEM 1 msg came on.  The hyd quantity was good; so I suspected a failed pump perhaps.Some time later and without an operating eng #1; the HYD PRESS SYS 1 msg came on.I was familiar with this qrh procedure; having done it at the training center a few times.   Gravity landing gear extension would be needed and the flaps would be on secondary mode.  My mind was then made up to continue to ZZZ1 where I was very familiar with the airport.  The weather forecasts I had obtained at the hotel before departure were good and were now checked again to be great.  No threat of nearby mountains like ZZZ and the winds would be almost lined up with the long ZZZ1 rwys.We sat-called dispatch/maintenance and after explaining our predicament; they were in agreement that continuing was the better option.  I was concerned that if ZZZ1 refused to handle our emergency arrival; we'd have to go to ZZZ2 or ZZZ3 (our planned alternate) but ZZZ1 fortunately agreed to handle us.  I insisted with the dispatcher that we'd need a tug to tow us off the rwy.It was at about this time that I took over PF duties from my FO.  I was going to let him fly and land the plane with an engine inop; but not with the #1 hyd system gone also.The former PF FO; now PM then did an amazing job of balancing fuel which became the real focus and hassle for the rest of the flight.We had advised ATC after shutting the engine down much earlier; but the ZZZ Center controller took it upon himself to give us priority handling.  I was glad he had done so; as I suspected that priority handling to still be better understood to everyone; as opposed to our declared advising".ZZZ1 had reserved their longest rwy; XXR for our arrival.  I managed to keep the plane on the rwy CL with the rudder and an occasional tap on the left or right brake as needed; but was happy at how steady the 747 remained without nose wheel steering.The good people of the ZZZ1 FD (Fire Department) had dispatched 4-5 trucks and did a visual inspection of our plane and #1 engine.  They reported seeing nothing unusual.The tug pre-arranged by the dispatcher and ground operations was waiting and promptly towed us to the ramp.After blocking in; the mechanics opened the nacelle on engine #1 and saw a lot of oil (or hydraulic fluid; they said they didn't' know which) pour onto the ground.I called ground operations the next day to ask if someone had determined by now why we had also lost hyd system 1 after losing the  #1 engine.  They said they really couldn't be sure.  They suspected either a failed demand pump or the entire accessory gear box having failed.  They were considering changing the entire engine.Cause: Not sure.  The engine had a massive leak of oil to the outside of the engine; not inside.  The previous crew experienced a loss of engine oil in ZZZZ; but never got an eicas msg; so didn't shut the engine down and continued all the way.I thought operations was closely monitoring the engines and trends remotely from their office.  Maybe everyone was off.Suggestions: I was concerned that in secondary mode the flaps would take longer to deploy than in the simulator.  I voiced my concern to my FOs and briefed that I would slow down early.  I really didn't want to go around because I had not allowed enough time for the gear and flaps.The qrh says to allow extra time for flap extension from 1 to 5 (4 minutes).  I slowed down and asked for flaps much too soon; before downwind.  I timed the flap extension with the stop watch.  It took only 3 minutes and 30 seconds.  The gear came down in alternate mode with all greens indicated in about a minute; or so.  If this ever happens to me again; I won't slow down and configure so early."

column121: Leaving 10k feet as we begin accelerating; we heard multiple loud bangs which felt to be under the right side of the cockpit. The captain was pilot flying; and he immediately turned off the auto pilot and auto throttle to begin leveling and slowing the airplane. We requested to level off at 12000ft and begin trouble shooting the issue. We had no indications on the EICAS; and the engines were within normal parameters.  We requested priority handling and informed that we would be returning to the field. The loud bangs continued ever few minutes in intervals of 2 or 3 bangs. We initially believed that it was a panel or door because it occurring during the acceleration period and seemed to occur when in turns. We decided to do a airport fly by to see if it could possibly be a gear door; but tower said they did not see anything. The flight attendant in the rear also stated that they felt the same sensation from the rear of the plane which led us to believe it had to be something different. We returned to the field with the bangs only occurring normally in turns. We landed below max landing weight and exited the runway. The fire trucks did not see anything of note; so we taxied back to the gate. We also received a remote Circuit Breaker trip; 'TAXI LT RH'. During the walk around everything seemed normal until 3 passengers seated behind the number 2 engine said they saw flames shooting out the rear of the engine every time the loud bangs occurred. This led us to believe that the number 2 engine was having intermittent compressor stalls that were not severe enough to show and create surges in thrust.

column121: We were flying the RNAV (GPS) Runway 29 approach into SBP this evening from KIKII; which requires a hold in lieu of procedure turn (HILPT). We were cleared for the approach prior to crossing CADAB. The approach had been armed; and we were on the vertical descent path when we crossed CADAB at approximately 6800 ft. MSL. It wasn't until just prior to CADAB that we noticed there is a published maximum holding altitude of 6000 ft. MSL. We expedited our descent to below 6000 ft. MSL and continued the approach as normal. What we did notice was that as soon as we crossed CADAB; the vertical deviation bar went from being on the path to being high. We were surprised that the aircraft didn't realize we needed to cross CADAB no higher than 6000 ft. MSL. Looking back at the constraints in the navigation database in the aircraft; all it shows is that we needed to cross CADAB at or above 5700 ft. MSL (no mention of the following maximum holding altitude). Nothing was mentioned to us by ATC; and the remainder of the approach was uneventful.

column121: During cruise; near Albuquerque; we began to lose GPS due to jamming in the area. Several other aircraft in the area were complaining of the same issue to ATC. The nav data page showed GPS 2 completely lost; and GPS 1 degraded to an AIDED" status and momentarily back to "NAV" status before completely being lost. With the autopilot engaged; the aircraft began a standard bank turn to the left; upon which I quickly selected "HDG" mode to regain the plotted ND (Navigation Display) course to our next fix within .2 NM laterally. After reporting the incident to ATC; we completed the approved QRH procedure for GPS Interference. After being unable to regain GPS accuracy; we deselected navaid function to continue to ZZZ. We were able to utilize IRS (Inertial Reference System)/DME/DME for the remainder of the flight; as our GPS remained jammed until landing. We also lost onboard WiFi connectivity after the jamming event. The FMS waypoint sequencing never was lost; and we landed without further incident in ZZZ. A logbook entry was made upon gate arrival in ZZZ.An unexpected jamming of our onboard GPS equipment. My sole recommendation is for a more appropriate method to conduct electromagnetic/gps testing which respects the integrity of onboard navigation equipment used by the flying public."

The target appeared to be a non-ICAO / dynamic / radar-track type target rather than a normal ADS-B target with a displayed N-number or aircraft type. I was unable to determine the aircraft registration or type from the cockpit display or public ADS-B replay.The alert occurred near my altitude and close enough to create concern for a possible near-midair collision or unsafe proximity. I do not know whether the other aircraft was civilian or military. Given the location near the Patuxent River operating area and the non-ICAO nature of the target; I am reporting this event for safety awareness and possible ATC/radar correlation.Contributing factors may have included lack of visible or identifiable ADS-B registration information for the target; possible radar/TIS-B rebroadcast traffic; and operation near an area with military and civilian traffic.I maintained aircraft control; continued to monitor the traffic display; and continued the flight. I am submitting this report to document the ADS-B traffic alert and possible near-midair event.

column121: I was flying patterns at ZZZ.  At approximately XA:30; I was on left downwind for RWY XX. There were several aircraft in the pattern.  I was unable to get the ATC recording but to my recollection I had been cleared to land.  ATC called me as traffic to a 172.ATC informed them they were gaining on me; 20kts faster and to widen their pattern. I was unable to see them at this point.  I do not recall if they acknowledged having me in sight.  LiveATC.com was incomplete and I have not heard any other recordings.  I confirmed later the 172 did veer slightly right.I was flying consistent patterns and having heard the instruction for them to widen; I proceeded normally to reduce power abeam the numbers; reduce speed; deploy 1st flaps; then began my base turn about 1nm to the west of the runway and about 1.5nm southwest of the intersection of XY/XX.As I rolled out of my turn on cross wind and looked left as my wing raised; I saw the 172 coming what appeared to be straight at me.  Simultaneously ATC directed them to 'Climb immediately!'  I received no instruction.  There was really no time for me to do anything but stay my course as they passed directly above me.  Close enough to make out the landing gear.I finished my stop and go and completed one more pattern to finish my flight. I do not recall any further radio communication about the near miss.Cause?  The 172 was flying faster than typical for a 172 and my PA-22 is slower to begin with.  Knowing they were gaining on me and inside I would have expected them to make a sharper turn to the right and slow down.  I suspect they did not have me in sight.ATC could have been less vague with them.  They also could have cancelled my landing clearance; extended my downwind; and let the 172 go first.  OR they could have had the 172 do a right 360.  But I do not know what traffic was behind them.For my part I might have had a closer look at ADSB; however at that critical phase I try to keep my eyes outside and not let the ipad interfere with my night vision.I also could have made a radio call to ask if the 172 was clear before I made my base turn.Things added up for potentially a very bad night for all.  I feel like we all got lucky.
